that if he had read over the Papers left, undoubtedly, in his Possession by his Predecessors, he would find what I stated to be strictly true; and that of course it could not be difficult to account for my Surprise, when, after being told that he and his Colleague were to take up the Negotiation precisely where they found it, it now became evident that it was to be flung back to the very Point from which we started, and flung back in a Way which seemed to threaten a Conclusion very different from that he foretold.

I shall not attempt to follow the French Minister through the very elaborate and certainly able, Speech lie made in Reply, with a View to convince me that the Enquiry into the Extent of my full Powers was the strongest Proof the Directory could furnish of their pacific Intention, and the shortest Road they could take to accomplish the desired End. It was in order to ive Activity to the Negotiation (" aftiver" was his Word) and to prevent its stagnating, that this Demand was made so specifically; and he intimated to me, that it was impossible for the Directory to proceed till a full and fa-tisfaftory Answer had been given to it. I interrupted him hereby saying, their Manner of acting appeared to me calculated to decide the Negotiation at once, not to give it Activity, since it must be known, I could not have Powers of the Description he alluded to; and even suppoling I had, the admitting it would be in Fast neither more or lefts than a complete Avowal of the

Principle itself, which once agreed on, nothing would be left to negotiate about. The other French Plenipotentiary interpofted here, by saying, that would not be the Cate; many Articles would still remain to be proposted, and many Points for important Distcufiion. I laid, every Word I heard seemed to present fresh Difficulties. Without replying to me, the first-mentioned Minister went on by endeavouring to prove, that the Avowal of having Powers to a certain Extent, did not imply the NeceL fity of exercising the m; that it was the Avowal alone for which they contended, in order to determine at once the Form the Negotiation was to take; that the Note, and the Time prescribed in it, were in conftequence of the most positive Orders from the Directory; and that if I drew from it a Conclusion different from the Assurances they had made me in the Name of the Directory,

I did not make the true Inference. I replied, that although the preftcribing the Day on which the Question was put to me as the Term within which I was to give my Answer to it, was both a very unuftual and abrupt Mode of proceeding, yet as a Day was much more than sufficient for the Purposte, I should forbear making any particular Remark on this Circumstance: That as to the Inference to be drawn from the positive Manner in which they appeared to maintain the Question put to me, I really could not make it different from that I had already expressed: That the reverting, after an Interval of Two Months, to a Question already anftwered, and which Question involved the Fate of the Negotiation, certainly could not be considered as wearing a very conciliatory Appearance: That in regard to my Answer, it could not be different from that 1 had given before: That my full Powers, which were in their Hands, were as extensive as any could be, and it did not depend on me to give them more or lefts Latitude; but that in Fast their Question went not to the Extent of my full Powers, but to require of me to declare the Nature of my Instructions; and on this Point they certainly would forgive me if I did not ftpeak out till such. Time as the Circumstances of the Negotiation called upon me to do it.

The French Minister strove to prove to me, what lie had before attempted, that the claiming a Right of Enquiry into the Nature of the discretionary Authority confided in a Minister, by no Means implied an Intention of requiring of him to act up to it to its utmost Limits. 1 obfterved, if no such Intention existed, why institute the Enquiry ? and if it did exist, why not lay so at once ? — He laid, what we now alk is little more than a Matter of Form; when you have given us your Answer, we shall follow it up by another Step, which we are ordered to take. I laid, my Answer wtis given Two Months ago; that, although I was ready to give it them again, and in Writing, as One to their Note, yet, as it could not be different, I did not fee why they should not proceed immediately to the other Step, by which I was told the Question was to be followed up. It would be premature, laid the French Minister; but in drawing up your Answer, do not forget the Force of the Arguments I have uled, or in your Report to your Court, the Assurances we have given of the earned: Wilh of the Directory to terminate the War.

I replied, that I still must maintain, that, from the Manner in which they thought proper to define full Powers, I could fee no Distinction between acknowledging the Power and admitting the Principle; and that the Question itself could not be put with any Other Ihtcntion — (Your Lordship will obilrve from the fubftequent Notes which passed between us, that I was perfectly grounded in this Assertion); — that in my . Reports, they might be fully allured I should aft up to that conciliatory Spirit, which, from the earliest Period of the Negotiation, had always decided my Conduct; and that, inauftpicious as Appearances were, I certainly would be careful not to make them look hostile. were most warm in their Protestations, that nothing could be lei's To; that the Idea of the Negotiation breaking off was as far from their Thoughts as from their Willies. At 6 P. M. the Note C was transmitted to me; to which at 8 P. M. I returned the Answer D, by Mr. Refs, whom I lent in order that he might bring me the Passports I asked for; but at a Quarter before io P.M. M. Derche, Secretary of the French Legation, delivered

to me the Paper marked E; and this Morning at 9 A. M. I replied by the Note F. which immediately produced that marked G.

The Notes sent me by the French Plenipotentiaries speak for themselves; and it is unnecessary to enter into any Reflections on them. I am willing to hope that the Anfivers I have made were such as became the Situation in which I (land, the Importance of the Cause intruded to me, and the steady but temperate Conduct which the Spirit of my Instructions injoin me to hold.

It was my Wish to give every Opening to the French Plenipotentiaries to recall the violent Step they had taken; and, if polhble, to convince them of its extreme Impropriety. And it was with this View, and with a most anxious Delire not to exclude all Hope of the Restoration of Peace, that I determined on luggefting the Idea of our Meeting once more before I left.

This Meeting took place Today at Noon: I opened it by observing. That the several Notes they had received from me since the preceding Evening had been too expressive of the Surprize I felt at the Measure the Directory had thought proper to adopt, to make it ne-celfaiy for me to enlarge upon it in this Conference; and indeed my foie Motive for suggesting that it might be for our mutual Satisfaction that it should be held, was, because this Measure appeared to me to be in such direct Contradiction to the very strong Assurances I had so constantly and repeatedly heard from them, and to the pacific Intentions with which they declared they were sent, that it was my earnest With (before I considered their Conduct as forcing me to a Step which muff so materially affect the Succcfs of the Negotiation), to be perfectly certain that I understood clearly and distinctly the precise Meaning of their official Notes. . On their admitting that nothing could be more reasonable than that I should, on so important a Point, require Explanation, or more satisfactory to them than to give it me (as far as lay in their Power), I proceeded by saying, that it appeared to me that I was called upon to produce immediately my full Powers, or rather my Instructions (for however different thcle were in themselves, in their Demand they seemed con-flantly blended), and that if either I refuted to consent to this, or if on contenting to it, it was found that I was not authorized to treat on the Principle they laid down, I was then in the Space of Twenty-four Hours

to leave Life, and return to my Court; and that I was required to obtain full Authority to admit this Piin ciple, if it was wished the Negotiation should proceed; This I said appeared to me to be the evident Sense of the Notes, and 1 begged to know whether I had mistaken it or not. One of the French Plenipotentiaries said,

" You have understood it exactly; I hope you equally " understand the Intention of the French Government,

" which is to accelerate Peace by removing every Obstacle which stands in its Way."

I replied, that having no Doubt left on my Mind as to their exact Meaning, and being quite sure notwithstanding the Observation they had made, " que j'avais fail! la veritable Intention de leur Note," it would, I feared, be a very unprofitable Employment of our Time to argue either on the Nature of the Principle they announced as a fine qua non, to even a preliminary Dif-cuffion, or on the extreme Difficulty of reconciling the peremptory Demand with which they opened their Million, to the pacific Professions that accompanied it; that if they were determined to persist in this Demand, it was much better to avoid all useless Altercation; and nothing in that same remained for me to do, but to ask for my Passports, and to signify to them my Intention of leaving France at an early Hour the next Morning. They said, they had their Hands tied by an Arrete of the Directory, and were bound to observe the Conduct they had followed by the most positive Orders and although we remained together some Time longer, not a Hint dropped from them expressive of a Willi that, instead of going myself for new Instructions, I should either write for them by a Messenger, or obtain them by fending to England Cne of the Gentlemen who are with me. I endeavoured' by every indirect Means to suggest to them the Necefiuy of adopting some such Modification, if they meant that their Withes for Peace, in the Expression of which they were this Morning more eager than eVer, should meet with the slightest Degree of Credit: I again brought to their Recollection that I was authorized to receive any Pro-polal, any Contre Projet they tendered to me, but that they must be aware that it was not possible for me to alter the Orders I had received, or to assume an Authority with which I was not inverted. I dwelt particularly and repeatedly on my being competent to take any Thing the y said for Reference; but this availed nothing, except drawing from One of them a Rernark, that the full Powers which authorized a Minister to hear Proposals, were widely different from those which would enable him to accede to them; and that it w'as such full Powers that the Directory required me to solicit.

An easy Answer presented itself to this Mode of Re?.-foning; but I saw no Advantage to be derived from prolonging a Conversation, which, after the positive Declaration they had made, could lead to nothing: I therefore ended the Conference by declaring my lte-solution to begin my Journey at a very early Hour ti e next Morning, and by saying, that immediately on my Arrival in England I would make an exact Report of every Thing that had parted since their Arrival.

I trust, my Lord, 1 shall not incur Censure for having declined to offer in distinct Terms to wait at Lijlt till I could know His Majesty's Pleasure on the peremptory Proposal made to me: But when I considered the Nature of the Proposal itself, the Avowal that this would not be the last, nor perhaps the most humiliating, Condition required of us, and the imperious Style with which I was enjoined to depart in Twenty-four Hours, it was utterly impossible for me to assume a Language or affect a Manner that could be interpreted into Solicitation or Entreaty: I felt myself called upon to treat the Whole of this extraordinary Proceeding with Calm-ness and Temper; and notwithstanding the deep and poignant Concern I mult feel at an Event which I fear will remove all Probability of an immediate Pacifica-

TRANSLATION of Note from the French Plenipotentiaries to Lord Malmesbury} dated Lisle, 29 Fruftidor, 5th Year.

The undersigned Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic, commissioned to treat of Peace with England, have the Honour to assure Lord Minister Plenipotentiary of His Majesty, that

the French Government wishes as sincerely, as strongly as ever, a Peace, desired by the Two Nations: But, unable to conclude any other Peace than such a one as is founded on the Laws and on the Treaties which bind the French Republic, persuaded that, to arrive at this End, it is necessary to explain itself with entire Frank-ness, and desirous of giving to the Negotiation the greatest Rapidity, the Executive Directory has expressly charged the Undersigned to demand of Lord bury, whether he has sufficient Powers for restoring, in the Treaty which may be concluded, to th Republic and to its Allies, all the Poflessions which, since the Beginning of the War, have passed into the Hands of the English.

The Undersigned are equally charged by the Executive Directory to demand from Lord Malmesbury an Answer in the Omrfe of the Day. They requeil him to accept the Assurances of their high Consideration.

(Signed)

Lijle, 29 Fru£lidor, 5th Year of the Republic.

Treilhard.

Bonnier.

By the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic, the Sec. Gen.

(B.)

TRANSLATION of a Note from Lord Malmesbury to the French Plenipotentiaries; dated Lijle, 16th September, 1797.

The undersigned Minister Plenipotentiary of His Britannick Majesty receives with great Satisfaction the Expression of the sincere Desire for Peace, which the Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic announced to him Yesterday in the Name of their Government. He has the Honour to assure them that the King his Master is animated with the same Desire, and has nothing more at Heart than to put an End to the Calamities of the War.

With regard to the Question which the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic addressed to Lord Malmesbury, concerning the Extent of his full

Powers, he considers himself as having already given the most unequivocal Answer upon this Subject, in the Two Notes which he delivered to their Predecessors on the 15th and 24th of July.

However, to avoid all Misunderstanding, he renews the Declaration, which he made Yesterday; that is to

say, that he neither can nor ought to treat upon any other Principle than that of Compensations; a Principle which has been formally recognized as the Basis of a Treaty equally just, honourable, and advantageous to the Two Powers.

Lord Malmesbury requests the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic to accept the Assurances of his high Consideration.

(Signed) Malmesbury.

Lijle, Saturday, 16th September,

1797, 10 A. M.

TRANSLATION of a Note from the French Plenipotentiaries to Lord Malmesbury; dated Lijle, 30 Frufti 5th Year.

The Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic, commissioned to treat of Peace with England, have the Honour to acknowledge the Receipt of the Answer of Lord Malmesbury to the Note which was presented to him in the Conference of Yesterday.

It appears from this Answer, and from the Two Notes of the 15th and 24th of , to which it refers, that Lord Malmesbury has not Powers for agreeing to the Restitution of all the Poflessions which His Britannick Majesty occupies, whether from the French Republic, or from its Allies.

In consequence, while they reiterate to Lord Malmesbury the most positive Assurances of the Sentiments of the French Government, the Undersigned apprize him of a Decree of the Executive Directory, which signifies that, in case Lord Malmesbury shall declare himself not to have the necessary Powers for agreeing to all the Restitutions which the Laws and the Treaties which bind the French Republic, make indispensable, he shall be to return, in Four-and-twenty Hours to his Court, to ask for sufficient Powers. Lord Malmesbury can fee in this Determination of the Executive Dire<flory nothing else than an Intention to hasten the Moment when the Negotiation may be followed up with the Certainty of a speedy Conclusion.

The Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic request Lord Malmesbury to accept the Assurances of their high Consideration.

(Signed) TTeilhard.

Bonnier.

Lijle, 30 FruRidor,

5th Year of the Republic.

{Sept, 16, 1797.)

By the Ministers Plenipotentiaries, the Sec. Gen. of the Legation,

Whatever Regret he may experience at seeing the Hope of a speedy Conciliation thus destroyed, he can return no other Answer to a Refusal so absolute to continue the Negotiation on Grounds which appeared to have been already agreed upon, than by demanding the necessary Passports for himself and his Suite, in order that they may set off within the Four-and-twenty Hours, and return immediately to England.

T R A N S L AT I O N of a Note from the French Plenipotentiaries to Lord bury; dated Lijleioth 6th

Year.

The Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic, charged to treat for Peace with England, have the Honour to inform Lord Malm that having sent a Copy of his last Note to their Government, the Executive Directory has directed them to declare in its Name, That it has never ceased to wish for Peace; That" it gave an unequivocal Proof of the Sentiment which animates it, when it ordered the Mfhifters Plenipotentiary of the Republic to require a categorical Explanation as to the Powers given by the English Government to its Minister Plenipotentiary; That this Demand had, and could have, no other Object but to bring the Negotiation to a speedy and successful Issue:

That the Order given to the Plenipotentiaries of the Republic to remain at Lijle after the Departure of Lord Malmesbury, is another Proof that the Directory had desired and foreseen his Return with Powers that should not be illusory, and the Limitation of which should no longer be a Pretext for delaying the Conclusion of Peace:

That such are {till the Hopes and Intentions of the Executive Directory, which enjoins the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the Republic not to quit Lijle till the continued Absence of the Negotiator shall no longer leave any Doubt of the Intention of His Britannick Majesty to break off all Negotiation: '

That consequently the 25th Vendemiaire (16th of October Old Style) is the Period fixed for the Recall of the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic, supposing that at that Time the Minister Plenipotentiary of His Britannick Majesty shall not have arrived at Lijle.

The Executive Directory will feel the greatest Regret that a Reconciliation, already twice attempted, should not be perfected; but its Confidence, and the Whole of Europe, will bear it Testimony, that it is the English Government alone that will have inflicted the Scourge of War upon the Two Nations.

The Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic entreat the Minister Plenipotentiary of His Britannick Majesty to accept the Assurances of their high Consideration.

(Signed) Fteilhard.

TRANSLATION of a Note from Lord Malmesbury to the French Plenipotentiaries; dated London,5th O 1797.

The Undersigned having laid before the King's Mi-niftry the Note of the Plenipotentiaries of the French Republic, is directed to observe to them,

That it is only in consequence of the formal and pofi-tive Injunction of the Directory that he quitted Lijle; That his Powers were neither illusory nor limited; And that nothing was omitted on his Part to accelerate the Negotiation, which has been only retarded by the Delays of the Directory, and which at this Moment is inly suspended by its Act.

Vol. 53 *

With regard to the Renewal of the Conferences, the Undersigned can only refer to his last Note, where he has explained with Frankness &nd Precision the only Means which remain for continuing the Negotiation; observing at the same Time that the King could no longer tfeat in an Enemyis Country, without being certain that the Customs established amongst all civilized Nations, with regard to Public Ministers, and especially to those charged to hQgotiate for the Re-establishment of Peace, would be respected for the future in the Person of His Plenipotentiary *

The Minister Plenipotentiary of His Britannick Majesty requests the Ministers Plenipotentiary of the French Republic to accept the Assurance of his high Consideration.

(Signed) Malmesbury.

Ordered, That the said Papers do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That the Thanks -of

this House be given to Admiral Lord Viscount Duncan, for his able and gallant Conduct in the brilliant and de -cifive Victory obtained over the Dutch Fleet on the nth Day of October, as well as for the Zeal, Courage, and Perseverance, which he has uniformly manifested during the arduous Period in which he has commanded His Majesty's Fleet in the North Sea.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That the Thanks of this House be given to Vice Admiral Sir Baronet, and to the several Captains and Officers in the Fleet under the Command of Admiral Lord Viscount Duncan, who, by their Bravery and gallant Conduct, contributed to the glorious Success of that Day; and that Admiral Lord Viscount Duncan do signify the same to them.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente<, That this House doth highly approve of, and acknowledge, the Services of the Seamen and Marines on board the Ships under the Command of Admiral Lord Viscount Duncan, in the late glorious Victory over the Dutch Fleet; and that the Officers commanding the several Ships do signify the same to their respective Crews, and do thank them for their gallant Behaviour.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do signify the said Refo lutions to Admiral Lord Viscount Duncan.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly desiring that His Majesty will be pleased to give Directions, that a Monument be erected, in the Cathedral Church of Saint Paul's, London, to the Memory of Captain Richard Rundle Burges, of His Majesty's Ship Ardent, who fell gloriously in the Naval Engagement of the nth of October, when a decisive Victory was obtained by Ad miral Lord Viscount Duncan over the 'Dutch Fleet; and to allure His Majesty, that this House will make good the Expence attending the fame.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council,

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

London, 5th Nov. 1797.

Sir,

lam honoured with your Letter of the 3d Instant, conveying to me the Resolutions by which the House of Commons, on that Day, manifested its unanimous Sense of the Services which myself, Sir Richard Onslow, and the several Captains, Officers, and Men, under my Command, rendered their Country on the 1 ith of OElo-ber last, which I shall not fail to communicate to them; and if, in fulfilling the Duties of my Station, I have been fortunate in rendering Service to my Country, I am raoft truly gratified, and feel the highest Satisfaction, not only in the Sense the House of Commons is pleased to entertain of my Conduct, but in the very flattering Manner in which you have done me the Favour to communicate the fame.

I have the Honour to be.

With the most perfect Respect and Esteem, Sir,

Your most obedient and

faithful humble Servant,

Duncan.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty upon Saturday last, with thefir Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My warmest Thanks for this loyal and dutiful Address, and for the Expressions of your affectionate Attachment to My Person and Government. The Assurances of your firm Determination to refill, to the utmost, the unwarrantable Pretensions and inordinate Ambition of the Enemy, afford Me the highest Satisfaction at this important Conjuncture: They juf-tify the Reliance which I have uniformly placed on the Vigour and Wisdom of your Councils, and leave Me no Room to doubt that the Strength and Resources of these Kingdoms will be effectually employed in supporting Our dearest Interests, maintaining Our happy Constitution, and vindicating the Honour and Independence of the Country.

A Petition of Peter Patten, of Sank, in the County Pala-tineof Lancaster, Esquire, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That the Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Newton, in the said County, came on on Friday the 13th Day of September last, and was continued until, and ended on, T.uefday the 19th Day of the same Month, at which Election the Petitioner and Thomas Langford Brooke, Esquire, were Candidates; and that, in taking the Poll at the said Election, several Persons were tern dered and admitted to give their Votes on Behalf of the said Thomas Langford Brooke who had no legal Claim or. Title to exercise such Right, and that several Persons, duly qualified to vote, who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, were rejected, and not allowed to vote; and that, after the Vacancy happened, and previous to,

and during the Time of the said Electiort, the said Thomas Langford Brooke, by himself, his Agents, Friends, and Managers, was guilty of many notorious and flagrant Acts of Bribery and Corruption, by giving divers large Sums of Money to several of the Electors of the said Borough, and by corruptly promising to the said Electors, or some of them, large Presents, Gifts, Advantages, and Rewards, in order to procure him, the said Thomas Lang ford Brooke, to lerve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said Thomas Langford Brooke, by himself. his Agents, Friends, and Managers, did, after the said Vacancy happened as aforesaid, and before and during the said Election, give, present, and allow, to divers Persons having Voice or Vote in the said Eieftion, Money, Meat, Drink, Entertainment, and Provision, and made Presents, Gifts, Rewards, and Entertainments, and made Promises, Agreements, Obligations, and Engagements, to give or allow Money, Meat, Drink, Provisions, Presents, Rewards, Advantages, and Entertainments, to and for several so having or claiming Right to vote in the said Election, and to and for the life, Advantage, Benefit, Profit, and Preferment, of such Persons so having or claiming Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure him, the said Thomas Langford Brooke, to be elected to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, and that, in consequence thereof, and of such llejedtion and Admission of Votes as hereinbefore Hated, a colourable Majority of Two Voices was obtained in Favour of the said Thomas Langford Brooke, who was thereupon returned as a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, so the great Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had an undoubted Majority of legal Votes at such Election, and was duly elected and ought to have been returned, and also to the great Prejudice of the legal Electors of the said Borough: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Name of the said Thomas Langford Brooke may be erased from the Return, and the Petitioner declared duly elected, or that they will grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday Fortnight, the 30th Day of this Irvstant November, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. tVilmot and Mr. Popham:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have Commanded us to acquaint this House, That His Majesty has appointed Three o'Clock Tomorrow, at His Palace of Saint , to be attended with the Address of both Houses of Parliament j and that the Lords intend to be there at that Time.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House being informed that Mr. , from the Exchequer, attended' at the Door; he was called

A Bill for continuing the Term; arid altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two several Acts, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, so far as the same relate to repairing the Road from Tadcaster. to Halton Dyal, in the West Riding of the County of York, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to Mr. Baldwin, Mr. Wilberforce, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Trustees for putting in Execution Two Acts of Parliament, the one, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act " for repairing and widening the Roads from the Town " of Manchester, by a Place called The White Smithy,

* in the Township of Crumpfall, to the Town of " dale, and from the said Place called The White Smithy,

* by a Place called BeJJ'es of the Barn, to the Town of " Bury, and from the said Place called of the

" Barn to Radcliffe Bridge, in the County Palatine of Lancafterand the other, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said former Act, and for empowering the Trustees under the same Act to repair a Lane called Sheepfoot Lane, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the said Acts, Turnpike Gates have been erected, and Tolls taken, according to the full Rates thereby authorized, the Produce whereof, together with a considerable Sum of Money borrowed, and remaining due upon the Credit of the said Tolls, has been applied to the Purposes of the said Acts, but the same have been found insufficient to complete and maintain the said Roads which are in a broken, miry, and ruinous Condition, and in many Places narrow and incommodious; and that the said Roads cannot be effectually amended, widened, improved, and kept in Repair, and the said Debt paid off, unless the Term of the said Acts be continued, and additional Toll Gates erected, and further Tolls granted; and that the Powers and Authorities requisite for the Improvement, Repair, and Maintenance of the said Roads, might be more conveniently executed if the said Acts were repealed, and the necessary Provisions for the same comprized in one Act; and also, if the said Roads were divided into Three separate Districts; and that it is expedient that the same Powers and Authorities should be declared to extend to the Road, through Part of the said Town of Bury, to the Dwelling House in the Occupation of the Head Master of the Free Grammar School there, Doubts having arisen whether that Part of the Road is included in the said former Acts: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Peele, Mr. Stanley, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Vol. 53,

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morn- Surfiy, defaring; resolve itself into a Committee of the whole rsd-House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Memorandum: '

By the Act passed in 1781, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company " of Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies, &c." The East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in proportion to the Number of Troops lent, or to be sent to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only , and as it will be necesiary to provide for the Subsistence of the Four Recruiting Troops, and Fifteen Recruiting Companies, remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting ac prefenc for this Purpose, the Sum of j£» 40,044. oj.-i d. which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the above Estimate.

King's An- ' Mr. Speaker reported, That both Houses attended d'-is ot both His Majesty, this Day, with their Address; to which ilouies. His Majesty was plealed to give this most Gracious

Answer:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Nothing could be more satisfactory to Me than this Unanimous Declaration of the Sentiments of My Two Houses of Parliament. They are such as the Conduct and declared Intention of the Enemy could not fail to produce. We are engaged in a Cause which is common to Us all, and contending for every Interest which a free and independent Nation can have to maintain. Undef thf Blessing of Providence, I look with Confidence to the Issue of this great Contest: But in every Event My Resolution is taken. It is such as I owe to God, to My Country, and to Myself; and it is confirmed by the Sentiments which you have this Day declared to Me. I will not be wanting to My People, but will stand, or fall, with them in the Defence of Our Religion, and in the Maintenance of the Independence, Laws, and Liberties of these Kingdoms.

Tower Ham- A Petition of the Commissioners of Sewers acting irts sewer Pe and fof the Limits of the Hamlets, exclusive

of St. Catharine's and Marshwas presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, from Time immemorial, there has been, ftiil is, and of Right ought to be, a Common and Public Sewer on Little Tower Hill, within the Tozver Hamlets, in the County of Middle/'x, called The Tower Hill Sewer, and which receives the Waters from the City Sewers; and that, tit the latter End of the Year 1794, such Sewer was blown up, occasioned-by a Defect which happened , in the City Sewer, as they are informed and believe, and, by an additional Quantity of Waters lately turned therein; that the Petitioners caused the same to be irepaired, but very recently the like Accident has happened again; and that, upon a careful and minute Inspection of such Sewer by skilful Surveyors and Workmen, the same appears, from its Size, not sufficient to carry off the great Body of Waters issuing from the City Sewer, great Part whereof has been recently turned therein, and which were formerly discharged in another Direction, and that a new Sewer is absolutely necessary to be made sufficient for that Purpose; and that the Petitioners have obtained Lefve from the Board of Ordnance to carry the Waters, for the present, into the Tower Ditch, but cannot obtain Leave to continue the fame, as, in the Opinion of that Board, it would be attended with great Inconvenience; and that the District, which has heretofore been rated towards the Repairs of such Sewer, is very small, and that a Rate of Two Shillings and Four Pence in the Pound has been very lately made upon them; and that the several Persons resident Within the City of 'London, who receive Benefit, or avoid Damage, are not fated, or pay towards the said Sewer, although they greatly exceed in Number the Persons within the District who pay thereto, and, as the general Law of Sewers now Hands, all Persons who receive a Benefit, or avoid 6

Damage, ought to contribute and pay in proportion to the Benefit they receive, or the Damage they avoid; but the Petitioners have not Powers, without the Aid of Parliament, to rate them, it not being within the Limits of the Tozver Hamlets, and the Petitioners have applied to the Commissioners of Sewers for the City of London', but they decline interfering the rein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable them to raile Money to make, such new Sewer, and that the Persons resident within the City of London, who receive Benefit, or avoid Damage . thereby, may contribute and pay, together with the Inhabitants of the District in which the said Sewer has its Cotlrfe, in proportion so the Benefit they receive,

Or the Damage they avoid; and that Powers may be given to the Petitioners to raile Money by Annuities, or otherwise, to enable them ta make such new Sewer, and to make Rates, from Time to Time, to defray the necessary Expences of such Sewer.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That an Act was passed in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for widening and improving the Entrance into the " City of London, near Temple Bar, for making a more " commodious Street or Passage at Snow Hill, and for " raising, on the Credit of the Orphans Fund, a Sum " of Money for those Purposes ;" and that a considerable Progress hath been made in putting the said Act into Execution, and it hath been discovered that the Powers thereof require to be altered, amended, enlarged, and rendered more effectual, in order to enable the Petitioners to complete the several Works by the said Act authorized and directed to be done; and that the taking down of the Church of Saint Clement Danes, as authorized by the said Act, will, as the Petitioners now conceive, be attended with great unnecessary Expence, as well as considerable Inconvenience to the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and that, by Plans and Surveys which the Petitioners have lately caused to be made, it appears, that a commodious and sufficient Enlargement of the Street, from Clement's, Church Yard to Temple Bar, may be made without removing the said Church, and at a much less Expence, by taking down certain Houses on the South Side of the Strand, and at the West End of Saint Clement's Church Yard, whereby the Communication between the Cities of London and will be

greatly improved: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for altering, amending, enlarging, and rendering more effectual, the Powers of the said Act, and for effecting the other Purposes above-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Report from Mr. Bragge reported from the Committee of Secrecy,

Committee of That the Committee had enquired into the Matter to 3' them referred, and had directed him to make a Report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.-

Your Committee have, in the First Place, examined the total Amount of Out-standing Demands on the Bank of England, and of the Funds for discharging the fame; and find, from the Examination of the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank, and the Documents produced by them, that the total Amount of Out-standing Demands on the Bank was, on the nth Day of this Instant 17,578,910;

'and that the total Amount of the Funds for discharging the same (without including the permanent Debt due from Government, of £. 11,686,800, which bears an Interest of £. 3 per Cent.) was, on the same Day, £.21,418,460; leaving a Balance of Surplus in favour of the Bank (exclusive of the above-mentioned Debt from Government) of £.3,839,550.

Your Committee next proceeded to examine the principal Articles of which the above-mentioned Sum of £.21,418,460, being the Credit Side of the Account, is made up, with a View of ascertaining how far the Bank might be enabled to resume its accustomed Payments in Calli, in case the Restriction at present subsisting should be removed: And Your Committee find, that the Advances to Government have, on the one Hand, been so much reduced, since the 25th of February last, as tp amount, on the said nth Day of this Instant , to no more than

the Sum of £. 4,258,140, while, on the other Hand, the Cafii and Bullion in the Bank have encreased to an Amount more than Five Times the Value of that at which they flood on the same 25th of February last, and much above that at which they have flood at any Time since the Beginning of September 1795.

Your Committee further find, that the Course of Exchange with Hamburgh is, at present, unusually favourable to this Country, and that, from the Situation of our Trade, there is good Reason 'to imagine it will so continue, unless Political Circumstances should occur to afiedl it.

Your Committee next proceeded to examine the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank, as to their Opinion of the Inconvenience which may have arisen from the Restriction impoftd on the Bank from making Payment in Cash, and of the Expediency of continuing such Restriction; and Your Committee find, that they are not aware of any such Inconvc- nience, and that they are supported in that Idea, by knowing that the Bankers and Traders of who

had a Right by the Act of Parliament to demand Three Fourths of any Deposit in Cash which they had made in the Bank, of £.500 or upwards, have only claimed about One Sixteenth: And Your Committee find, that the Court of Directors of the Bank did, on Vo t.53.

the 26th of Octoberf 797, corrte to a ftel'olution 4

Copy of which is subjoined to this Report.

Your Committee having further examined the Governor and Deputy Governor, as~to what may be meant by the Political Circumstances mentioned in that Resolution, find, that they understand by them, the State of Hostility in which the Nation is Hill involved, and particularly such Apprehensions as may be entertained of Invasion, either in Ireland or this Country, together with the Pofllbility there may be of Advances being to be made from this Country to Ireland; and that from those-Circumstances so explained, and from the Nature of the War, and the avowed Purpose of the Enemy to attack this Country by Means of its Public Credit, and to dirtrefs it in its Financial Operations, they are led to think that it will be expedient to continue the Restriction now subsisting, with the Reserve for partial Issues of Cash, at the Discretion of the Bank, of the Nature of that contained in the present Acts; and that it may be so '

continued, without Injury to the Credit of the Bank, and with Advantage to the Nation.

Your Committee, therefore, having taken into Consideration the general Situation of the Country, are of Opinion, that notwithstanding the Affairs of the Bank, both with respect to the general Balance of its Accounts, and its Capacity of making Payments in Specie, are in such a State that it might with Safety resume its accustomed Fundtions, under a different State of Public Affairs; yet, that it will be expedient to continue the Restriction now subsisting on such Payments, for such Time, and under such Limitations, as to the Wisdom of Parliament may seem fit.

Copy of a Resolution of the Court of Directors of the Bank.

" At a Court of Directors, at the Bank, on

Thursday the 26th October, 1797;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Court,

That the Governor and Company of the Bank of England are enabled to issue Specie, in any Manner that may be deemed necessary for the Accommodation of the Public; and the Court have no Hesitation to declare, that the Affairs of the Bank are in such a State, that it can with Safety resume its accustomed Fundlions, if the Political Circumstances of the Country do not render it inexpedient: But the Directors deeming it foreign to their Province to judge of these Points, wish to submit to the Wisdom of Parliament, whether, as it has been once judged proper to lay a Restriction on the Payments of the Bank in Cash, it may, or may not, be prudent to continue the fame."

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed.

That there are, within the said Township or Liberty, several Open Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commons, and Waste Grounds, containing, in the Whole, 1,500 Acres, or thereabouts, and which, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; and that it would be advantageous to the Owners and Proprietors thereof if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Parts allotted to them respectively: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commons, and Waste Grounds, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

ReportExpir- Mr. Hobart reported from the Committee, who were ing Laws. appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be' revived or continued; That the Committee had made a further Enquiry,' and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to continue several Acts, made in the Thirty-fifth and Thirty-sixth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, respecting the Admission " of certain Articles of Merchandize in Neutral Ships, " and the issuing of Orders in Council for that Purpose, for a limited Time," which was to continue in Force until Six Weeks after the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act authorizing His Majesty, for, a " limited Time, to make Regulations respecting the " Trade and Commerce to and from The Cape of Good " Hope," which was to continue in Force until the Expiration of Six Weeks from the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Hobart, Mr. Rose, Mr. Long, and Mr. Ryder, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

A Copy of the said Return or Answer here followeth; to wit,

John Darke, Esquire, and Richard Jenkins, Gentleman, Bailiffs of the Borough of in the County of Gloucester, do hereby return and certify unto the Sheriff of the said County of That having

in the Afternoon of Saturday the Eighteenth Day of November Instant received the Precept hereunto annexed from the said Sheriff, requiring them to cause to be elected a Burgess for the said Borough, they did, from Ignorance of the Act of Parliament herein after mentioned, between the Hours of Five and Six o'Clock in the Afternoon of the same Day, make Proclamation of the Election of a Burgess, to be held on the

Twenty-second Day of the same November, on which Day the said Bailiffs intended to proceed to the said Election: That before any Proceeding in the said Election, the said Bailiffs were, on the said Twenty-second Day of November, and not before, informed, that by a Statute passed in the Thirty-third Year of His Majesty's Reign, such Proclamation is required to be made, from the Twenty-fifth Day of to

the Twenty-fifth Day of March, between the Hours of Eight o'clock in the Morning and Four o'Clock in the Afternoon, and that therefore the Proclamation which had been, so as aforesaid made between the Hours of Five and Six o'Clock in the Afternoon was illegal and void: That the said Bailiffs were all'o advised that no fresh Proclamation of the said Election could then be made, so as to proceed therein within Eight Days next after the Receipt of such Precept, giving Four Days Notice thereof, according to the Form of the Statute in that same made and provided; and that x therefore no Election could legally be made of a Burgess under the said Precept: That by Reason of the Premises, the said Bailiffs did not further proceed in the Execution of the said Precept, nor cause any Election to be had, or any Return of a Burgess for the said Borough to be made according to the Tenor of the said Precept. In Witness whereof they the said John Darke and Richard Jenkins, Bailiff's of the said Borough, have hereunto set their Hands, and the Seal of Office of the said Borough, the Twenty-fifth Day of in the Year of our Lord One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-seven.

Given under my Hand, this Twenty-seventh Day of November 1797,

Joseph Baldwin, Deputy Clerk of the Crown.

Setting forth, That, by the great Increase of the Trade and Commerce of the Cities of London and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, the present Legal Quays and Wharfs on the River Thames, and those used by Sufferance as Wharfs and Quays, are found inadequate to the Accommodation of the Shipping, which has been in a State of Increase during the last Hundred Years, and to the Purposes of landing and shipping of Goods and Merchandizes, and, from the crowded State of the River, the Navigation is much impeded, and many ln-conveniencies, Delays, and Accidents, as well as Losses and Damages, are occasioned to the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London; and that, by Reason of the increased Navigation of the said River great Damages and Delays are sustained by the Owners of, and Persons interested in Ships and Vessels retorting to the said Port of London; and that the said several Grievances might be removed, if good and sufficient Wet Docks or Basons, and Cuts, with proper Outlets, and other necessary Works, were made, in convenient Situations near the said River, for the Reception and Discharge of Vessels, which would give Protection and Dispatch to Shipping, Accommodation to Commerce, and Security to the Revenue; and that, for carrying into Effect the Purposes aforesaid, it will be necessary to purchase certain Lands, Buildings, and Premisses, which cannot be done without the Aid and Authority of Parliament; and that the Petitioners have caused Surveys, Plans, and Estimates, to be made of the several Works necessary to be done for providing Docks, Basons, and Cuts, and other Accommodations, as aforesaid, and have raised a Subscription for carrying the same into Execution: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the said Purposes, by such Ways and Means, and under such Regulations and restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty has appointed Tuesday, the 19th Day of this Instant December, to be observed as a Day of Public Thanksgiving to Almighty God, for the many signal and important Victories obtained by His Majesty's Navy in the Course of the present War: And, for the greater Solemnity of that Day, His Majesty will go to Saint Paul's Church, as Has been accustomed in former Times in this Kingdom, to return Thanks to Almighty God for the fame; and that His Majesty hath been plealed to give the necessary Orders for providing convenient Places in the said Cathedral for the Members of this House.

That, in consequence thereof, the Counsel for the said several Petitioners delivered in a Statement, as follows:

" That the Right of Election for the Borough of " Newton, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, is exclusively vested in the Freemen or Burgefl'es of the " said Borough; that is to say, in any Person seised " of an Estate of Freehold, in any House, Building, " or Lands, within the Borough, of the Value of " Forty Shillings a Year and upwards; and, in case of " Joint-Tenants, or Tenants in Common, no more " than One Person has a Right to vote for One and " the same House or Tenement."

That the Counsel for the Sitting Member, Thomas Langford Brooke, Esquire, delivered in a Statement, as follows:

" That the Right of voting for Members to serve in " Parliament for the Borough of Newton, in the County " of Lancaster, js in Persons having an Estate of Freehold, or for a Term, or Residue of a Term, of 99 " Years or upwards, determinable on One or more Life " or Lives, in any Messuages, Lands, or Tenements, " within the Borough of Newton ;"

That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the said several Petitioners, the said Select Committee have determined.

That the Right of Election, as set forth in the said Statement, is not the Right of Election for the said Borough of Newton:

That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Right of Election, as set forth in the said Statement, is not the Right of Election for the said Borough of Nezvton:

That the said Select Committee, having duly considered the said Statements, and the Evidence adduced before them, touching the Right of Election for the said Borough of Nezvton, have determined,

That the Right of Election for the Borough of ton, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, is exclusively vested in the Freemen or Burgefl'es of the said Borough, that is to say, in any Person leifed of a corporeal Estate of Freehold in any House, Building, or Lands, within the Borough, of the Value of Forty Shillings a Year and upwards; and, in case of Joint-Tenants, or Tenants in Common, that nb more than One Person has a Right to vote for One and the same House or Tenement:

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House,

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for. a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on this Trade with Safety, and protect His Majesty's Subj-eds in the Dominions, it has

been found necessary that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Con-fuls, and Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in other Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and where English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence nvheteof has beeil borne by the Turkey Company, which; together with many other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on this Trade, have of late Years amounted to about £. 8,000 per Annum; and that the Petitioners acknowledge, with Gratitude, the several Grants they formerly received from Parliament, and although they did not apply for further Assistance lo long as they found thern-iclves in a Situation to support their Expences, they are Jenfible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary and unavoidable Expences, un-lel's relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take these Premises into Consideration, and grant‘them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

liefolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means forraif-ing the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.'

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, 'fen of the Clock; ‘

A PETITION of the there-undersigned Inhabi- Newark upon tants of" the Parish of Newark u in the cVivlitionP County of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting Forth, That the said Town is a large, populous, and commercial Town, lying upon the great North Road from London to Edinband that the Streets, Lanes, and Public Passages, within the same, are not sufficiently cleanled and lighted, and many of them not properly paved; and that it would be of great Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and all Persons resorting thereto, if the said Streets and Public Passages were effectually paved and kept iii Repair, and properly cleanled and lighted; and that; certain Shambles, or Shops, were several Years ago . erected and built for the Convenience of exposing Butchers' Meat to Sale, but the same have never been occupied for that Purpose; and that it would be a' great Convenience to the said Inhabitants if such Shambles, or Shops, and other convenient Places, were used for exposing Butchers' Meat to Sale, instead of the same being iold in the Public Streets; and that sundry Estates, of very considerable Yearly Value, are now vested in the Mayor and Aldermen of the said Borough, and other Trustees, and the Rents and Profits thereof, after certain Applications and Payments made thereout, are dire died to be applied for the common Good and Weal of the said Town; and that the Surplus of the Rents and Profits of the said Estates, after the several Annual Payments wherewith the same are respectively charged are made, will be considerably more than sufficient to defray all the Expences necessary and incident to the several Purposes aforesaid, and it would be for the Benefit of the said Town if the same were so applied: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better paving, lighting, and cleansing, the Streets and other Public Passages in the said Town of Newark upon and for removing the Market for Butchers' Meat into the new Shambles there, and regulating the fame, and for applying Part of the Rents and Fronts of the said Trust Estates for those Purposes, with such Powers and Provisions as to the House shall seem meet.

Report from Mr. Ryder reported from the Committee, who were appointcdto appointed to consider of the Manner of this House consider of the going to Saint Paul's Church, on the 19th

M-eros £)ay of this Inilant , and of such Regu-

saur».°" lations as may be necessary to be observed for the Pre-

servation of Order upon that Occasion; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had agreed to report, that the following are proper Regulations to be observed on the said Occasion; and he read the Report in his Place i and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was iread; and the Regulations therein mentioned are as, followeth; viz.

First, That this House do go from the House to Saint Paul's Church, on Tuesday the 10th of this Instant December, to the Solemnity of the Public Thanks-

giving.

Secondly, That the House be going to their Places prepared for them in Saint Paul's Church, on Tuesday the 19th of this Inilant by Eight o'Clock ill

the Morning.

Thirdly, That the House be called over; and that the Speaker do go last; and that no Cartiage belonging to any Member of this House be permitted to Follow that of the Speaker.

Fourthly, That the Serjeant at Arms do order Two Messengers to precede, on Horseback, the First Carriage going from the House; That, at their Arrival at Saint Paul's. One do proceed to conduct such Carriage to the Place appointed to Wait in, and the other re-tnain to attend in like Manner the last Carriage in the Procession j and that they do take into Custody any Coachman, Footman, or other Person, who may be disorderly, or violate any Orders given him, or interrupt the Execution of any Rules made for the Accommodation Or Dignity Of this House.

Fifthly, That the Members do go to Saint Paul's in their own Coaches, with a Pair of Horses only to each Coach; that no Hackney Coaches be permitted; and that each Carriage do pass. One by One, within the Chains in Old Palace Yard; and that each Member do direct his Servants to keep the Ranks during the Procession. '

Sixthly, That no Carriage, of any Sort whatever, be permitted to stand or pass between Temple Bar and Palace Yard, front Six o'Clock in the Morning till Five in the Afternoon, except th,e Carriages of such Persons as belong to the Members of either House of Parliament, and Foreign Ministers, or to the Procession of Their Majesties and the Royal Family; and that no Member of this House do come down to the House by the Strand Eastward of Saint Martin's or by Pall Mall.

Seventhly, That the Serjeant at Arms do station One or more Messengers of the House on Horseback, who may assist in preventing any Person from violating this Order, and may take into Custody any Person falsely pretending to belong'to either House of Parliament.

Eighthly, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Justices of the Peace, the Bailiff of Westminster, and other proper Officers, to assist in the Preservation of Order, and the due Observance of these Regulations; And,

Lastly, That the Serjeant at Arms, and other Officers of the House, do attend at Saint Paul's, to conduct the Members to their Seats, to prevent any Other Persons from taking Possession of the fame; and be ordered to take into Custody any Person who may violate or obstruct these Orders.

The said Regulations being read a Second Time, were agreed to by the House.

Mr. Dudley Ryder also reported. That the Lord

Mayor of Ionian had communicated to the said Committee certain Regulations for the Arrangement of Car-: riages within the City of Lond, which the Committee approved, so far as the same related to the Carriages of the Members of this House; and the said Regulations are as follow:

REGULATIONS proposed for the Accommodation of Their Majesties and the Royal Family, the Members of both Houses of Parliament, the Foreign Ministers, the Aldermen, &c. of London, and others, passing to and returning from the Cathedral Church of Saint Paul, on Tuesday the 19th Day of December 1797.

That there be Three Avenues to the Church kept, with diflSnft Outlets from each, for the Carriages to pass off, and prepare to fetum.

WEST AVENUE, for Their Majesties, the Royal Family, the Members of both Houses of Parliament, and the Foreign Ministers:

That the great Street or Avenue, from Temple Bar to the Church, be reserved entirely for the Passage of Their Majesties, the Royal Family, the Members of both Houses of Parliament, and the Foreign Ministers all their Carriages to pass in single Rank, and no othet Carriage whatever to be admitted. It being understood that Their Majesties and the Royal Family Will enter the Church at the West Door, their Carriages are to drive in at the West Gate of the Church Yard, put down at the Bottom of the Steps, draw off to the North Side of the Church, and there wait until' Divine Service is over; then return to the Bottombf the Steps to take up. It is recommended that the Carriages of the Members of both Houses of Parliament, and of the Foreign Ministers, put down at the South West Gate of the Church Yard; and that they order their Servants to proceed with their Carriages on the South Side of the Church Yard Eastward, through Watling Street and Budge Row, to turn up IValbrook, pass the West Side of

the Mansion House, and return through th into

Cheapside, and to remain on the South Side of Cheapside, in Three Rows, with the Horses towards the Church, until called for.

NORTH AVENUE, for the Nobility (not in Parliament) and other Person from the West End of the Town:

That the Nobility, Gentry, and others coming into Holborn from the West End of the Town, he requested to proceed along Snow Hill and Newgate Street, turn to the Right down Warwick Lane, and then to the Left along Paternofier Ron), and be fef down at Canon , Opposite the North Door of the Church; then 'to order their Servants to proceed with their Carriages to the End of Paternofier Row, and turn round to the Left into Newgate Street, then down St. Martin's le Grand, into Aldersgate Street, keeping the Left Side of the Street to Long Lane, and return on the Right, there to remain in a Double Row, with the Horses towards Newgate Street, until Divine Service is ended; and then so return the same Way to take up.

EASTERN AVENUE, for the Corporation:

That the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, and Four Gentlemen of the Committee, proceed from the Mansion House, rather before Nine o'Clock, through Cheapside, round the South Side of Saint Parts Church Yard, and up Fleet Street to Temple Bar; put down at Messrs. Child and Company; then direct their Carriages to drive through Temple Bar, turn short about, and follow each other down Fleet Street, round Saint Parts Church , and along Cheapside, turn to the Left down King Street, and wait in Guildhall Yard till called for.

That the Aldermen and City Officers immediately follow the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, and Gentlemen of the 1 Committee,

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Parish of -enwell, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Parish is a populous District, and contains about 21,000 Inhabitants; that the Clock and Watch Manufactory has for many Years been carried on therein to a very great Extent, and that nearly 7,000, being about One Third of those Inhabitants, are dependent upon the different Branches of this Manufactory for their Support; and that the Clock and Watch Manufacturers, as well as the other Inhabitants of the Parish (who are collaterally connected with them) from the Effects already produced by the Act, passed in the last: Session for granting certain Duties on Clocks and Watches, cannot but lament the serious Inconveniencies to which those Trades are thereby subjected, and the grievous Burthen which the Parish mult sustain by the greatest Part of the Workmen, formerly employed therein, having, since the passing of that Act, become unemployed.

Numbers of whom have been under the Necessity of applying to the Parish for Relief for themselves, their Families, and Apprentices, and many others mull speedily be reduced to the same deplorable Situation, J and that, if the said Act should continue in Force, the Mailer Manufacturers will be unable to carry on their Trades, a Diminution of more than one Half having already taken place in the Sale of Clocks and Watches, and of the various Articles used in the making of them, and the Sale thereof is daily decreasing; and that the Articers and Workmen, who, from these Causes, cannot obtain Employ, have already begun to emigrate, and many more will, from their Distrelfes, be induced to do the fame, and leave their Families and Apprentices chargeable upon the Parish J That the Manufactory of Clocks and Watches is of great National Importance, inasmuch as it employs so many Thousands ot Workmen, who, by the mere ingenious Operation of Manual Labour, increase the Value of BnMaterials, otherwise of small Estimation, to a very extraordinary De: gree; and that the Annual Rental of this Parish, as allblled to the Poor Rates, is £.54,780; that the different Taxes to which it is now rated amount to the Sum of £. 28,000 and upwards; and that these Taxes are to an alarming Degree becoming unproductive; and that, if the said Act should be continued, a very great Addition to the Poor Rates mult take place, in order to raise the necessary Support for those Workmen and Manufacturers, and the Persons dependent upon them, who, from the Causes before-mentioned, are and will be driven to the Necessity of applying to the Parish for Maintenance: And therefore praying the House to take this Subject into its serious Confederation, That the said Act may be repealed, and that the Petitioners may, if necessary, be heard, by themselves and their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of this their Application.

A Petition of the Vestrymen of the Parish of Saint petition from Luke, in the County of Middlesex, in Vestry assembled, vestrymen of on Behalf of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, par- "d0. u es' ticularly those in the several Brandies of the Clock and Watch making Trades, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the said Parish, there is a considerable Number of Poor Mechanics, and Perr fons who keep small Shops of various Delci iptions, and on a fair Calculation, it is computed there are among them some Thousands of Artificers, hitherto employed in the several Branches of the Trades of Clock and

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, zvard Smith Godfrey, Esquire, being examined, said, That the said Town is a large, populous, and commercial Town, and that the Streets, Lanes, and public Passages within the same are not sufficiently cleansed and lighted, and many of them not properly paved; and that it would be of great Advantage to the Inhabitants thereof, and all Persons relorting thereto, if the said Streets and public Passages were effectually paved and ' kept in Repair, and properly cleansed and lighted; and-that it would also be of great Convenience to the said Inhabitants, if certain Shambles or Shops, which were several Years ago built for the Convenience of exposing Butchers' Meat to Sale, but never occupied, were now used for that Purpose.

THE House being met, in order to their going to Saint Paul's Church to the Solemnity of the Public Thanksgiving;

Refo/ved, That this House be now called over, for their more orderly proceeding to Saint Paul's Church.

Then the Members were called over, by the Clerk, by their Counties, as usual; and they went to Saint Paul's Church accordingly.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Note, The House being called over, soon after Eight o'Clock in the Morning, the Members went accordingly in their Carriages from the House, along Parliament Street, by Charing the

Strand, and Fleet Street, directly to Saint Paul's Church: The Clerk 'Afliffant, the Chaplain, and Deputy Serjeant at Arms went first in one of Mr. Speaker's Carriages, being preceded by some of the Messengers of the House on Horse-back, all the Way, and also by the Constables of PVeJlminster, as far as Temple Bar. The Mem-

bers, on their coming to Saint Paul's, were conducted through the Iron Gate at the South-weR Corner, into the large Area before the Church, and from thence into the Church by the Door on the South Side of the Great WeRern Door: Mr. Speaker, in his Coach, attended by the Clerk and Serjeant at Arms, went the lass, and fat in the Middle of the North Side of the Choir, with the Mace before him (in the Place where the Lord Mayor of London usually fits) and the Clerk and Serjeant were -in the Seat below him. The Members fat in the Places provided for them, which confified of the Whole of the Gallery on the South Side of the Choir (except such Part of the back Seats thereof as were let apart for the Admirals and Naval Officers who attended this Solemnity) and One Half of the Gallery on the North Side of the Choir, at the Weffern End nearefi the Organ, which proved to be sufficient for their Accommodation. — No Interruption or Inconvenience happened during the Procession, or in any Part of this Proceeding; the Whole was conducted with perfect Regularity and good Order, and in a Manner suitable to so great and solemn an Occasion, and to the' Dignity of the House.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person assessed to any of the Rates or Duties now payable on Houses, Windows or Lights, or on Inhabited Houses, or on Dogs, or Clocks, Watches, or Time-keepers, to the Amount of Twenty Pounds (ex-, cept such Persons who shall be eventually made subject to a lower or other Rate of Duty) shall be charged Annually, during a Term to be limited, with an additional Aate or Duty, in proportion to the Amount of the said Duties to which such Person is assessed, according to the last Yearly Assessment or Assessments, made prior to the 6th Day of April 1798, in pursuance of any Act of Parliament now in Force, and the Proportion thereof shall be as follows; videlicet, where the said Duties shall

Amount to Twenty Pounds, and shall be under Thirty Pounds, a Duty equal to Three Times the Amount and One Half the Amount thereof; where the said Duties shall amount to Thirty Pounds, and shall be under Forty Pounds, a Duty equal to Four Times the Amount thereof; where the said Duties shall amount to Forty Pounds, and shall be under Fifty Pounds, a Duty equal to Four Times the Amount and One Half the Amount thereof; and whe're the said Duties shall amount to Fifty Pounds, or upwards, a Duty equal to Five Times the Amount thereof; and that where any Person shall be so charged by every such Assessment made for a less Term than a Year, the additional Rate or Duty shall be computed on the Aggregate Amount of the Sums contained in such Assessment, and of such further Sum to be added thereto as would become payable thereon if the same were made for a whole Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person assessed to any of the Duties now payable on Male Servants, on Carriages, or on Horses (other than those granted on florfes and Mules by Two Acts, passed in the Thirty-sixth and Thirty-seventh Years of His present Majesty's Reign) shall be charged Annually, during a Time to be limited, with an additional Rate or Duty, in proportion to the Amount of the said Duties to which such Person is assessed, according to the last Yearly Assessment or Assessments, made in pursuance of any Act of Parliament now in Force prior to the 6th Day of April 1798, and the Proportion thereof shall be as follows; that is to say, where the Amount of the said Duties, now payable, shall be under Twenty-five Pounds, a Duty equal to Three Times the Amount thereof; where the said Duties, now payable, shall amount to Twenty-five Pounds, and shall be under Thirty Pounds, a Duty equal to Three Times the Amount and One Half the Amount thereof; where the said Duties, now payable, shall amount to Thirty Pounds, and shall be under Forty Pounds, a Duty equal to Four Times the Amount thereof; where the said Duties, now payable, shall amount to Forty Pounds, and shall be under Fifty Pounds, a Duty equal to Four Times the Amount and One Half the Amount thereof; and where the said Duties, now payable, shall amount to Fifty Pounds, or upwards, a Duty equal to Five Times the Amount thereof; and that where any Person shall be so charged, by any such Assessment, made for a less Term than a Year, the additional Rate or Duty shall be computed on the Aggregate Amount of the Sums contained in such Assessment, and of such further Sum to be added thereto as would be payable thereon if the same were made for a whole Year.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of, and Dealers in, Petition of Clocks and Watches resident within the Cities of Lcn-don and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and Weilminrter, the Vicinities thereof, whose Names are thereunto l'ub-feribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting \Vutch forth. That, in consequence of the Act, passed in the Duty Act. last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for " granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Clocks " and Watches," the Petitioners have sustained great Losses: That, should this Act continue in Force, they will daily be exposed to still greater Hardships; and that, from the Effects it has already produced,-they entertain the most alarming Apprehension of the Dangers to which they will be subjected: That, fmee the passing of the said Act, the Petitioners have, with much Anxiety, observed a gradual Increase in its -injurious Operation; it appears, from their own Experience, as well as from numerous Documents received from almost every Part of Great Britain, by a Committee appointed, last July, to examine and state their Grievances (which were then severely felt) that, prior to the Month of November last, a Diminution of more than One Half had taken place in the making of Clocks and Watches, and their various accompanying Ornaments, and the Implements used in making the same, and the Manufacture and Sale thereof has since decreased, and con- /

tinues diminishing so rapidly, that the Home Trade must very soon be nearly annihilated: That the Artificers in the various Branches of the Clock and Watch Manufactory, who, from the Causes before-mentioned, cannot obtain Employment, have already begun to emigrate, and many others will, from their DillrelTes, be induced, and probably encouraged by Foreigners, to do the fame; that such Artificers will be loft to this Country, and carry with them the most. valuable Secrets which have hitherto given the Manufacturers and Dealers of Great Britain a decided Superiority and Advantage in the Markets Abroad; and, if speedy and,

9 effectual

Sicklinghall and Wood hall Inclosure Petition.

Report of AC-

felted Taxes

additional

Duty Bill, further consider-cd.
