effectual Relief be not granted to the Petitioners, they most fcrioully apprehend a great and continued Decrease, and eventually an entire Destruction of their Foreign Trade: That the Home and Foreign Trades are particularly connected, so far as regards the Instruction and Employment of the Workmen, because, the Foreign Trade being only Periodical, the Manufacturers cannot, without the Home Trade, employ the Workmen at those Times when they are not getting up and executing Orders for the Foreign Markets: That the Cotton and Woollen Manufactories are entirely indebted for the State of Perfection, to which the Machinery used therein is now brought, to the Clock and Watchmakers, great Numbers of whom have, for Several Years past, at Times been employed in inventing and constructing, as well as Superintending, such Machinery, and that those Persons, from their Want of Employment in the Clock and Watch Trade, will also be induced to emigrate, and carry with them the important Knowledge not only of improving and encouraging, but of establishing. Cotton and Woollen Manufactories Abroad, which the Petitioners Submit will certainly be very prejudicial to the Commercial and General Interests of this Country: That the Manufactory of Clocks and Watches mult appear to be of great and peculiar National Importance, when it is considered how many Thousands of Artificers are employed therein; and that through the mere productive Operation of their Labour, the Materials used in the Machinery of those Articles are rendered from Fifty to Five hundred, and progressively, in many Instances, to more than One thousand Times their original Value: That, from these Considerations, the Petitioners are actuated by Motives of Duty, as well as Interest, to lay the foregoing Statement of Facts before the House, and, at the same Time that they intreat its Relief, to declare, that they arc desirous to contribute their full pecuniary Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, and the Support of the Constitution, but that, unless the Said Act be repealed, they will be totally unable so to do: And therefore praying, That the said Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, laying Duties on Clocks and Watches, may be repealed; and that the Petitioners may, if necessary, be heard, by themselves, and their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of this their Application.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

And the Question being put. That those Words be there added; "

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of several Owners of Estates in the Parish of Ranworth, in the County of was presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there being, within the said Parish, several Lands and Grounds, called Whole Year Lands, Common Fields, Half Year or Shack Lands, Commons, and Waste Grounds, belonging to the Petitioners and others, which were subject to various Rights of Sheepwalk, Shackage, and Common, and great Part of the said Whole Year Lands, as well as the said Half Year or Shack Lands, being very inconveniently situated for the several Owners and Occupiers thereof, and the said Common Field Lands laying intermixed and dispersed in small Parcels, and being of little Value, the Petitioners and other Persons interested, conceiving it would be of great Advantage to all the Parties if such Rights of Shackage, Sheepwalk, and Common, were extinguished, and if all the said Lands and Grounds, Commons and Wastes, were divided, and specific Parts Or Shares thereof set out and allotted to the several Proprietors, and all other Persons interested, according to their several Estates, Rights, and Interests, agreed thereto; and that by certain Articles of Agreement, bearing Date the 18th Day of December 1797, the said Rights of Shackage, Sheepwalk, and Common, were agreed to be extinguished, and Commissioners were appointed for dividing and allotting the said Lands and Grounds, Commons and Wastes, to the several Proprietors, and all other Persons. interested, according to their several Estates, Rights, and Interests therein, and the Commissioners named in such Agreement have made their Award in the Premises, but which Agreement and Award, cannot be confirmed without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purpose aforesaid, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Hobart and Mr. AJiley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Clock and Watch Makers of the City of Bristol ',was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, deeply impressed with a just Sense of the Necessity, at this important Crins, of supporting the extraordinary Exigencies of the State by every' Means in their Power, feel the most poignant Regret at being compelled to solicit the Interference of the House in Behalf of themselves, their Workmen, and their Families: That, in consequence of an Act, passed in the last Session, imposing an Annual Tax on Persons wearing Watches, or using Clocks, the Trade in those Branches is fo° much diminished as to amount nearly to an Annihilation thereof, whereby many excellent Workmen, with their Families, are reduced to the utmost Distress; and that the Business of the Petitioners has been already in a very high Degree affeftetf by the Tax, and they can, without Exaggeration, declare, that it will (unless speedily repealed i prive them of all Prospect of supporting themselves and Families, prevent their contributing to the present Exigencies of their Country, and eventually prove their utter Ruin: And therefore imploring the House to take their same into Consideration, and, by a Repeal of the said Act, to afford them the wished for Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Sj>eaker,

The Lords, having, taken into Consideration the ift, 3d, 4th, 5th, and 6th of the Resolutions which, in the lull Session, were agreed to by both Houses of Parliament, relative to the'Promulgation of the Statutes, and allb the Resolution of the House of Commons communicated to the Lords by Message on the 22d Day of December last, have come to the following Resolutions: Resolved, That the Copy Fee to be paid to the Clerk of the Parliaments, and the Clerk Assistant, by the Party or Parties interested in any Private Bill, who shall request a Clause to be inserted therein, that the fame

A. 1798.

may be declared a Public Act, shall be the same as is now paid, and has been established ever since the Year 1725, for the Copy of any Record or Proceeding of Parliament; videlicet, One Shilling for every Copy Sheet.

Resolved, That, in order to secure effectually to the Public 200 Copies of every such Private Bill so requested to be, and declared accordingly to be, a Public Act, the said Copy Fee'of One Shilling per Sheet shall be paid by the Party or Parties soliciting such Private Bill before the Third Reading thereof; and shall allb, before the Third Reading of such Bill, pay to His Majesty's Printer a Sum proportioned to the Rate of One Pound Five Shillings for every Twenty-five Copy Sheets that such Bill, when printed, shall contain. The Amount of such Copy Fee, and Expence of Printing, to be refunded to the Party or Parties soliciting such Bill, if the same shall not pass into a Law.

Resolved, That a Fee of Five Shillings upon every such Private Bill shall be paid to the Clerk of the Journals, the Clerk of the Papers, and the Doorkeeper attending the Private Committees, in lieu of the Emoluments which they have been used to receive from the same.

38 Geo. III. ii0 Januarii 181

of the Reports of the Commissioners who 'were appointed by an Act, passed in the Year 1786, " to enquire into the State and Condition of the' Woods,

" Forests, and Land Revenues belonging to the Crown," and to " suggest such Plans for the future Management and Improvement of those Estates, as they should think best calculated to render them most " productive and advantageous to His Majesty and the " Public."

Those Commissioners, after a minute and laborious Investigation, the Result of which was stated in Seventeen different Reports to Parliament, pointed out the Defects and Errors in the ancient Mode of Management, under which little Benefit had arisen to the Crown, or the Public; and recommended, instead of it, a System totally different, and from \phich a gradual Increase of Revenue, to a very considerable Amount, and many other Advantages, might be expected to arise.

The most material of those Defects were stated to

and advised that proper Clauses for the Preservation and Improvement of the Property should be introduced:

That Leases of Houses or Building Ground should *

be authorized to be granted for 99 Years, instead of Building 50 Years, to which the Crown was confined by the Tease.

Civil List Act of Queen Anne; the Power of granting Leases for that longer Term being found advantageous in the Management of private Estates:

That Leases of Houses, except where re-building Perils of A -was necessary, should not be renewed till'within 20 new 1. Years of the End of the existing Terms, nor Leases of Lands till within 5 Years; so that only One Renewal should take place in the Course of any Lease:

That no Fines should be taken for Land Estates or Proportion) Building Ground, and that the Fines to be taken for of Fine and Houses should not exceed the Proportion of One Third enU‘

Part of the Annual Value, and in no same be computed at more than the highest legal Interest c

be; '

1 ft. That Leases were granted, frequently, without having Surveys taken of the Property, and that the Surveys, when taken, were never confirmed by the Oath of the Surveyor, nor any other Means employed for ascertaining the Value of the Estates which could be attended with Expence, no Fund being provided for defraying that Charge.

2dly. That Lessees were permitted to renew their Leases, as often as it happened to suit their Convenience; and that the Expence of the Lease, which, in consequence of the Fees payable at the different Offices, is known to be great, being deducted from the Fine, was no Loss to the Tenants, but a heavy Burthen on the Estate of the Crown.

3dly. That at least Seven-Eighth Parts of the Value were taken in Fine, and only One-Eighth Part in Rent; and that the Fines were, in all Cases, computed at very high Rates of Interest; the wasteful Effect of which Mode of proceeding was, that the Crown actually received more from the One-Eighth Part let for Rent, than from the Seven-Eighth Parts for which Fines were taken.

That the new Rents to be reserved should be clear of New Rents to all Deductions, so as effectually to guard against the former Error, by which Land Tax had been very commonly Twice allowed:

That all Fees and Perquisites should be prohibited, Feestobeabo-and adequate Salaries given instead of them: Uflied *

That all the remaining Fee Farm Rents belonging to Fee Farm the Crown should be fold, and the Price invested in to the £. 3 per Centum Consolidated Bank Annuities: 0

That when Vacancies should happen in the Offices Number of of the Receivers, the Number should be gradually re- e lelfcned10 duced, and a less expensive Mode adopted in the Col- |yth Repo‘t

Page 20.

lection of the Rents:

That instead of the separate Offices of Surveyor Ge- A Board robe neral of the Crown Lands, and Surveyor General of the established Woods and Forests, a Board should be established, to consist of Three Commissioners, for the Management of the Whole:

And, that Reports should be made to Parliament, Reports to be at stated Periods, in which a full Account should be Par *

given of their Proceedings, and of the Improvements made, and at what Expence.

4thly. That Crown Leases were passed through various Offices, apparently instituted as Checks on their mutual Proceedings; but that no Benefit arose from th t Regulation, the Offices not having any useful Connection or Communication with each other; in consequence of which it had happened that the Land Tax was very commonly Twice allowed to the Lessee, by which Error alone a Loss was sustained of about £. 1,500 or £. 1,600 per Annum.

5thly. That no Copies, Entries, or Counterparts of the Leases were kept in the Office of the Surveyor Ge-. neral, so that the Officer to whole Care the Protection of the Estate was principally committed, had not before him the Covenants to be observed by the Lessees.

And finally, that, by injudicious Provisions in the Civil List Act of Queen Anne, those who were entrusted with the Management were restrained, in Cafes where more Latitude would have enabled them to improve the Estate; and too much Power was given to them where the Advantages of the Lessees, and the Perquisites of the Officers, could be most increased, and the Interest of the Crown most injured.

The Commissioners therefore advised that this unwise System should be abolished; and they explained very fully the Principles on which the Plan of Management and Improvement propostd instead of it was founded.

They suggested "Alterations in the Form of the Leases, Vox.. 53.

And after observing, that the Writings relative to 17th Report, the Estates of the Crown were dispersed through many Page ' different Offices of Record, and Repositories of Public Papers, and that much of their Time had been taken up, and considerable Expence incurred, in searching for them, the Commissioners advised, that in the Office office to be which they recommended to be established, should be kept and arranged, not only the Entries, Counterparts, tion of Books, and Assignments of all Leases, but all Surveys, and Surveys, and other written Documents tending to shew the Rights ,f>ocu of the Crown in any of its Estates, or Copies of them, where any Objection should be found to arise to the Removal of the Originals from the Places where they were deposited: And that distinct Calendars should be made of those Documents, and Registers of all Grants containing any Remainder or Limitation in favour of the Crown.

Proceeding Under these Circumstances, and this being the First ttemwpfan PeP?rt which the Surveyor General has made to the into Execu- Legislature since the parting of that Act of Parliament, tion. he conceives it to be incumbent on him to state, not

only what his Proceedings have been in carrying the new System of Management into Effect, but what general Regulations he has proposed to the Treasury to be established for his Guidance, and that of his Successors in Office; and in order to do this in the clearest Manner, without swelling this Report to an improper Length, he will place in the Appendix Copies of some of the Memorials or Letters to the Treasury, in which the most material of those Regulations have been proposed, together with the Answers from that Board. On a Reference to those Documents, a Judgment may be more easily formed whether the Principles of that System have been uniformly kept in View, and whether the Measures which the Surveyor General has recommended are well calculated to produce, in the End, that Improvement in the Land Revenue of the Crown which the Public has been led to expect.

After these preliminary Observations, which the Cir- The demifed cumstances seemed to call for, the Surveyor General cfow how ‘ humbly reports to this Honourable House, That the situated. demised Estates of the Crown, which comprehend the greater Part of what is under his Management, consist of a great Number of Manors, Lands, and Houses, dif-perfect in almost every County of England and Wales.

The most valuable Part of that Property is situated in London and Westminster, in which there are about London and 1,900 Houses belonging to the Crown, exclusive of the Westminster. Palaces, Public Offices, and other Buildings of a Public Nature, and of Houses possessed in Right of Offices; and besides Lands of very considerable Extent, so closely adjoining to the Town as to make it probable that, after Peace shall be restored, a great deal may be fot as Building Ground.

This being the Part of the Crown's Estate not only The earliest of the greatest Value at present, but susceptible also of t[ suj1£"due the greatest Improvement, it naturally called for the provoneat. earliest Attention.

Many entire Streets belong to the Crown, and considerable Districts most advantageously situated, but co-. vered with Buildings of very little Value, the Accels to them in many Places inconvenient, and the Streets or Lanes narrow and irregular.

Under these Circumstances, it appeared obvious that Necessity of the Property could not be brought to its highest State GenendPlan of Improvement solely by a Consideration of the fepa- madeofthi rate Parts comprized in different Leases, as Applications Part of the might be made for Renewals; and that a general View roperty should be taken of the Whole, before determining what Leases should be renewed, or what Alterations or Improvements might be practicable and advantageous.

But though there were detached Plans of almost every Part of the Crown's Property in Houses and Building Ground, there was no accurate General Plan of the Whole, from which the relative Connection between the different Parts could be traced: Nor, indeed, A General could such a Plan have been necessary under the former System of Management. The Idea of any Improve- the former ment of the Property, by an Enlargement or Alteration Management, of the Streets, the Removal of any Buildings irregularly situated, the opening of any new Accel's to them, or altering the Size or the Number of the Houses, I'o as to accommodate them to the Demand, or the Taste of the Times, seems not to have occurred, or, if it did occur, to have been deemed impracticable.

The Changes which had taken place in the Manner of leafing this Part of the Property had, indeed, an of-pofite Tendency, and had rendered any such Improvement much more difficult. Formerly a considerable Number of Houses, often entire Streets, and in some Instances several Streets, were granted in One Lcale; and these reverting to the Crown at the same Time,'

Alterations of this Nature might have been found easily practicable: But it had happened that, where a Lessee had fold his Interest in any One or more of the Houses comprized in his Lease, the separate Parts of the Property had been afterwards considered as distinct Estates, and reversionary Leases of those Parts had been granted separately to the Purchasers, without any Care having been taken that the Leases of the different Parts should terminate at the same Time; and thus, in every such Instance, a new Obstacle had been thrown in the Way of the general Improvement.

This Proposal having met with the Approbation of the Treasury, Two Surveyors of Eminence, employed in the ordinary Business of the Office, were authorized to make a General Plan of the Crown's Estate in London and Westminster; a Measure which, though attended with some Expence, was extremely necessary, not only for the Object which has been mentioned, but as affording the belt Means of ascertaining the Boundaries of the Property of the Crown, and the best Security against Encroachments.

Such a Plan has accordingly been made; and many Alterations have occurred, which, when completed, will not only greatly increase the Value of the Crown's ' Estate, but contribute to the Accommodation of the Public, and the Ornament of the Capital; — Consider-tions which, undoubtedly, are confident with the Dignity of the Crown, and which it becomes the Duty of those who are entrusted with the Management of its Estate to attend to.

Those Alterations and Improvements cannot, however, be rapidly made; because, in most of the instances of this Nature, there is some existing Lease to interrupt or delay the Execution. All that can be done is, to fix on the Plan of Improvement, and to take Care that no Lease be granted to counteract it; so that the Alterations may be begun when the first Leases in those Parts fall in, or when a Re-building becomes necessary, and may proceed gradually, as other Leases shall expire or be surrendered,

- Pursuing this System of Improvement, sundry Memorials have been presented to the Treasury by the Surveyor General, proposing Alterations and Improvements in different Parts of the Town, and in the Lands adjoining to it; and Architects have been invited to offer Plans, some of which have been approved of, and some Progress has been made in carrying them into Effect.

Within the Limits of the ancient Palace of Whitehall there is a considerable Space of Ground, partly open, and partly covered with Houses, many of which are old and ruinous, and which are held during Pleasure, yielding no Rent to the Crown, but attended with an Expence to support them. By removing those Houses, and granting Leases of the Ground for building, according to a Plan proposed to the Treasury by the Surveyor General, the Crown would obtain Rents to a very considerable Amount, and that would be made one of the most beautiful Quarters of the Town. The House and Office built for the Surveyor General, are the Beginning of an intended Street leading to the River, and opening a View of Saint Paul's and Black-friar's Bridge.

The Crown is possessed of a large Estate, formerly called Marybone Park, adjoining on the South to Portland Place and Harley Street; over which it is probable that, on the Return of Peace, the Town may be extended.

In consequence of a Report of the Surveyor General, relative to the Steps to be taken for the Improvement

Vojl. 53. ' '

of that Estate, he has been authorized by the Treasury to offer a considerable Reward to any Architect who shall produce a Plan for an Addition to the Town in that Quarter, which, after being laid before His Majesty, shall be adopted; and, with this View, a very accurate Plan has been taken of that Ground, and an Engraving has been made of it, in order that Copies may be given to such Architects as may be willing to offer Plans for the proposed Improvements. The Extent is no less than 543 Acres, and the Situation and Form of the Ground extremely beautiful; and if the Plan adopted shall be such as to induce Builders to give a Preference to that Situation, a great Part of it may be covered with valuable Houses at no very distant Period, and yield an Income which it would, at present, seem extravagant to mention.

The Crown had been in the Practice of granting Grants of Licences during Pleasure to the Proprietors of Houses adjoining to the Parks, to inclose small Pieces of confident Ground for their Accommodation, reserving Rents of with the Act j only a few Shillings a Year, by Way of Acknowledgment,. for the Preservation of the Crown's Right to the *

Ground; and on these there were several Examples of Bow Windows, or other Buildings having been raised, in Addition to the adjoining Houses. Grants of this Kind did not seem to be confident with the Spirit Of the Act of Parliament lately passed for the Improvement of the Crown's Estate; nor did the Property noradvan-held under them seem to be put into a State that could w tk '

be advantageous to any of the Parties interested. The Crown received little or no Rent for it; the Continuance of the Grant, after it had been made, was considered as no Favour; and the Resumption would have been felt as an Injury: The Property being held by no certain or legal Tenure, would not, on a Sale, bring any considerable Price; and it could not be agreeable to the Possessors to hold Property dependent on the Will of another, however small the Chance might be of its being resumed.

With the View to put an End to a Practice liable to so many Objections, the Surveyor General addressed a Representation to the Treasury on this Subject; proposing that all Persons who had such Grants should be informed that they might have Leases on Conditions authorized by the Act. This Suggestion having been adopted, Applications were very soon made by the Proprietors of all the Houses adjoining to the Green for Leases of those Gardens which have been since inclosed at their Charge; and, in consequence of this Improvement, the Houses on that Side of the Park are rendered much more pleasant, the Inhabitants are accommodated, the Park is ornamented, and Rents to the Amount of about jf. 400 a Year are added to the Land Revenue of the Crown, without incurring any Expence whatever.

At the West End of Piccadilly, adjoining to Hyde Parky the Houses in Hamilton Street, which are in a ruinous State, are intended to be removed, and the Ground appropriated to the building of one Row of Houses, of a Size fit for that Situation, preserving the View over the Park, by preventing any thing from being raised to the West that might obstruct the Pro-speft; and at the upper End of that Row, and behind all the Houses from thence to the Gate into Hyde Park, the Inhabitants are to be accommodated with Gardens, similar to those in the Green Park; and the Increase of Rent, in consequence of these Alterations, will be very considerable.

A more parti-, cular Description of those intended Improvements is purposely avoided here, left it might have the Effect of mcreasing the Difficulties which stand in the Way of their being soon accomplished, by inducing the present Holders of the Leases to demand unreasonable Conditions, as the Price of their Concurrence in the Plans proposed.

An Example of this Kind of Improvement is now going on in the Street called Street (formerly

called Shug Lane) which is a very great Thoroughfare for Carriages from the Houses of Parliament, the Theatres, etc. to the principal Streets and Squares in the North West Quarter of the Town, and to the Crown's Estate of Marybone Park. That Street was so narrow and irregular as to occasion frequent Interruptions, and great Inconveniencies, both to the Inhabitants and to Passengers. In order to remove those In donveniencies, the Whole of one Side of the Street being the Property of the Crown, and the Houses very old, it was directed by the Treasury, on the Recommendation of the Surveyor General, that on renewing the Leases, the Houses should be rebuilt, and the Fronts let back, so as to widen the Street Ten feet. More than Half of that Side of the Street is already rebuilt on this improved Plan, partly in consequence of the Expiration of former Leases, and partly by Treaty with the Tenants for the Surrender or Renewal of Leases which had several Years to run. This has been effected without any other Expence to the Crown than the small Sum of £. 90, towards making a new Common Sewer; and Arrangements are making for completing that Improvement, so soon as the remaining Leases shall expire, or the Parties can be treated with on reasonable Terms for rebuilding the rest of the Houses.

It is obvious that this Improvement, and others which the Surveyor General is attempting in the same Line, must tend to increase the Value of the great Extent of Building Ground belonging to the Crown, by rendering the Communications with the Parts before mentioned more easy and convenient; and, if the same Mode of Proceeding shall be continued, and uniform Attention shall be given, these Objects may be accomplished with very little Expence, and the Rents of the Crown's Estate be greatly increased.

The postponing of the granting of Leases in those Districts at present under Lease, and in which Alterations are intended to be made, but where it shall be found difficult to make Arrangements with the Lessees on reasonable Conditions, can be of no Disadvantage to the Crown. Leases of Houses are allowed by the Act of Parliament to be renewed at any Time within Twenty Years of the Expiration of the existing Terms; and it is immaterial to the Crown at what Time, prior to the End of a subsisting Lease, a new Lease shall be granted. No Loss can arise from deferring a Renewal, except to the Officers, who, being paid by Fees, may suffer by the Delay.

Leases of Land Estates are not allowed to be renewed till within Five Years of the End of the existing Terms, except for erecting new Buildings, or for some other Purpose of Improvement; and no Renewal has been applied for of any very considerable Estate, since the passing of the Act; so that no great Improvement can yet have arisen from the Renewal of Leases of Property of that Nature.

In Rockingham Forest, which contains Three Bailiwicks, each subdivided into several Walks, there are large Tracts of Woodlands which formerly belonged to the Crown, but which have long been alienated in Perpetuity. Those Woodlands, however, remained subject to the Pasturage of the King's Deer, and the Cattle of the Commoners; and in One of the Walks, the Oak Trees of a certain Size are excepted to the Crown, though the Underwood and the Soil of the Woodlands are granted in Fee. The Offices of Forester or Keeper of the different Walks are also granted in Perpetuity; and in each Walk there are inclosed Pasture Lands called Lawns, in the Whole of considerable Extent, appropriated to the Feeding and Preservation of the Deer, and not subject to Rights of Common.

These Lawns are possessed by the Keepers of the respective Districts; and, in some of them, the Soil and entire Property of the Land are claimed by the Grantee of the Keeperships, though the Custody only is considered to be granted. Ia the Walks of Sulehay and

In the Forest of Sherwood the Forestrial Rights belonging to His Majesty extend over large Tracts of Commons and other Lands, of which the Soil does not belong to the Crown; and Acts have been passed for the Division and Inclosure of Lands in Eight different Parishes within the Bounds of the Forest, and for setting out Allotments of Land in Compensation for the Forestrial Rights.

The different Acts which have been passed since the Appointment of the present Surveyor General, for the Division and Inclosure of Lands within Manors belonging to the Crown, and for the Drainage, Embankment, Improvement, Exchange, and Sale of Lands, making Navigable Canals, and other Purposes, in which the Interests of the Crown are concerned, and which were referred from the Treasury to the Surveyor General, for his Confutation and Report, previously to His Majesty's Consent being given thereto, are enumerated in a Schedule annexed to this Report. Among them are several which embrace Objects of considerable Magnitude, and which are likely to be productive of much Benefit to the Country, and Improvement to the Land Revenue; particularly the Act for the Inclosure of the Commons and Waste Grounds in the Isle of Axholme, in the County of Lincoln, which contain about 12,000 Acres, estimated to be worth not less than 20 s. per Acre, and considered to be improveable to more than Twice that Amount.

Many Applications for Leases having been made to the Treasury, and referred to the Surveyor General, he proceeded upon them according to the Directions of the Ad, and the Rules laid down by the Treasury. He ordered Surveys to be taken, and verified on Oath; and made such Enquiries as were necessary to enable him to judge whether any Alteration would tend to the Improvement of the Property; and on many of these Applications, on which the Surveys and Enquiries have been completed, he has reported to the Treasury the State of Fads, and the Value of the Premisses, with his Opinion on what Terms and Conditions such Leases might be granted

In the official Course of proceeding in granting Leases from the Crown, after the Terms and Conditions on which a Lease shall be granted have been approved by the Treasury, a Warrant is issued from that Board, directing the Surveyor General to make forth a Con-fcat, or lend to the proper Auditor for a Particular of ‘the Premiil'es, and to rate the fame, in order to the passing of the Leaie; and to suggest what Covenants Clauses, and Provisoes, are proper to be inserted therein. The Constat, or Particular, and an Instrument called The Rate, in which are specified the Term of Years, the Rent, and the Fine, or other Consideration for granting the Lease, together with the Covenants ;and Conditions judged proper to be inserted, are transmitted by the Surveyor General to the Treasury, and fjom thence to the Clerk of the Pipe, with another

Report of the Surveyor General, in Answer to a Reference from the Treasury, transmitting the Opinion of the Attorney and Solicitor General on certain Clauses of the Act for the better Management of the Land Revenue, and directing him to report what Alterations in the said Act might be advisable to be submitted to the Consideration of Parliament - - 226

' ' N° 1. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of

His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

Though it is not advisable that Leases of the de-miled Estates of the Crown should be renewed, until an improved System of Management shall be adopted, except in Cafes where the Property would materially suffer by the Delay of a Renewal, it is undoubtedly expedient that such Steps should, in the mean Time, be taken, as may enable those who shall be entrusted with the future Management to proceed in carrying it into Effect as speedily as possible.

With this View 1 submit what follows to the Consideration of your Lordships:

The Crown is possess'ed of an Estate in Houses in London and Westminster of very great Value, and comprehending many entire Streets. Of this Estate there is no accurate general Plan in my Office, though there are detached Plans of almost every Part of it: But these Plans give no View of the relative Connection between the different Parts of the Estate. A general Plan could not, indeed, be necessary, under the System of Management which has been followed. , The Idea of any Improvement of the Property, by an Enlargement or Alteration of the Streets, a Removal of any Buildings irregularly situated, the Opening of any new Access to them, or altering the Size or the Number of the Houses, so as to accommodate them to the Demand, or the Taste of the Times, seems not to have occurred, or, if it did occur, to have been deemed impracticable.

The Changes, indeed, which have taken place in the Manner of leafing this Part of the Property of the Crown have had an opposite Tendency, and have rendered any such Improvement much more difficult.

Formerly a considerable Number of Houses, often entire Streets, and, in some Instances, several Streets, were granted in One Lease; and these reverting together to the Crown, Alterations of the Nature which has been ftiggefted, might have been found easily prac-. ticable: But it has happened that in Cafes where a Lessee has fold his Interest in any One or mofe of the Houses comprized in his Lease, the separate Parts of the Property have been considered as distinct Estates; and, partly, from that Consideration, and partly from the natural Effect of the Profit to the Officer of the Crown, by an Increase of their Fees, from an Increase of the Number of Leases, Reversionary Leases of those Parts have been readily made to the Purchasers, whenever they have been applied for, without any Care being taken that the Leases of the different Parts, formerly under One Lease, should terminate at the same Time; and thus, in every such Instance, a new Obstacle has 5

been thrown in the Way of the general Improvement! I am, however, of Opinion, that in some Parts of the Crown's Estate, where the Streets are narrow and in- convenient, and the Openings too few, considerable Improvements may still be made by the Means which have been mentioned.

To prevent, therefore, the Continuance of this Evil, and to remedy it as far as may now be practicable, I would humbly propose to your Lordships, that I may be authorized to cause a General Plan to be made of the Whole of the Crown's Estate in Houses and Building Ground in London and W; and that gra-

dually, or as Applications for Grants or Renewals of Leases shall occur, the Opinion and Report of an Ar-chiteft of Eminence may be obtained, not relative to the State and Value of the Property applied for only, but to the Street in which it is situated, and to the Improvements which are practicable under the existing Circumstances, and advisable on the Part of the Crown. In every future Report by the Surveyor General, or by the Office entrusted with -the Care of this Part of the Property of the Crown, relative to any Grant or Renewal of a Lease, Reference will naturally be made to the Opinion of the Architect who has been employed, and a Copy of so much of it as may be necessary', will, in the usual Course of Proceeding, be transmitted to your Lordships with such Report.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

John Fordyce,

July 12 th 1793. Surv1 Gen1.

N 1. (B.)

Sir,

, To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

The Memorial of John Fordyce, Esquire, Surveyor General of His Majesty's Land Revenue:

My Lords,

Your Lordships having, by your Minute dated the 4th Current, signified your Pleasure that eminent Architects should be desired to offer Plans for the General Improvement of the Buildings on the Crown's Estate, and that no Lease should be granted which might be inconsistent with such Improvement, I conceive it to be my Duty now to bring under your Lordships' Consideration the State of the Property of the Crown within the Palace of Whitehall.

Before the Fire, which destroyed the principal Parts of the Palace in the Reign of King , from which

Time it ceased to be a Royal Residence, the Houses and Buildings in the Three Scotland and White-

hall Court, &c. were chiefly occupied by the different Officers and Servants attendant upon the Palace. Afterwards, the Court being removed to Saint James's, Leases were from Time to Time granted of different Parts of the Scite of Whitehall, and Houses erected thereon for the Residence of the Grantees. Nearly the Whole of Privy Garden and Whitehall Court have been thus granted by Lease, and are now held as Part of His Majesty's Land Revenue. Some Leases have also been granted of Parts of Scotland Yards; but the greater Part of the Buildings there, though they ceased, upon the Removal of the Court, to be employed for the Service of the Royal Household, have continued in the Posses-iion of different Officers in the Appointment v of the Lord Chamberlain and Lord Steward.

Upon the Reduction of the Civil List Establishment, in consequence of the Act passed in 1783, several of the Offices with which Houses or Apartments had been held were abolished; and in 1787 an Act was passed for the Sale (among others) of upwards of Twenty different Houses or Tenements in Scotland Yards: But it -being afterwards found that the Sale of those Houses Would be a very great Impediment to the Improvement of the rest of His Majesty's Property in Whitehall, it was deemed advisable not to fell them j and by the Act of the last Session of Parliament for the better Management of the Land Revenue, the Act which authorized the Sale was repealed, and the Houses and Grounds were put under the same Regulations as the rest of the Land Revenue.

In consequence of the Authority given to me by your Lordships' Letter, dated the 20th Day of July 1793, to cause a General Plan to be made, of the Crown's Estate in Houses and Building Ground in London and Westminster, a Map or Ground Plan has been made of -the Property of the Crown in; which is of

.considerable Extent and great Valuer though, in its present State, it yields little Advantage to the Public j and 1 humbly propose to your Lordships; that I may be authorized to lay Copies of the Map, which I have mentioned, before Architects eminent in their Proses-fion, for their Information and Assistance, and to offer a Reward of £.200 to the Person who shall produce -such Plans and Elevations for new Streets and Buildings in Whitehall and Scotland Yards, as shall meet with lyour Lordships' Approbation.

Those Architects should be instructed to -form their <Plans in such a Manner as not to affect the principal and most substantial of the Houses now Handing in this Part of the Crown's Estate, nor render the Access to them less commodious; but to pay no Regard to Houses or Buildings which are in a ruinous State, or of little Value, and which may be found to £kand in the Vox.. 53.

Way of the belt Plan for the Ornament, Accommodation, and Improvement of that Quarter of the Town. If, in consequence of the Alterations which may take place, in carrying into Execution the Plan which may be adopted, any same of particular Hardship shall arise,

I shall think it my Duty, in pursuance of the Spirit and Principle of your Lordships' Minute, to state the Circumstances to the Board of Treasury, that your Lordships may be enabled to judge of the Compensation to which the Parties may be entitled.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

John Fordyce,

Surv' Gen1,

May it please your Lordships, .

In obedience to your Lordships' Commands, signified to toe by Mr. Long's Letter of the 14th Current, ! have coolidered the Proposal of the Duke of to relinquish his Rights of Way through Park, and to give a Piece of Land; Tart of his Grace's -Farm at Barrow Hills, in exchange for an Acre and a Half of Land on the North Side of the Road opposite -to Nottingham Place', and for a Slip of Land, i,6od Yards in Length; and 54 Feet, Or 18 Yards, in Breadth, computed in the Proposal; and on the Plan which accompanied it; to contain about, or nearly. Two Acres, but which, according to my Computation, contains 5a. . 3X. 32P. or nearly Six Acres. Both of these Pieces of Land are Parts of the said Estate, called Marybone Park, belonging to His Majesty;

The Objects of the Duke of Portland are stated in -the Proposal to be, to provide a Situation for a new Parish Church for the Parish of Marybone, on the Piece of Ground containing an Acre and an Half; and to make a Road on the Slip of Land, to communicate with a Spot of Ground now belonging to the Duke, and intended for a new Burying Ground.

This being the First Time in which I have been, called upon, since my Appointment as Surveyor Ge->

neral, to give an Opinion tin any pfoptifed Alteration or Improvement of any of the Estates of the Crown, I think it proper to observe to your Lordships, that until the Reports of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue shall have been considered, and a Plan for the future Management adopted-, I shall think it my Duty to keep in View the System of Management and Improvement which they have.recommended. But as they thought it right, for Reasons which they have assigned, to make their Reports on the Grown Lands general, and not to give a minute Description of each Estate, or of the particular Gircumstances to be attended to in the Improvement of it, and as this is one of the most valuable and improveable of the demised Estates now belonging to the Crown, I think it necessary to be more full in this Report than the Circumstances stated in the Proposal may, on the first View, seem to require.

I have perused all the Papers within my Power relative to this Estate, and have often personally viewed it as well during the Time that the Landed Estates of the Crown were under my Consideration, as Ohe of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue, as in conseqtience of the Reference which your Lordships have now made to me.

Marybone Park is situated in the Parishes of Saint Mary-le-bone and Saint Pancrai, and extends from Alsop

Street, and the Buildings on Mr. Estate,

Northward of Portman Square, on the West, nearly to Tottenham Court Road on the East; the great New Road From Paddington to Islington, made about 27 Years ago, pafftis through it; and Portland Charlotte

Portland Place, Harley Street, Devonshire Place, -bone High Street, and Nottingham Place, abut on it on the Soutlf; and every one of the Streets which lead Northward from Oxford Street, if continued in the fame

Direction, would pass through it; on the North, towards Hampstead, it extends to the Bottom of

Hill-, and the whole contains, by a Survey made in 1753, 554 a. -r. 13P., and isTythe free.

This Estate was formerly kept as a Park, in the Possession of the Crown, flocked with Deer; and was full of valuable Timber. A Particular of it, taken from a Survey made during the Usurpation of Crdmwell, is preserved in my Office. ' Soon after the Restoration it was granted for 65 Years to Sir Henry Bennett, Secretary of State, afterwards Earl of Arlington, at a Rent of £.36. 14 s.6d. without any Fine, after a Report of Sir Charles Harbord, then Surveyor General, in which he stated that a Lease of it for 31 Years was worth £. 6,000 in Fine, referring a Rent of £.200 a Year.

The Whole was comprehended under One Lease, and many subsequent Renewals took place, - to different Pe rfons, at the same reserved Rent, but for different Fines, until the Year 1764, when, at the Delire of Mrs. Lucy Jacomb and Mr. Jacob Hittde, who were at that

Time Joint Tenants in a Lease ending 24th July 1785, a new Lease was granted of Fifteen Twenty-fourth . Parts of the Estate to Mrs. Jacomb, for a Rever-

lionary Term of Ten Years, reserving a Yearly Rent of £.22. 19s.-, and at the same Time another Rever-lionary Lease was granted to Jacob Hinde of the remaining Nine Twenty-fourth Parts of the Estate, for the tfame Term of Years, reserving a Rent of £. 13. 15 r. 6 d.

To both these Leases jk Years were added in 1772,

' to commence from the 24th July 1793; and the Rents, according to an Alteration adopted a short Time before in the Management of the demised Estates, were increased to £.96.. 3 J. 4 d.for the Fifteen Twenty-fourth

-.Parts, and £. 57. 13 s.ii{d. for the Nine Twenty-fourth Parts.

And in 1780 a ReverOonary Term of Eight Years, to commence in 1803, was granted to Jacomb of the Fifteen Twenty-fourth Parts, reserving the same Rent of £. 96. 35. \d. -, but Hinde, the Lessee of the remaining Nine Twenty-fourth Parts, being a Lunatic, no Renewal was obtainedfoifhim. . -.: , .....j

The Lease to Jacomb has been lately purchased by the Duke of Portland. ' ' '

The Estate is undivided, and is all let to One Sub-Tenant, whole Lease, I am, informed, expires in 1803, being 1 \ Year after the Termination of the Lease to Hinde, and Six Years before the End of that bought by the Dlike of Portland.

This undivided Property will, therefore, according to the present Leases, be held, in the-Proportions above-mentioned, by the Duke of Portland and Mr. Hinde for pr Yeats, and by the Duke of Portland and the Crown for Eight Years afterwards.

From the Mixture of Rights which has been created by granting Two Leases in an undivided Property, and to One Lessee for a longer Term than to the Other, from the Circumstance of Mr. Hinde having granted a Lease of his Proportion for a longer Term than he had himself obtained from the Crown, as well as from the ancient Mound, or Ring Fence, which was placed round the whole Estate, having, in different Parts, been removed in digging the Foundations of the adjoining Buildings, it is obvious t;hat some Enquiry, and some general Arrangement among the Parties interested, should speedily be made, to prevent Disputes or Embarrass'ment; but it is in this, Instance particularly to be regretted, that the Practice of granting Reversionary Terms should have postponed the great Improvement which may be expected on this valuable Estate to so remote a Period; and Care must be taken not to add to the Embarrass-. ment, or still farther to impede the Improvement; By any previous Proceeding or partial Alteration. ' ‘

The Road proposed to be made by the Duke of Portland would extend along the West Boundary of the Estate for near a Mile, and would cut obliquely through all such Streets, Westward of Nottingham Place, as should be extended over this Estate. This Circumstance, as well as that of the proposed Road being made a Passage to a Burying Ground for so large and populous a Distriift, might perhaps be found to lessen the Value of the Ground for Building to such a Degree, as no Price or Value that could be expected to be given to the Crown for the Land desired would be found sufficient to compensate.

I must therefore humbly recommend, that before agreeing to this or any other Proposal for the Alteration or Disposal of any Part of Mary bone Park, a general Plan should be formed , for the Improvement of the Whole of it, left such partial Alteration should afterwards be found inconiiftent with what should, on full Consideration, and the belt Advice, be deemed most for the Benefit of the Crown.

And, in order to enable your Lordships to determine on the best Information what Plan it would be prudent to adopt, I would humbly propose that I should be authorized to employ a Surveyor to examine the Accuracy of a Plan of Marybone Park, made about 40 Years ago, and now in my Office, and to add to it a general Sketch of the Streets leading to it, and of such of the Lands adjoining to it as appeared to be materially connected with the Improvement of this Property; that an Engraving should be made of that PJari, which I apprehend might be done at no great Expence; that One of the engraved Plans should be given to every Architect of Eminence in London, and that a considerable Reward should be given to the Person who should produce such a Plan for an Addition to the Town on those Grounds, as, after having been laid before His Majesty and your Lordships, should be adopted. Such Archite&s as may be willing to offer Plans should be'desired not only to delineate the Streets, Squares, public Buildings, and the Course of the Sewers, but to suggest also the Means of providing a Supply of Wattir for the Inhabitants, the Scarcity of which is already complained of in the new Streets in that Quarter. i

The Expence of obtaining a Plan in this Manner would idoubtless-.be amply compensated by the additional

To the Right Honoumbic the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

Mr. Long, by his Letter of the lift of April, has transmitted to me a Memorial of Robert Esquire,

praying His Majesty's Permission to extend the Iron' Railing in the Green Park, before his House in James's Place, to range in a Line with the Rails before the House of Lord Viscount Malden, and to erect a Bow Window to projeCl into the Park as far as his present Bow Window, and desired that I would slate, for the Information of your Lordships, in what Manner it ought to be carried into Execution.

I find by the Entries in my Office, that Mr. Smith's House is built partly on Freehold Ground, and partly on a Piece of Ground belonging to the Crown, containing 16 Feet 5 Inches in Front or Breadth towards the Park, and 29 Feet 7 Inches in Length from Eaffc to West; that the last mentioned Piece of Ground is held under a Lease from the Crown, granted 4th January 1753, to Sir John Cope, Baronet, for a Term of which Nine Years were unexpired on the 4th of January last at a Rent of 40 Shillings per Annum; and that the Area in the West Front of the House was inclosed from the Park, and a Bow Window erected on Part of it, by virtue of a Licence from his late Majesty, by Warrant under the Hands of the Lords Justices, dated the 13th of June 1745, to hold during his Majesty's Pleasure i which Licence having expired on the Demise of his late Majesty, and not having been renewed, the Bo\v Window, with the Area in the Park, have been held from that Time without any Title or Authority, and without the Payment of any Rent or Acknowledgment.

I have caused the annexed Plan to be taken, which describes both the Ground comprized in the Lease to Sir John Cope, and that which was granted during his late Majesty's Pleasure, and also the additional Ground now desired to be taken from the Park, and the Extent of the proposed new Bow Window.

On former Applications- for Leave to inclose small Pieces of Ground from the Parks, for the Accommodation of adjacent Houses, Licences have usually been granted by Warrant under the King's Sign Manual, to hold during His Majesty's Pleasure, reserving a Rent of 20 Shillings a Year, or other small Sum, as an Acknowledgment, and for the Preservation of the Right of the Crown; and there are several Examples of Buildings, in Addition to adjoining Houses, having been raised on Ground held under such Grants: But an Act . having recently passed for the better Management of the Land Revenue of the Crown, it becomes more particularly my Duty to suggest any Objections which may occur to me, to the Continuance of any Practice, however long established, which appears to be either contrary to the Spirit of that Act, inexpedient in itself, or hurtful to the Crown's Estate; and to recommend such Rules of Proceeding, as it may be prudent in every similar same to pursue.

By the Provisions in the Act, Ground may be let for Building, for any Term not exceeding 99 Years, or Three Lives; and such Rent must be referred as the Lords of the Treasury shall deem a reasonable Rent or Consideration for the lame: But there is nothing in the Act which can be understood to authorize "a Licence to build on a Grant during Pleasure, reserving an inadequate Rent; neither would it seem to be expedient to grant such Licences for Building, even if the Act could be construed to admit of it.

Where a permanent Building is erected, and a confi derable Expence is incurred, on a Grant expressed to be relumable at the Will of the Proprietor, some Con 3 D fidenct

194 n° Januarii. . 1798.

fidence in the Grantor, or some (ecret Understanding mud be suppofld to exist, which would always give Rife to Complaints against the Crown, if the Grant should be resumed, and against the Officer who should think it his Duty to recommend, either that the Rent should be increased, or that a Period should be put to the Grant.

The Property seems, indeed, to be put by such Grants into an unprofitable State for all the Parties interested :-The Crown receives little Advantage in Point of Revenue; the Continuance of the Grant, after it has been made, is thought to be no Favour; the Resump-tion Would be felt to be an Injury; and the Grantee, if he should desire to fell his Interest, would find that a Purchaser would not give any considerable Price for Property held by no legal or certain Tenure; besides that it cannot? be agreeable to hold Property entirely at the Will of another, however small the Chance may be of its being resumed.

That your Lordships may have a jud View of the Grants of this Kind which have been made, and may be enabled to judge of their Expediency from pad Experience, I shall subjoin to this Report a Lid of all the Grants during Pleasure that now exid, with their Dates, and the Rents payable for them, divided into Two Clares, the one containing those on which Buildings hive been raised, and the other those used only as Garden or Pleasure Ground. From the Date of some of those Warrants during Pleasure, it appears that they have been held for a much longer Time than could have been granted by Lease under the Civil Lid Act of Queen Anne., and without the Payment of any Rent or Fine; and dill it would be thought a Hardship even now to resume them.

If it shall, therefore, be His Majesty's Pleasure to grant the Favour desired by Mr. , I would humbly recommend that an Edimate may be made by Surveyors, in the Manner directed by the Act of Parliament recently passed, of the Ground comprized in the Lease to Sir John Cope, and of that granted during his late Majesty's Pleasure, and also of the additional Ground now desired to be taken from the Park; and that One Lease may be granted of the Whole; for such Term as may be deemed proper, when the State of the House already built on Part of the Premifies, the Nature of the proposed Addition, and other relative Circumstances, have been considered, reserving such Rent as your Lordships shall think a reasonable Consideration for the fame: And I would farther, with great Deference, propose that the same Mode of Proceeding should be followed in all similar Applications; and that those Persons who have already erected Buildings of any Importance on Grants during Pleasure, may be informed that they may have Leases on similar Conditions.

But though Leases may be granted in all Cases of this Nature, where any valuable Building has been erected, as the Regulations proposed for abolishing Fees have not yet been adopted, the same Alteration, however de-firable, cannot be made on Grants during Pleasure where there are no valuable Buildings erected, or proposed to be erected, on Account of the present Expence of Crown Leases.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

John,

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

Applications having been made to your Lordships by Lord Grenville and Mr. Errington, the Duke of Bridge-

water, Earl Spencer, Mr. Smith, Lord Malden, and the

Marquis of Salisbury, for separate Grants of small Portions of Ground in the Green Park, near to their different Houses, I have, in obedience to your Lordships' Orders of Reference, taken their Memorials into Consideration, and have referred also to the Act ktely passed for the better Management of the Land Revenue, and to the Rules which your Lordships have been pleased to establish for the Regulation of my Proceeding, in Cafes where not only the private Accommodation of Petitioners, but the more general Improvement or Embellishment of the adjoining Property of the Crown, may be in question. \

The Parties making these Applications are all Proprietors of Houses situated on the East Side of the Green Park. The Objects set forth in their Memorials or Petitions are to remove certain low Buildings or Sheds, which are applied to Purposes which'render them extremely offer.five to the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Houses; to construct subterraneous Offices; or to have Flower Gardens on the Portions of Ground applied for which would not only be a great Accommodation to them, and an Ornament to their Property, but would keep the Cattle, and Persons frequenting the Parks, at a greater Diflunce from their Windows, and at the same Time preserve the View over the Park.

In the Line with those Houses there are various others which would, in the same Manner, be benefited by similar Allotments: But the Improvement of that Side of the Park would be incomplete, unless the Plan should be made general; and it is probable that all the Proprietors will apply to your Lordships for such Grants as soon as they shall see the Effect of the proposed Improvement.

I thought it right, therefore, to view the Ground with Lord Evjion, the Ranger of the Park, and to point

out to his Lordship the general Line of Inclosure which would, in my Opinion, be most conducive to the Beauty of the Park, and at the same Time give to the Parties applying all the Advantages they desired; and that Line having met with his complete Approbation, I ordered an accurate Plan to be made of the Whole of that Side of the Park, in its present State, with the low Buildings and Sheds which it is proposed to remove, and directed th.e Surveyors to delineate upon it, not only the general Boundary of the proposed Inclosures, but also the particular Limits and Dimensions of each Allotment. That Plan will be laid before your Lordships with this Report, in order that the Inconveniences from;which each particular House will be relieved, and the Advantages it will acquire by the intended . Alteration, may be under View at the Time that the Rents proposed to be reserved are taken into Consideration, so that a Judgment may be formed, whether they are such as the late Act requires, namely, a reasonable Consideration for the Grant or Lease, and whether they are rated in a just Proportion to each other.

To guide the Surveyors in estimating the Allotments, as far as it was right for me to do so, by pointing out the Principles which they should have in View, I directed that in no Instance the Rents to be proposed for the Ground to be now taken from the Park, should exceed the additional Value which they should be of Opinion the Houses would acquire by having those Allotments annexed to them; and no other Instruction than tfiis appeared to be requisite in estimating the Ground to be granted to Lord Grenville, Part of which the Surveyors have valued at .1 s. a Foot in Front, and the Remainder at ior. a Foot, making a Rent of £.33. t8r. 4 d.per Annum: But it became necessary to give farther Instructions with respect to the Parts lying opposite to the Property of the Duke of Bridge-water, and to a Part of that of Earl Spencer, where those Houses and Sheds are situated, which are justly complained of as a Nuisance to the Dwellings near them, but which are of some Value to the Crown; for other

Under these Circumstances, in order to give your Lordships a distinct View of the Plan, which I mean to propose, as well for the Preservation or Increase of the Beauty of the Park, as for the Accommodation of the noble Petitioners; and at the same Time to enable your Lordships more ealily to judge whether the Rent to be proposed is that " reasonable Consideration" which is required by the Act of Parliament, I thought it necessary to direct the Surveyors to make Two Designs, one for building Dwelling Houses upon that Ground, and another for Stables and Coach Houses, each to be lb situated as to be as little inconvenient as possible to the neighbouring Houses; and to estimate what Ground Rent the Crown might easily obtain for either.

In pursuance of those Instructions, the Surveyors have made a Plan for the Building of Dwelling Houses, and a Valuation, certified on Oath, in which they estimate the Part of this Ground, proposed to be granted to the Duke of Bridgewater, at 30 j. Foot, making a Rent of £.98. 5 s.; and the Part of the Ground pro- posed to be granted to Earl , which is now cover-

ed with low Buildings, but which has more Depth than the Duke of Bridgwater's, at 35 per Foot, making a Rent of £. 136. 18 r 9 d.per Annum; and they have sent a Plan also, and a Valuation, on Oath, of the same Ground, disposed of for the Purpose of building Stables and Coach Houses, where the Ground Rent of the Duke of Bridgeivater's Part of this Plot is 125. per Foot,

- making a Rent of £-39- 6s. and the Ground Rent of Earl Spencer's Part is i8r. p Foot, making a Rent of

£.70. 8r. 6 d.

Taking all the Circumstances into Consideration, I beg leave, with great Deference, to submit to your Lordships, whether it may not be a reasonable Arrangement between the Crown and those noble Persons, that the Grants should be made to them reserving the lowest of those Rents, namely, the Rent for the Ground disposed of as for Stables; and that they should be, at the same Time, restrained from erecting any Buildings higher than the present Surface, or from applying the Surface to any other Use than that of ornamental Gardens.

By this Arrangement the Crown would, for the Sake of embellishing the Park, and of adding to the Accommodation of the Duke of Bridgewater and Earl Spencer, make a Sacrifice of the Difference between that Rent and the higher Rent for Dwelling Houses, reserving at ithe same Time such a Rent as might, according to the Spirit and Principle of the late Act of Parliament, be reckoned a reasonable Consideration for the Grant; and though theft noble Persons would give up the Advantage which might arlfe to them, as Lessees under the Crown, from building Stables and Coach Houses, yet their own Houses would, by that Sacrifice on their Part, be rendered more plealant and beautiful, and consequently of greater Value.

If this Plan should be adopted, I would humbly propose that the exterior Fence of the whole Inclosure should be a plain simple Iron Rail, all of an uniform Plan, and the Divisions between the Allotments a Fence of the same Kind; and that the erecting of any Buildings or Walls on any Part of the Ground, and the planting of any Thing that may impede the View or Prospect from any of the Houses, should be strictly prohibited.

If the Plan shall be completely executed, it will, I humbly apprehend, prove a very great Ornament to the Park, and produce a considerable Addition to the Land Revenue: A very ftnall Expence will be. incurred, and a Fund provided for defraying a Part of the Charge which the Crown sustains, of keeping the Parks, and the Roads, and Walks in them, in Repair, for the Benefit ‘ of the Public $ while the Grantees, by converting the Ground into ornamental Gardens, bounded only by an Iron Rail between their Houses and the public Walk,

will

will add to the Beauty of the Situation: the Nuisances and offensive Circumstances which they have complained of will be removed, their Residence rendered more pleasant and undisturbed, and the Value of their Property increased, much beyond the Amount of the Rents which the Surveyors have put on their different Allotments.'

Most of the Proprietors of Houses on that Side of the Park are already possessed of small Slips of Ground, inclosed from the Park, under Licences from His Majesty, or the late King, which are edmprized in the Valuations made by the Surveyors, and will, of course, be included in any Leases that may be granted j and some of them also hold their Houses under Leases from the Crown, and are desirous of renewing the m. I have not thought it necessary to state thele Circumstances minutely in this Report; but if your Lordships shall so far approve of the general Plan here proposed, as to think it proper to lay it before His Majesty, for His Royal Pleasure thereon, and His Majesty shall be graciously pleased to direct it to be carried into Execution, I shall make separate Reports, consistently therewith, on such Applications as have already been referred, or which may afterwards be referred to me, by your Lordships, from any of the Proprietors of the Hdufes adjoining to the proposed Improvements.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

N° 6. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury. '

My Lords,

I think it necessary to represent to your Lordships, that the Street called Tichborne Street (late Lane) with Part of Marybone Street (being a principal Avenue from the middle and lower Parts of the Town to Golden Square, Hanover Square, Oxford , and the numerous

Streets and Squares in their Vicinity, and forming a Part of the most direct Communication from the Houses of Parliament and Westminster , to the principal Streets in the upper Part of Marybone) is at present very narrow and incommodious, so as not only to occasion frequent Stoppages of Carriages, and other Inconveniences, but likewise to affect the Value of the Property, both in these Two Streets, and in others with which they communicate.

The Houses on the North Side of Street

are private Property, belonging to different Owners. The Whole of the South Side-of that Street and both Sides of Marybone Street, Air , Vine , and other adjacent Streets, belong to the Crown. The Crown is also possessed of a large and valuable Estate at Marybone, formerly called Marybone , adjoining to the Ends of Harley Street and Portland , and very advantageously situated for building. The widening and improving of Tichbornt Street and Marybone Street would, therefore, I apprehend, not only increase the Value of the Crown's Estate in that Neighbourhood, but at the same Time, by improving the Access to the Marybone Park Estate, would tend to enhance the Value of that Property, by affording additional Inducements to build thereon. 1

In order to promote Objects so desirable, I directed . the Surveyors, employed in this Department, to form a Plan for widening Tichborne Street and Marybone,

to examine the State of the Buildings, and report their Opinion on the Subject. A Copy of the Plan is transmitted herewith for your Lordships Inspection; and the Surveyors have certified that all the Houses on the South Side of Tichborne Street are very old and flight Buildings, and some of them in a ruinous Condition;

and have recommended that the Whole should be rebuilt, and the Fronts set back, so as to widen the Street to the Breadth of about 40 Feet; and they have valued the Remainder of the Ground to be let on Building Leases, at Ground Rents which exceed what the Houses have hitherto produced, by the Rents and Fines for former Leases.

Some of the Houses in Marybone Street within the Limits of the proposed Plan arc at present substantial, and do not require to be rebuilt; but these are situated in a Part of the Street where the Alteration may be deferred with the least Inconvenience to the Public or Prejudice to the Estate of the Crown. There are, indeed} but few Examples where any extensive Plan for the Improvement of the Estate of the Crown in London can be carried at once into complete Effect, without incurring greater Expence, or making greater Sacrifices, than I should think it prudent to recommend. My Intention, therefore, is to propose that those Plans, if approved of when laid before your Lordships, shall be gradually executed, as the Terms of the Leases expire; and I accordingly earnestly recommend to your Lordships the Adoption of this Plan for the Improvement of Tichborne Street, by which the Public will acquire the Benefit of having a much frequented Thoroughfare materially improved, without any Expence, or Sacrifice of Income, on the Part of tire Crown, and with a Prospect of very confulcrable Advantage to the Land Revenue, from its Influence on other Parts of that Estate; and as it happens that Nine of the Houses in Tichborne Street are now out of Lease, arrd the Lessees of several others have applied to renew their Leases, and are willing to concur in the proposed Plan for widening the Street, the present is a favourable Time for beginning this Improvement.

This Plan will be connected with another Advantage to the Neighbourhood, by the Continuation of the new Sewer recommended by me to be built in Tichborne Street and Marybone Street, and already in Part executed (as Hated in my Report of the 12th last on the Petition of James Taber) the Remainder of which Sewer it is proposed should be built, progressively, by the Persons to whom new Leases shall be granted of the Property of the Crown in those Streets.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

John Fordyce,

'31st May 1796. Surv'Gen1.

N 6. (B.)

Sir,

Having laid before the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury your Report of 31st of May last, submitting to their Lordships a Plan for improving and widening Tichborne Street, with Part of Mary ben: Street, which you propose shall be gradually executed as the Leases expire, and will, as you apprehend, increase the Value of the Crown's Estate; and suggesting that as several of the Lessees have applied to renew their'Leases, and are willing to concur in the proposed Plan, the present is a favourable Time for beginning this Improvement; I am commanded by my Lords to acquaint you that they approve of the said Plan being carried into Execution, in the Manner suggested by you.

I am,

Sir,

Upon the bed Judgment I am able to form of the whole Matter, I humbly conceive that the remaining Rights of the Crown, within the Walks of Sulehay and More hay, are as follows:

1. The Right to the Timber Trees in Sulehay

according to the Exception in the Grant of 13 Elizabeth.

In the Year 1764, the then Earl of for the Sum of £. 1,710, purchased of the Crown 2,750 Trees within this Walk, which were reported to be the whole Number of the Timber Trees then Handing on the Premisses, exclusive of Saplings liicely to become Timber. Some of those Trees are claimed by Lord Westmorland to be still Handing; but all such Trees as have become Timber since that Sale, and the Right to such as shall hereafter become Timber, arc admitted to belong to the Crown; and for these Lord Westmorland v agrees to pay an adequate Price in Money.

2. The Right to the Deer, and to Herbage and

Deer Browse in the Woodlands in both Walks, from the End of the subsisting Lease of the Herbage and Deer Browse for Three Lives.

Lord Westmorland claims not only to be entitled to the Deer during the Term of that Lease, but to be exempt from any Obligation to leave a Stock of Deer at the End of the Lease, or to restore them afterwards, in case he shall think fit, in the mean Time, to destroy them.

3. The Right to the Lodges, with the Lawns, and

other inclosed Lands, held by virtue of the Grants of the Kecperships.

4. The Right to the Soil of the open Ridings, Plains,

and other uninclosed Lands, and the Herbage thereof for the Deer.

I conceive Lord Westmorland to be entitled, as Forester or Keeper, to the Possession of the Lodges, and the Custody of the Lawns, and other inclosed Lands, applicable only to the Purposes for which the Keeperships were instituted, namely, the Care and Preservation of the Deer; but that the Lands belong to the Crown, subject to his Interest as Keeper and as Lessee of the Herbage and Deer Browse. Lord Westmorland does not admit them to be held under that Title, but claims to be entitled to the Lawns, and all other Lands in both Walks, and to the Ground and Soil thereof, by virtue of the Grants of the Woodlands.

The Matters in Dispute on the Part of the Crown, and of the Earl of Westmorland, are, consequently, the Rights specified under the 2d, 3d, and 4th Heads above Hated: And, in order that they may be submitted to the Consideration of the Arbitrators to whom the Subject may be referred, I have prepared a Statement of the Grants and other Documents on which the Rights in Question are founded; in which Statement are infected the Observations and Arguments advanced on

3

1798 *

Behalf of Lord Westmorland, as delivered to me Irt Writing by his Lordship's Agent, with such Answers thereto, and such Observations and Arguments as occurred to me in Support of the Rights claimed on Behalf of the Crowtl. The Statement is transmitted herewith for your Lordships' farther Orders; and as. this same involves Matter or Law, and the Determination upon it may, in its Consequences, be of consider-able Importance, as establishing Principles on which similar Questions, both in this and other Forests, may hereafter be decided, I submit to your Lordships whether it may not be proper that the Statement should be revised by your Lordships Solicitor, and, if necessary, laid before the Attorney and Solicitor General, to consider of the Propriety of the Arguments used, and to suggest any other that may be proper to be added, previously to the laying the same before the Arbitrators.

Lord Westmorland has named Mr. on his

Part, and your Lordships will be pleased to name the Arbitrator whom you may think fit to appoint on Behalf of the Crown; and when the Decision shall have taken place 1 shall proceed, under your Lordships' Directions, to ascertain the Value of the Rights which shall be determined to belong to the Crown, and submit the same to your Lordships, in order to the fixing the Consideration to be paid for the Grant which Lord 'Westmorland has applied for.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

John Fordyce,
