Land Revenue Office Ofibber 24th, 1794 *

My Lords,

As your Lordships have not yet signified to me your Pleasure as to the Price at which I may, at present, dispose erf Fee Farm Rents, and as new Applications are received every Day for Information on this Subject, and new Offers made to purchase, I think it my Duty to bring the Matter again under your Lord ships' Notice, and humbly to submit to your Lordships' Consideration, whether some general Regulation, as to the Price at which the Surveyor General may be authorized, at all Times, to fell those Rents, may not, with Safety, be established, by fixing the Proportion which the felling Price of those Rents shall, at all Times, bear to the Price of the Funds at the Time of Sale.

For since the Act of Parliament enjoins that the Produce of the Sale of those Rents shall be laid out in the Purchase of Stock, it becomes a Sort of Barter of Rents for Dividends; and it is of little Consequence what the Price of the one i$, if the Proportion to the Price of the other shall be preserved; and this general Regulation will save the Trouble to your Lordships of new Applications from this Office,' for Directions as to the Price of Sale, on every considerable Fluctuation in the Price of the Funds.

I take the Liberty, therefore, to submit to your Lordships' Consideration, whether it may not be' expedient to authorize the Surveyor General to fell Fee Farm Rents, at all Times, when he can obtain such a Price as shall be 10 per Centum at lfeaft higher than the current Price of 3 per Centum Consolidated Bank Annuities at the Time of the Sale.

It is true, that as the greater Part of the Rents are very small, an Alteration in the Price of the Funds may happen after some have been fold, and before the Price shall amount to a Sum sufficient to be inverted in Stock} but this is unavoidable, whether the general Regulation shall be established or not.

By a Sale under this Limitation, the Advantage to Government will be certain and considerable: It will be 10 per Centum, or more, on the Capital; and the Interest will be received Half Yearly, Without Expence or Diminution; whereas the Rents are irregularly paid, much in Arrear, and collected at considerable Expence.

To prevent any Misapprehension of what is meant by proposing to fell at a Price at least 10 per Centum higher than the Price of Stock at the Time of Sale, it may be proper to (late, that in my former Memorial on this Subject, when the Price of Stock was near to 64 per Centum} I proposed that Rents should be sold at

25 Years Purchase, at which Rate a Rent of £.3 would produce £. 75; but £. 64 would purchase £. 3 of Dividends of Consolidated Bank Annuities, which would leave a Profit of £.11 on £.75, or about 14 per Centum.

I have the Honour to be.

My Lords,

Your Lordships'

Most obedient humble Servant,

John,

Surv' Gen.

The Right Honourable

The Lords Commissioners of the Treasury.

N 14. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

Several Applications having been made for Grants or Renewals or Leases from the Crown, in Cafes where VOL. 33.

Houses are proposed to be re-built, or other new Buildings to be erected, it becomes necessary to establish some general Rules for regulating the Extent of Term to be granted by the Crown in the different Cafes of this K.ind now depending, or which may hereafter occur.,

The Act for the better Management of the Land Revenue authorizes the granting of Building Leases for any Term not exceeding 99 Years; but that Term being the longell which the Cr< wn is empowered to grant, or which the Owners of private Estates are in the Habit of granting, for Houses of the largest Size and most expensive Stile of Building, it seems proper to make some Difference in the Terms to be granted for Houses of inferior Value, and, as far as may be practicable, to adapt the Length of the Lease to the Size and Quality of the Building to be erected.

The Act of the Fourteenth of His present Majesty, for the better Regulation of Buildings and Party Walls, specifies Four different Rates or Classes of Dwelling Houses, and the different Degrees of Thickness required, both' for External and Party Walls, in the Houses of-each Ciafs. It is, however, to be observed, that the Degrees of Thickness prescribed by that Act are the least which the Legislature has thought fit to allow of, in regard merely to the Public Security: And it is found that Houses may be built in strict Compliance with that Act, and yet be so flight as to be hardly capable of (landing out the Term of an ordinary Building Lease. The Object and Intent of the Act was. indeed, chiefly to provide against Accidents from Fire } but the Interest of the Ground Landlord requires that Attention should be paid to the Strength and Durability of the Houses, from which alone his Estate can derive any lading Improvement; and for effecting that Object some additional Substance in the Walls is deemed, by experienced Surveyors, to be requisite, beyond what the Building Act absolutely requires.

The shortest Term for which Building Leases are commonly granted, I am informed, is 61 Years; but I understand that the more usual Term is 99 Years, efoe-cially in Leases for the covering of Ground not before built on. In treating with several of the Tenants of the Crown who have applied for Building Leases, I have found them, in general, unwilling to build upon act Years Lease, and Thill more to exceed the Degree of Strength which the Building Act requires, if confined to that Term; and I have found them willing to pay larger Ground Rents on Leases for longer Terms: I am, therefore, of Opinion, that it will be conducive to the permanent Improvement of the Revenue to grant longer Leases, and, in return, to require some additional Substance in the new Buildings. There are, I believe, few, if any, Situations upon the Crown's Estate, where it would be right to permit Houses to be built of so inferior a Kind as those of the Fourth Rate or Ciafs described in the Building Act; and upon con-fulting with the Surveyors employed in this Department,. I have thought it advisable to form Three Classes for Building Leases to be granted by the Crotfn, of different Lengths, according to the Size and Substance required for the Houses in each Cla(s;

First Ciafs, 7 All Houses exceeding Nine Squares Term 99 Years. 3 of Building on the Ground Plan, exclusive of Offices detached from the main Building (each Square containing 100 superficial Feet) and having not less than Four Square Stories, including the JBafement Story.

Second Ciafs, 7 All Houses exceeding Five Squares of Term 80 Years.) Building on the Ground Plan, and not exceeding Nine Squares, and having not lets than Four Square Stories.

3 I Third

214 11° Januarii. A. 1798.

Third Class, ? All Houses not exceedingFive Squares Term 70 Years.,) of Building on the Ground Plan, and having not less than Four Square Stories.

By my Direction, the Surveyors have drawn out a Specification of the different Thicknesses of Walls, Kinds of Materials, and other Particulars, to which the Tenants should be required to conform in the building of Houses of each Class; and which, without adding materially to the Expence of the Buildings, will contribute elsentially to their Strength and Durability, and consequently to the Advantage of the Revenue. A Regulation of this Kind will be conducive likewise to the Accommodation of the Tenants, who will thereby have the Option of taking a Building Lease for either of the Terms specified, by erecting their Buildings of the Size and Substance required for that Term; and if it should happen that a Tenant who proposes to build a House of the Size specified in the Second or Third Class, should w'ifh for a Lease of greater Length than the Term prescribed, I should think it no Detriment to the Crown to grant him the Term proposed for the next higher Class, on Condition of erecting his Building of the Strength required for such Class, it being, as I conceive, of more efl'ential Advantage to the Estate of the Crown to encourage the building of substantial Houses, by the Addition of a few' Years to the Building Leases, than to permit the erecting of flight Buildings on Leases for shorter Terms. A Copy of the Specification is transmitted herewith.

It is usual with Ow'ners of private Estates, on granting Building Leases, to allow a certain Time (from One to Three Years, according to Circumstances) for erecting the new Buildings, and during that Time to forbear the Acceptance of Rent. In the same of the Crown, when it happens that a new House is to be built on Ground which is out of Lease, and where the new Ground Rent would be payable from the Date of the new Lease, I would recommend that an Allowance should be made, not exceeding the first Two Years Rent; but when it happens that a House is to be rebuilt during the Term of an existing Lease, and a reversionary Term is added to prolong the same to a building Term, and the new Ground Rent payable only for the reversionary Term, the former Ground Rents being in general very trifling in comparison of the Value of the Ground, I should not, in such Cases, recommend any Forbearance of Rent.

If your Lordships shall be pleased to approve of the Regulations herein suggested, or to prescribe any other for my Direction on this Subject, I shall proceed accordingly on such Applications for Building Lcalcs as are or may be referred to me.

All which is humbly fubuiitted to your Lordships.

1 ith October 1796. Survr Gen.

N° 14. (B.)

Sir,

Having laid before the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury your Memorial, dated the nth of October last, on the Subject of the general Rules to be established for regulating the Extent of Term to be granted by the Crown in Leases where Houses are proposed to be rebuilt, or other new Buildings erected, I am commanded by their Lordships to acquaint you, that they approve of the Regulations suggested in the said Memorial.

I am.

Sir,

Your most humble Servant, Treasury Chambers, Charles Long,

14th February 1797.

John Fordyce, Esq; \

Surveyor General of the Land Revenue.

N° 15. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

In obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference, dated the 6th of August last, I have considered the annexed Memorial of Sir John Smith Burges, Baronet, and Drummond Smith, Esquire, praying your Lordships to grant them a new Lease or Leases of a Parcel of Ground, with the Houses and other Buildings thereon, situated at Hyde Park Corner, and extending from the House of Earl Cholmondeley, at the Corner of Lane,

on the East, to that of Earl at the Entrance of

Hyde Park, on the West, and from Piccadilly to the Wall of the Park, including both Sides of Hamilton Street, to fill up their present Term therein to a Building Term of 99 Years.

The Premisses of which the Memorialists desire anew Lease consist of a large Parcel of Ground, with the Buildings thereon, bounded as above del'cribed, extending in Front to Piccadilly, about 540 Feet, and containing Two Acres and a Half, or thereabouts. This Ground was formerly Part of Hyde Park, which having been disparked and fold during the Usurpation of Cromwell, the Ground in question, on which several Tenements had been erected, was left out of the Park, when it was restored and walled round by King Charles the Second; and a Lease thereof was granted, in the Year 1665, to a Trustee for James Hamilton, Esquire, then Ranger of the Park, under a Rent of 10 per Annum. In 1695 (July 3d) a farther Lease of the Premisses w'as granted by King William and Queen Mary, to Elizabeth Hamilton, Widow', for a Term of 99 Years, from the 30th of November 1695, at the same Rent; and in 1757 (May 19th) the Premisses were farther demised, by his late Majesty, to the Honourable George Hamilton, for a Term of 12 Years and a Half, from the nth of December 1794, when the former Lease expired, at the same Rent of ioj.; which last mentioned Term will expire on the nth Day of June 1807.

In the Year 1770, this Estate was assigned to the late Sir Robert Bernard, Baronet, and after his Decease, in the Year 1789, was purchased by the Memorialists, for the Remainder of the Terms granted by the Leases

It becomes my Duty to solicit the particular Attention of your Lordships to the Claims both of the Lessees of the Crown, and of the Sub-Lessees, in these Petitions, that, on deliberate Consideration, Precedents may be established by which I may be guided in Cafes of a similar Nature, which may be referred to me; and that One uniform Rule of Proceeding being laid down,

Statement of O.iiins of the LetfVes of the < rown, and , Sub-Lt flees.

any Doubt or Difficulty in such Questions may in future be obviated.

After considering, with all the Attention in my Power, the late Act of Parliament, and the general Rules laid down by your Lordships to direct my Proceedings, I conceive it to be clearly understood, that though, after the Expiration of the Terms in the existing Leases, the Estates will revert to the Crown, and Government has the legal Right of granting new Leases to any Persons, and on any Conditions consistent with the Provisions in that Act, yet that it is intended to give a Preference to the present Lessees in every same where the Subject remains entire, and has not been altered or embarrafied by Acts of the Lessee himself, in which the Powers granted by the Lease have bsen exceeded; that, on the other Hand, in Cafes where the Lessee has taken on himself to enter into Engagements with others to grant Sub-Leases beyond the Duration of his own Lease from the Crown, where Money has been laid out in the Improvement of the Estate, in the Confidence that those Engagements would be fulfilled, and where it is expected that Government will accept of less than the improved Value, with a View to the making an adequate Return for the Money so laid out, the Lessee will not, in every such Case, be enabled, implicitly, to fulfil those Engagements; but the actual Circumstances will be considered, in order that the Liberality of the Crown may be properly directed, and the Benefit of the Abatement, if any shall be made from what Government has a Right to demand, may go to the Person by whom the Money has really been expended, and the Confidence reposed; and that, in the Consideration of every such Question, it is my Duty to keep in view the general Object of the Legislature, and the Principle of the Act of Parliament, and of the Rules laid down by your Lordships, namely, the Improvement and better Management of the Estates of the Crown.

In the present Cafe, in consequence of the various Transactions which have been referred to, the Property granted by the Lease to Mr. Hamilton appears to be divided into Fout Parts, in each of which different Parties are interested, and different Regulations seem to apply to them.

The First is the Part of which no Sub-Lease has been granted, containing any Covenants for Renewal beyond the Term granted by the Crown, and which is now held by Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond Smith, as it was by Mr. Hamilton and Sir Robert Bernard, without any other Alteration of Circumstances than that of the Sale and Transference of the Crown Lease to them.

The Second Part comprises the Ground on which Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond Smith have themselves erected valuable Houses, and for which they have obtained a new Lease from the Crown of 50 Years, whereof 46 Years remain unexpired.

The Third Part consists of the Ground on which the House formerly in the Occupation of Mr. De Calonne is situated, since altered, enlarged, and divided into Two Houses, in the Occupation of Mr. Cockerell and Mr. Craufurd, for which a similar Lease with that last mentioned has been granted by the Crown to Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond Smith.

And the Fourth comprehends those Parts of the Property granted by Sub-Lcales to Messrs. Dixon, Cavendish, and Claggett, with Covenants for Renewal beyond the Term of the Lease from the Crown, and which have not been included in any new Grant from the Crown.

The original Lease purchased by Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond Smith, so far as relates to the First of these Divisions, falls under that Regulation of your Lordships, by which it is declared, that the Lessees of the Crown shall have a Preference over others in granting a new Lease; and I am of Opinion, that, con-fiftently with the Act of Parliament, a Renewal may be granted

'The Second Part is that on which Houses have been built by Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond on a Lease of no more than 50 Years, that having been the longest Term which could be granted prior to the late Act of Parliament; and as those Houses have been erected at greater Expence, and are more substantial than could have been expected under a Grant for lo short a Term, the Lessees have, in my Apprehension, a reasonable Claim to an Extension of the Term; and your Lordships are empowered to grant it by the Provisions ot that Act: And if your Lordships shall approve of such farther Lcale being granted to the Me-morialists, the Surveyors must not only re-value the Ground comprehended in the Lease already granted to those Gentlemen, and the Rent take place from the Expiration of that Lease, but they must also ascertain the Rent of the additional Ten Feet of Ground over which they have extended their new Buildings, though not comprehended in that new Grant, such Rent to take place from the End of the Lease to Mr. Hamilton, and likewise the Rent of the Ground inclosed from the Park without Licence, which must commence from the D ate of the Lease now proposed to be granted to them.

itefpefting the Third Part, being that on which the Houses occupied by Mr. Cockerell and Mr. Craufurd are situated, a new Lease of those Houses having been already granted by the Crown, of which 46 Years remain unexpired, it does not, from any Circumstances which have come before me, appear to be necessary, at present, to grant any farther Term therein; nor have any Facts been stated to me which would seem to authorize a Renewal of that Lease under the late Act, while more than Twenty Years of the existing Term remain.

In regard to the Fourth Part, it appears, from the Circumstances which have been stated, that the Lessees oft the Crown, and their Sub-Tenants, all acted on a -Presumption that the Crown would not only continue to grant Renewals of the general Lease to Mr. Hamilton, or to his Representatives and Assigns, but that the Rent and Fine to be paid would be very far inferior to the real Value. In consequence of that Presump-fion, the Lessees came under Engagements to grant new Leases to those Sub-Tenants, for much longer Terms than they had any legal Right or Power to contract for or fulfil; and by Means of those irregular Engagements, the Lessees doubtless obtained larger Fines and Rents, during the Term which had been granted to them by the Crown, than they could have obtained, if they had not entered into those Engagements for Renewals.

The Sub-Tenants, on the other Hand, in consequence of those Covenants for Renewal, not only paid more, in Rent and Fine, than the Value of what could. In a legal and valid Manner, be transferred to them by the Lessee of the Crown, but, from the Confidence they placed in those Covenants, laid out large Sums in erecting valuable Houses on the Estate of the Crown; and trusting that the ancient System of Management would be continued, and that the;Estates would be let at much less than the Value, they agreed ;iot only to

Vol. 53.

continue to pay to the principal Lessee the Rents re served by thote Leases, but also a proportionable Part of the Fine, Fees, and other Expences of obtaining the successive Renewals of the Lease from the Crownf and the Expences of the Under-Lease and Counterparts: But, after all those Trahfactions had taken place, the Legislature determined that an entirely new System of Management should be adopted for the Improvement of the landed Property, of the Crown, under which System it is intended that the real Value shall be ascertained, and a fair and reasonable Consideration taken for every Estate granted; leaving, however, with your Lordships, such Powers as might enable you to lave Lessees from the Rilk of Penalties, in consequence of Engagements entered into on the Expectation that the former System would be continued, and to prevent Loss to those who had laid out Money, or cauled it to be laid out, in the Improvement of the Estate of the Crown, when no adequate Term of the Lease remained.

Pursuing the Object of the legislature in those Provisions, considering that, in the Examples which occur in the present Cafe, the Money has been advanced, and the Confidence shewn, by the Sub-Tenants, and not by the principal Lessees,' who, though they engaged to grant farther Terms, in case they should obtain them from the Crown, do not appear to have, in any Respect, made themselves responsible for the Lei's which the Sub-Lefi'ees would sustain, in case a Renewal should not be obtained; and looking forward to the Efleft upon the general Improvement of the Estate of the Crown, which the Precedent now to be established will be likely to produce, I confess I am humbly of Opinion, that, in the Part of the Estate comprized in this last Division, the Sub-Tenants have a stronger Claim than the immediate Lessee of the Crown to new Leases, for such Terms and on such Conditions, as may give them an adequate Enjoyment of their Improvements, in return for the Money expended on the Prg-perty of the Crown.

I have thought it necessary to lay this preliminary Report before your Lordships, in which I have considered the Claims of he Lessees of the Crown and their Sub-Tenants, and brought them into view at the same Time; and if your Lordships shall signify your Approbation of the Opinions I have given, I shall then make a separate Report on each Reference, and submit to your Lordships' Consideration the Terms and Conditions on which Leases may be granted to Sir John Smith Burges and Mr. Drummond Smith, and to the other Parties before named.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships.

N 16. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

The Memorial of John , Esquire,

Surveyor General of His Majesty's Land Revenue.

My Lords,

In order to accompli lb the Object of the Legislature in passing the late Act of Parliament for the better Management of the Land Revenue of the Crown, it is extremely desirable that some general Principles should now be established by which the Proceedings on such Business as your Lordships may be pleased to refer to my Consideration may be regulated.

With this View I shall take the Liberty to submit to your Lordships' Attention some Points on which I am anxious to receive your Instructions; and shall, with great Deference, suggest what has occurred to my own Mind, which may pollibly tend to save your Time in judging of them.

The Circumstance which naturally comes first to be considered, and which mult occur in every same where Application is made for a grant of any Part of the Estate of the Crown already in Lease, is the Degree of Weight which ought to be given to what is called the Tenant-Right, or Claim of Renewal. Finding that this Subject had come under legal Difcullion in the House of Lords, in a Question concerning a Lease from the Crown, I have attentively perused the Cafes on both Sides, in which it is argued and admitted that the Tenant has no legal Claim, nor any certain or even contingent Right or Interest beyond the subsisting Term of his Lease, but only a Chance or Right to expect a Favour: It becomes material, therefore, to consider on what that Right is founded, and what are the Circumstances which ought to be kept in view in judging of this Claim, on Applications for the Renewal of Crown Leases.

In almost every Lease there are Covenants for the Care and Preservation, if not for the Improvement, of the Property j and if any Lease has been granted without such Covenants, it must be understood that a Confidence has been placed by the Proprietor in the Lessee, that he would preserve it: It is, therefore, the Duty of the Lessee to perform those Covenants, or not to abuse that Confidence.

If the Lessee has fulfilled that Duty, he certainly has a Right to-expect a Preference over others on the granting of a new Lease; but if, instead of improving, or even preserving the Property, he has injured it, or suffered others to injure it, as it cannot be said that a Person should be rewarded for having broken his Covenants, committed Waste, or ifcufed his Trust, I should humbly conceive that the Right to expect the Favour of,a Renewal is loft.

This is not only just between the Parties, but is also for the Advantage of the Property, as it rewards Care, and encourages Improvement.

But though this general Rule should be kept in view on every Application for the Renewal of a Lease, and the actual State of the Property, and the Observ-

ance or Neglect of the Covenants in the Lease, should, perhaps, be noticed in every Report from this Office on such Applications, yet there must be many Cafes which require more particular Consideration; Cafes in which this Rule alone cannot be a sufficient Guide, and in some of which, from the just and liberal Conduct of Government, somewhat more than a mere Preference over other Offerers may be expected:

For Exam,

1 ft, Where the Lessee of the Crown has entered into Engagements to Sub-Tenants which extend beyond the Term of his Lease, or the Powers vested in him, but to which he may have, in some Degree, been led by the System of Management which has been long continued.

2dly, Where Houses have been built, or great Sum expended, by the Lessee, in expectation of a Renewal, at a Time when no adequate Term remained of the existing Lease, and where the Interest of the Tenant of the Crown in the Houses so built or repaired has, in some Instances, been transferred to Purchasers.

3dly, Where the Lessee of the Crown has fub-let to several Tenants, whole Conduct has been different, some having improved, others merely preserved, and others wasted the Property they occupied.

In many of the Cafes now before me, under Reference from your Lordships, there is a Mixture of the Circumstances which have been described: it does not therefore seem necessary or ul'eful to divide any Observations which have occurred to me into the same Number of Heads; and I submit, with great Deference, to your Lordships, whether, in Cafes where a Lessee has, for a profitable Consideration to himself, and without the Knowledge or Authority of the Crown, come under Engagements or Covenants to be fulfilled after the Expiration of an existing Lease, it may not be consistent with the Liberality which ought to prevail in the Management of the Estate of the Crown, that the Lessee should be so far enabled to fulfil the Covenants, as not to incur Penalties., and should be allowed to retain the Share of the Advantages which fairly belonged to the Term of his Lcale, but without admitting any Right to claim more; that where Houses have been built or repaired, or Improvements made, in Expectation of a Renewal, at a Time when no adequate Term of the Lease remained, it may be reasonable now , to add such a Number of Years to the existing Lease, as will make up the Term which the Surveyors, to be employed in pursuance of the Provisions of the late Act of Parliament, shall be of Opinion, after taking into Consideration the Nature and Quality of the Building, or the Extent and Value of the Repairs or Improvements, ought to have been granted at the Time of building, repairing, or improving the Premisses, if the Circumstances of the same had then been stated to your Lordships, and the Law had allowed of the same Extent of Term as may now be granted; that where a Re-building has taken place, the Rent should oe equal to the present Value of the Ground for building, with some Addition for the old Materials which were then upon it, and which were the Property of the Crown j and that, where the Improvement has consisted in Repairs of an expensive Kind, the Rent should be such as the Surveyor shall, upon Oath, certify the Premisses to have been worth on a Repairing Lease for a Term of Years suitable to the Condition of the Buildings, and the Nature and Extent of the Repairs.

This Rule, it is apprehended, cannot be deemed injurious to any of the Parties: the Lessee will not fuf-

fer

Rate of Advantage to be allowed the Tenants of the Crown over those of private Proprietors *

11

Januarii.

219

fer from having been milled by the former System of Management, but will receive all the Advantage which would have been allowed to him under the new System, or if he had applied for a Grant before erecting the new Buildings, or carrying on the Repairs or Improvements. The Purchaser from the Lessee can have acquired no Right which the Lessee himself was not pof-leffed of, and can, therefore, have no separate Ground of Claim; and the Grown will, at the End of the Term of the Lease, during which the Money was expended, receive back the Property with the same Advantages only as if no such Improvements had taken place.

In the Third same described, namely, where a Lessee having fub-let to several Tenants, some of them have improved, and others injured, the Property intrusted to them, more could not certainly be expected by the Lessee of the Crown, than that he should be understood to have preferred his Claim of Preference of Renewal to that Part of the Estate let to him which has been preserved or improved; for, being responsible by his Lease for the Whole, it was equally incumbent on him to protect every Part front being injured, by those to whom it was fub-let by him for his own Advantage; and the Tendency of this Rule will be to excite more Attention in the Lessees henceforward to the Protection and Improvement of the Estates granted to them.

The Subject which I shall next submit to the Consideration of your Lordships, and on which I request to have your Instruction, is, in what Manner, or by what general Rule or Rate, in proportion to the Value which may be put, by Surveyors acting on Oath, upon the Estates of different Kinds belonging to the Crown, the Net Rent to be paid by the Lessees shall be ascertained; and whether the Rate, in proportion to the Value, shall be the same on each Kind of Property, namely;

1 ft. On Houses.

2dly, On Land Estates at a Distance from the Metropolis.

3dly, On Building Ground.

By the Act lately passed it is provided, that, before granting any Lease or Renewal of a Lease, " a Survey " shall be made by Surveyors acting on Oath, and an " Estimate of the true and fair improved Annual Worth " or Value of the respective Estates so by them surveyed and valued, dear of all Taxes, Assessments, " and Reprizes whatever."

This Rule would serve to ascertain the Value at which such Estates should be let, if they were private Property; but, for various Reasons, it may, perhaps, be deemed advisable by your Lordships, that the Rents of the Estates of the Crown should be somewhat lower than would be demanded for similar Estates by Individuals. '

Under the System of Management which has long prevailed, Leases from the Crown have been very beneficial; and the greater Part of the Value having been paid in Fines,# computed at a high Rate of Interest, the Rents have been very low in proportion to their Worth. To demand, under the new System, a Rent or Fine equal to the utmost Value, might, perhaps, be complained of as going from one Extreme to another.

It would seem to be desirable that the Rent, though near to the Value, should be so reasonable as that the obtaining a Crown Lease may still be reckoned a Favour; that Government may not, after a Lease has been granted, be disturbed with Applications for new Allowances or Deductions, or, if such Applications should be made, may deem it unnecessary to attend to them; that the regular Payment of Rent, and the Performance of Covenants, may be inforced, without any just Ground of Complaint; and that, notwithstanding that uniform Regularity, the King may still

Vol. S3 %

be reckoned a more desirable Landlord than a Subject attentive to the Management of his Property.

If experienced Surveyors, both of Land and of Buildings, shall take every Circumstance into view, and make proper Allowances when they fix the Net Rent, so as to to put the Lessees of Houses on an exactly equal Footing with the Lessees of Land, nd Reason can remain for making the Rates of Deduction different on those different Kinds of Property; but it is not easy to determine what Rate of Deduction from the Net Rent so ascertained by the Surveyors will answer all the Purposes which have been described without sacrificing too great a Part of the Value. It is with great Diffidence that I submit to your Lordships Consideration, whether the Deduction of One Eighth Part of the Net Rent of Land Estates, and Estates in Houses, would be sufficient.

It may, perhaps, be a Matter of some Doubt, whether the same Kind of Deduction from the Rent is necessary; or ought to be made, in Leases of Ground for building. As the Crown has a great Extent of Ground of this Description adjoining to the Metropolis, a general Deduction from the estimated Value, which will always be regulated by the current Price of Building Ground, may, perhaps, only have the Effect, when generally known, of obliging other Proprietors of Building Ground to make a similar Abatement, and consequently of lowering the current Value, by which Means the Object of obtaining a Preference from Builders, from the Circumstance of the Rent being lower, would be defeated; and as the Ground Rent forms but a small Part of the Value after the Buildings have been ere died, there is little Danger that such Rents will not be regularly paid.

Those who are entrusted with the Management of the Estate of the Crown, to which the Attention of Government is more particularly called, should, perhaps, endeavour to obtain a Preference to the Building Ground belonging to the Crown by other Means; by procuring from the most eminent Architects the best: Plans, in point of Beauty and Convenience, for the Extension of the Buildings oyer the Crown's Land; by the best Disposition of public Sewers, the best Mode of lighting the Streets, the most plentiful Supply of Water; by having Stations for Watchmen, Patroles, and Fire Engines, properly placed, so as to afford the rea-dieft Assistance, and the best Security to the Persons and Property of the Inhabitants; all which Advantages should be described on those Plans.

There are many other Circumstances concerning which it is desirable, for my Regulation, that I should have some general Idea of your Lordships' Opinion.

In several Parts of the Estate of the Crown in London, the Streets are narrow and inconvenient, and the Houses old and ruinous: By preventing some from being re-built, Openings may be made, which will add to the Accommodation of the Public, and, at the same Time, increase the Value of the Rest of the Area for new Buildings.

In all such Situations I would humbly propose that Leases should not be renewed till a Plan, to the Satisfaction of your Lordships, shall have been prepared of the new Streets or Openings which should be made in those Places, with a View to the Improvement of the Estate, and the Accommodation of the Public.

I think it proper also to state to your Lordships, that in the Management of the Crown's Estate, it has hitherto been the Practice, before granting the Renewal of a Lease of Houses, to employ a Surveyor to estimate the Value of the Premilfes in their actual State at the Time of taking the Survey. In doing this the Surveyor is presumed to take into his Consideration the Repairs or Re-building which may become necessary during the Term proposed to be granted; and the Lease has been always made out as soon as the Proposal has been agreed to by the Treasury; but the Work to be done has been

left

Opening of new Streets, and widening others.

left entirely to the Discretion of the Lessee; and it has not been usual, in any Case, for the Surveyor of the Crown to attend to the Execution, to see that the Work is well and substantially done; nor is any Schedule an ✓nexed to the Lease, of Fixtures, Fastenings, or other particulars, which should be left on the Premisses when the Term expires.

In the Management of Private Estates, the Practice, in most Instances, is different: The Rind of Building to be erected, or the Nature and Extent of the Repairs agreed on, are previously stipulated by a Contract between the Parties; a Surveyor is employed by the Proprietor to attend to the Execution, and makes his Report when it is completed , the Lease is not granted till the Party is known to have properly fulfilled his Engagement, and a Plan of the Buildings, with a Schedule of Fixtures, are then annexed to the Lease.

There are Circumstances relating to the Crown's Estates, which would render this Rule of withholding the Lease difficult, or, perhaps, in some Cafes, impracticable.

But in all Cases, either a Contract may be executed, and the Completion of the Lease postponed till the Plan and Schedule can be annexed to it, or the new Lease may contain Covenants for allowing Plans and Schedules to be taken whenever the supposed Difficulties shall be removed.

If it is your Lordships' Intention that what has thus been recommended should be carried into effect, the Necessity of an Office, in which all those Records and Documents may be safely deposited, must be rendered still more obvious.

Upon the whole I mull beg leave, with great De- Establishment ference, to represent to your Lordships, that if it be your Desire that, until the State of public Affairs shall necefciiy for give Time to consider whether Commissioners should be appointed for managing the whole landed Estates of the o/the Vifice. Crown, I should, in the mean Time, under your Authority, attempt to carry into effect the Plan of Management of the demifable Part of the Crown's Ellate, recommended in the Reports of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue, and authorized by the late Act of Parliament, an Establishment of Officers, similar to what they supposed would be found necessary to enable a Board to execute the same Business, will be required for my Assistance.

Under the former System of Management, where Leases were renewed as often as the Lessees desired, with little Alteration in the Terms and Conditions of successive Leases, and without any View to the Improvement of the Estate; when Surveys were not always taken, and never upon Oath, as they are now required ta be; and when the Leases were granted without Schedules annexed, or even necessary Covenants inserted, leaving the Property almost wholly at the Discretion of the Occupier, it is obvious that the Execution could not be attended with very great Labour or Difficulty; but, if Surveys are to be made, and Means to be used in all Cases to obtain the fulled Information of the State and Value of the Property; if, for Estates in,

Houses, Contrafts are to be made first, and Leases granted afterwards, with Schedules annexed to them; and if, for Land Estates, Covenants are to be inserted for their Improvement, and Care is to be taken that the Engagements of the Lessees shall be fulfilled; and if complete Registers are to be kept, both of the Property and the Documents concerning it, in the Manner which has been proposed, there mull obvioully, be a great deal of Business to be done in this Office, and uniform Attention bellowed. The Number of Officers which, I apprehend, must be required for the Business described, and for the Sale of Fee Farm Rents, cannot be less than,

A Secretary, or Deputy, to the Surveyor General.

A Register of the Crown Lands; and,

Four Clerks; besides,

A Porter or Messenger, and an Office Keeper.

I would, therefore, humbly propose,.that such of the Officers employed under the Commissioners of the Land Revenue, as have, by the Authority of your Lordships, been continued since the Expiration of their Commission, and employed in this Office, should receive the

Read Memorial of John Fordyce, Esquire, Surveyor General of Crown Lands, dated the 5th August last, relative to the general Principles to be established for regulating the Proceedings in his Department, with respect to the granting of Leases of the Lands and Estates ,of the Crown, under the Authority of the Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, wherein the Surveyor General requests the Directions of this Board on the several Points therein mentioned, and submits Vql. 53.

his Observations upon the Subject to the Consideration of their Lordships.

Read the Act of the last Session of Parliament, for< the better Management of the Land Revenue of the' Crown.

My Lords are of opinion, that the Lessee of the Crown should have, in all Cases, a Preference over others in granting a new Lease; that no Retrofpedl should be had whether he has improved the Property or injured it; but that all Lessees of the Crown should be informed, in future, that the Preference to Renewal will be forfeited on their Part, if the Property is not' preserved, or if it is injured. When more than a mere Preference over other Offers is proposed, a special Report upon the Cafe, from the Surveyor General, will be expected. 1

The Lessee of the Crown will not be enabled to fulfil Engagements he may have entered into with his Sub-Tenants beyond his existing Term, unless upon the same Conditions, and at the same Rate, as would now be required under the Act j for the additional Term, if no such Engagements had been entered into. Where Hc\uses have been built, or Improvements made, in Ex- . pedtation of a Renewal, at a Time when no adequate Term of the Lease remained, my Lords are of opinion, ‘ that a certain Number of Years should b6 added to such Lease, but reserving the same Rent fot' the additional Term as would have been required, previous to the building, if the Regulations of the Act of last Session had then been in force, my Lords being of opinion, that, they cannot give up so much of the Crown Estate as they would relinquish in agreeing to more favourable Terms of Renewal in this Cafe.

My Lords agree with the Surveyor General, that the Crown should be considered as a more desirable Landlord than a private Individual; but they are of Opinion that the Dedudiori of One Twentieth of the Net Rent, ascertained by the Surveyors, in the Manner prescribed by the Act of the last Session of Parliament, will be sufficient; and they agree with the Surveyor General, that no Deduction should be made in Leases of Ground for building.

My Lords coincide perfectly in Opinion with the Surveyor General, that eminent Architects should be desired to' offer Plans for the general Improvement of the Buildings on the Crown Estate j and that no Lease . should be renewed which is inconsistent with the general Improvement. If, in adopting this Rule, any Cafes of Hardship arise, they must be determined according to their respective Merits, on Application for Relief being made to this Board.

My Lords approve of the Mode being adopted with " respect to the Crown Estate, in granting Building Leases, which is stated by the Surveyor General to be adopted in the Management of private Estates; but where this is not practicable, the new Lease should contain Covenants for allowing Plans and Schedules to be taken, whenever any Difficulties which prevented it at the Time of making the Lease may be removed.

My Lords approve of building an Office for the Surveyor General, and of the Establishment of Clerks and Assistants proposed; and are of opinion that a Building for the Purpose may be properly erected on the Spot luggefted by the Surveyor General, for which they will give Orders for an Estimate to be prepared.

Transmit a Copy of this Minute to the Surveyor General, and direct him to govern himself accordingly.

Direct the Officers of Works to consult with the Surveyor General respecting the building a new Office, and to transmit an Estimate of the Expence thereof fox the Information of their Lordships.

N 18. (A.)

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of 'His Majesty's Treasury.

My Lords,

Before the passing the late Act of Parliament for the Improvement and better Management of the Land Revenue, of the Crown, the Mode of paying the Surveyors employed in this Department was, generally, to include the Charge for the Survey among the Expences of the Lease, and to deduct the Amount of both from, the Fine. This Mode of Payment was not inconsistent with the System which was then pursued: The Leases were renewed as they had been originally granted, with little Alteration, except in the Rent or Fine; and the Rule naturally, and very properly, followed, was, that each particular Estate should be charged with the Expences incident to it: Nor does there now seem any Reason for departing from that Rule in the Mode of paying for Surveys of any of the Estates of the Crown, which are not situated in the Metropolis, and which, lying dispersed and at a Distance from one another, the Effect of the Expence laid out on any one Estate cannot be of advantage to another, nor could any very

considerable

38 Geo III. 11° Januarii. 223

considerable Portion of them be conveniently inspected by One Surveyor.

But the raofl: valuable Part of the Crown's Estate consists of Houses and Building Ground in and near London; and many Plans are projected, and some have already been agreed to by your Lord ships, for opening new Streets, or widening others, making Sewers, removing Markets, and other Alterations, by which, though the whole District adjoining will probably be very much improved, each Lease cannot be charged with its just Proportion of the Expence inairred.

Be'fides the Business of making Surveys preparatory to the granting of new Leases, the Care and Attention which lo valuable a Property requires furnish various Occafidns for employing Surveyors after Leases are granted, to see that Houses are re-built or repaired in a substantial Manner, and that Covenants are duly performed. There are also frequent Occasions of con-fulting Surveyors on the laying out of Ground for building; and by continuing to employ the same Persons, they become more completely informed of all Circumstances respecting the Estate, and better able to suggest useful Advice to those entrusted with the Management.'

These Circumstances seem to render it advisable and necessary to have One or more Surveyors of Houses constantly engaged. I have hitherto employed Two, namely, Mr. John Marquand,.who has for a great Length of Time been in the Service or this' Office, and - Mr. Thomas Levbrton; and I would humbly recommend to your Lord ships, that in' this very important Part of the Bufiiiefs of this Department, there should always be Two Surveyors employed, so as to form a Check on each other.

I have endeavoured to learn in what Manner the Surveyors employed «by the Corporation of,

and other Proprietors of large Estates, are paid; and I am informed, that, in some Instances, the Payment is partly by a Salary, partly by a Poundage or Commission on Monies expended, and partly by Bills of Charges for making Surveys, Plans, and Designs, fu-perintending Repairs or Re-buildings, and attending the Committees or Persons entrusted with the chief Management; and that fonie are paid by the Proprietors, and others by the Tenants.

It is obvious that, whatever the Mode of Payment may be, the Expence mull fall ultimately on the Proprietor. It is, perhaps, mtore likely that the Surveyor will Interest himself in his Service when paid directly by him, and become a more attentive Check on the Tenant, than when he is to receive his Payment from the latter; and, after an attentive Consideration of the Subject, the following Arrangement appears to me the most eligible tq be adopted in paying the Surveyors employed upon this Part of the Crown's Estate:

id. That' the Charge for Surveys and'Valuations' made previously1 to the granting of Leases should still be considered as Part of the Expence Of the Lease, and be paid by the Lef-lees, and an adequate Abatement made from the Fine and Rent on that Account; and that this Charge should be proportioned to the Number and Value of the Houses contained in each Survey, according to a Rate or Table of Charges previously established by the Surveyor General, and no other Payment whatever be received by the Surveyors from the Tenants:

adly. That in lieu of a Poundage or Commission Tor surveying new Buildings or Repairs, and of Bills of Charges for their Attendance, when required, to be consulted by the Surveyor General on any Subject connected with their Appointment, they should be allowed a mo derate Salary; which should also be considered

Vol. 53.

as a Compensation for their Trouble in giving their Opinion on any Subject referred to them, accompanied, if necessary, with Sketches ' or Ground Plans for the better explaining the Idea suggested in their Reports on such Occasions, as also for the periodical or occasional Inspection of Houses, to see the State of the Repairs, and for taking Inventories, where it may be judged necessary, and be directed by the Surveyor General; and that this Salary should be One Hundred Pounds per Annum to each of the Surveyors: And,

3dly. That for taking Plans of any Part of these Estates; other than upon the granting of " Leases, and for making Designs for Improve-;

ments thereon, accompanied with Plans and Elevations, or particular Estimates, under a special Order from your Lordships, or the Surveyor General, they should be paid a moderate and reasonable Recompence, upon a Bill of Charges to be delivered to the Sur veyor General, and submitted to your Lordships, previously to the Payment thereof.

I have proposed this Arrangement to Messieurs -qiiand and Leverton, subject to your Lordships Ap-

probation, and upon this Condition, that if, after a reasonable Trial, their Emoluments should be found either to exceed or to fall short of what may be deemed a suitable Recompence for their Trouble, it shall be subject so any Alteration that your Lordships may think proper; and if your Lordships shall be pleased to approve it on that Condition, I would humbly propose that Messieurs Marquand and Leverton should be paid one Year's Salary, commencing from the 5th of July 1794 (their Employment before that Time having been chiefly confined to the taking of the general Plan of the Crown's Estate in London and Westminster, directed by special Order from your Lordships) and that the future Payments may be continued Half Yearly; with the other Part of the Establishment, until your Lordships may think fit to make any Alteration therein.

All'which is humbly submitted so your Lordships.

John Fordyce,

APPOINTMENTS.

The Office of Surveyor General has been usually granted by Letters Patent, during Pleasure.

The Surveyor General appoints such Clerks and Assistants as he thinks necessary; and their Appointments re held during his Pleasure. — The ordinary Establishment of the Office consists of:

The Surveyor General..... now vacant.

A Deputy, or Principal Clerk - -

And one other Clerk William Hollijler.

Since the Death of the late Surveyor General, in January 1791, the Lords of the Treasury have appointed Mr. Harrison to transact the Business of the Office during the Vacancy.

N® 22.

To the Right Honourable the Lords Coirtmissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

The Memorial of Peter Burrell, Esquire, Sur- veyor General of His Majesty's Land Revenue.

My Lords,

On examining the Schedule of Plans, Surveys, Books and other Records, directed to be delivered to me by your Lordships Warrant of the 8th of I, find

many Surveys, Rent Rolls, and Returns to Commissions, loft and missing. On Enquiry I am informed that they were not delivered to my Predecessor, Mr. Herbert by the Executrix of Lord Gallway, on which Account he never would sign tlfe Schedule, nor could they ever be recovered, though the most diligent En-. quiry was made after them, and AdVertisements pub-llshed with considerable Rewards. Many Instances of great Confusion and Difficulty have arisert 'on the Death j of Surveyors General, for Want of a regular Office for the Custody of the Records, and the Lessees of the Crown to apply to; and, not long finCei, a great' Cause of Sir George Wynne's, was loft, solely by not being able to come at the Books, then in Confusion, and the Custody of Bxecutors, from whom they could not be obtained, even by a' special and peremptory Order from the Lords of the Treasury.

The very great Importance of them, both to the Crown and the Subject, is sufficiently apparent, as well as the Danger they are now liablfe to from Accidents (being deposited in Two or Three different Places) particularly Fire, to which but a few Months ago they were exposed by one happening very near them. I, therefore, with great Deference, submit to your Lord ships Consideration_the ..Necessity.-there is for some Place of Safety to be fixed on, where they may be deposited, not to be removed. _

I find that an Office was intended to be settled a few Years ago, and a Piece of Ground, now vacant, reserved for this Purpose, the Lords of the Treasury having it under contemplation; but it was probably dropt on Account of their Attention being taken up by more pressing Affairs, War breaking out at that Time.

7

If your Lordships should think proper-to carry such a Plan now into Execution, and apply some Part of the Fines to that Purpose, there cannot be a more ednve-nient Opportunity, as many Applications are now before your Lordships for Renewals.

But if your Lordships should not think proper, I feel so great Anxiety for such a Charge committed to my Care, that I will beg leave to petition for a Piece of Ground to build ohe, with a Clause of Resumption in the Power of the Crown.

All which is submitted, with great Respect, to your Lordships Wisdom.

Peter Bun ell,

June 19th, 1769. Survr Qen1.

My Lords,

According to the Construction which the Attorney and Solicitor General have put on the Clauses of the Act referred to their Consideration, it appears that if a: subsisting Lease comprizes more than One House, and an Application is made for A Renewal, in Consideration of a Contraft to re-byild One or more of those Houses, or to erect new Buildings on any Part of the Ground comprized in such Lease, a new Lease cannot be granted, while more than 20 Years of the subsisting Lease remain unexpired, of any other of the Houses than such as are contracted to be re-built, nor of any other Part of the Ground than that on which new Buildings are to be erected.

A Petition of the Most Honourable Thomas Marquis of Bath, and the humble Petition of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of, or interested in, the Open and Common Fields and Downs, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, and Commonable Places, within, or belonging to, the Parish of Veny, in the County of Wilts, on Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Lands and Grounds are, in their present State, incapable of any considerable Improvement, and it would be veiy advantageous to all Persons interested therein if the lam 6were divided and allotted in Severalty: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and allotting, in Severalty, the said Lands and Grounds, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Baldwin and Mr. Joshua Smith do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act to enable the Right Honourable Richard Lord Braybrooke, Baron of Braybrooke, and Richard Neville, Henry Neville, George Neville, and William Neville, and all and every other Son and Sons of the said Richard Aldworth Lord Braybrooke, and their Issue Male, re-l'peftively, when they shall respectively become beneficially entitled to the Pofiession, or to the Rents and Profits, of certain Estates devised by the Will of the late Right Honourable John Griffin, Lord Howard de Walden and Lord Braybrooke, deceased, or shall become entitled to the Peerage of the Barony of Braybrooke in Pofiession, to use and take the Surname, and bear the Arms, of Griffin, pursuant to the said Will, was read the First Time.

A MESSAGE by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Afient to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Duke of Portland, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as folio wet h; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty an Aid and Contribution for the Prosecution of the War:

An Act for allowing, during the Continuance of the present War, a certain Proportion of the Men, raised in pursuance of Two Acts of the last Session of Parliament for augmenting the Militia, to enlist into His Majesty's other Forces, and to lerve until Six Months after the Conclusion of a General Peace:

An Act for continuing for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two several Acts, one passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the other in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty, lb far as the same relate to repairing the Road front Tadcaster to Halton FfyA, in the West Riding of the County of York;

An Act for dividing and allotting the Commonable Pastures within the Parish of Chedzoy, in the County of Somerset:

An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Common Fields, Commons, Commonable Lands, and Waste Grounds, within the Parish of Hetherfett, in the County of Norfolk:

A Petition of the Manufacturers of, and Dealers in, Clocks and Watches, and Clockmakers and Watchmakers Tools, resident in the Town and Neighbourhood of Prefcot, in the County of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in Consequence of an Act, passed in the last Session, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Clocks and Watches, the Petitioners have sustained great Losses, and, should this Act continue in Force, they will hereafter be exposed to (till greater Hard ships, and that, from the Effects already produced, they entertain the most alarming Apprehensions of the Difficulties to which they

Petition of Watchmakers, See of Prelcot, for repeal of the Clock and Watch Duty Act.

38 Geo. III. 8 ° Februarii.233

they will be subjected; and that, since the passing of the said Act, the Petitioners have, with much Anxiety, observed a gradual Increase in its injurious Effects, and it appears, from their own Experience, as well as from Documents received from the Neighbouring Towns, in the said County of , and from the

Committee appointed by the Clockmakers and Watch makers in London, to examine and Hate their Grievances, that, prior to the Month of November last, a Diminution of more than one Half had taken place in the making of Clocks and Watches, the Tools and Implements employed therein, and the various Ornaments used therewith, and that the Manufacture and Sale thereof has since generally decreased, and continues diminishing so rapidly, that the Home Trade mull very soon be nearly annihilated} and that the Artificers of all the Branches in the Clock and Watch Manufactory, who, from the Causes before mentioned, cannot obtain Employment, have already begun to emigrate, and many others will from their Distresses be induced, and probably encouraged, to do the fame: That such Artificers will be loft to this Country, and carry with them the most valuable Secrets, and which have hitherto given the Manufacturers and Dealers of Great Britain a decided Superiority and Advantage in the Markets Abroad, and, if speedy and effectual Kelief should not be granted to the Petitioners, they mull feribully apprehend a great and continued Decrease, and eventually an entire Destruction of their Foreign Trade; and that the Home and Foreign Trades are particularly connected, so far as regards the Instruction and Employment of the Workmen, because, the Foreign Trade being only periodical, the Manufacturers could not without the Home Trade employ their Workmen at those Times when they are not getting up and executing the Orders for the . Foreign Markets; and that the Cotton and Woollen Manufactories are entirely indebted for the great State of Perfection to which the Machinery used therein is now brought to the Clock and Watchmakers, great Numbers or whom have for several Years past at Times been employed in inventing and constructing, as well as superintending, such Machinery, and that those Persons, from the Want of Employment in the Clock and Watch Trade, will also be induced to emigrate, and carry with them the important Knowledge not only of improving and encouraging, but establishing Cotton and Woollen Manufactories Abroad, which, the Petitioners submit, will certainly be very prejudicial to the Commercial Interests of this Country; and that the Manufactory of Clocks and Watches must appear to be of great and peculiar National Importance, when it is considered how many Thousands of Artificers are employed therein, and that, through the mere productive Operation of their Labour, the Materials are rendered from Fifty tp Five Hundred, and progressively, in many Instances, to more than One Thou-i'and Times their original Value; and that, from these Considerations, the Petitioners are actuated, by Motives of Duty as well as Interest, to lay the foregoing Statement or Fads before the House, and, at the same Time they solicit its Interference by granting them Kelief, to declare that they are willing and desirous to contribute their full pecuniary Proportion to the Exigences of the State, and the Support of the Constitution of the Country, but that they will be unable so to do unless the said Act be repealed: And therefore praying. That the said Act, laying Duties on Clocks and Watches, may be repealed, and that the Petitioners may, if necessary, be heard, by themselves, and their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of this their Application.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House being informed, that the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; they were called in and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London; and Setting forth, That the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London, by virtue of, and under divers Charters recognized and confirmed by divers Acts of Parliament, have had and exercised, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and exercise the Office of Bailiff and Conservator of the Water of Thames, to be exercised and occupied by the Mayor of the same City, for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or by his sufficient Deputies, in, upon, and about the Water of Thames (that is to say) from the Bridge of the Town of , in the County of Middlesex, towards the East unto London Bridge, and from thence to a certain Place cstWtd Kendall, otherwise Tenland, otherwise to-

wards the Sea and East, and in Medway, and in the Port of the City of London aforesaid, and upon whatsoever Bank, and upon every Shore, and upon every Wharf of the same Water of Thames, within the Limits and Bounds aforesaid, and in, upon, and about all and every of them; and also, for all the Time aforesaid, held Jurisdiction over the fame, and have had and taken, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and take to their own proper Use, by the Mayor of the same City, for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or his sufficient Deputies, all Wages, Rewards, Fees, and Profits belonging to the same Office of Bailiff j and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners would be invaded, and the Trade and Commerce of the said Port of London, where it has flourished for a great Length of Time, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the City of London, and the Kingdom in general, would, in a very material Degree,' be removed to a new Scite, out of the Controul and Superintendance, as well as out of the Care and Protection, of the Petitioners; and that such Removal would not only be a Violation of the ancient Customs and Privileges of the Petitioners, but also be productive of the most ruinous and distressing Consequences to divers incorporated Societies and Companies, as well as to great Numbers of Individuals, the Value of whose Property, or the Profits of whole Labour and Industry, in a great Measure, depend on the Trade and Commerce of the City and Port of London being continued to be carried on within the Limits and Jurisdiction of the said City; and that the Petitioners and their Predecessors, ever careful of the Rights and Welfare of their Fellow Citizens and anxious to accommodate, promote, and increase the Trade and Commerce of the City of London, have, from Time to Time, deviled and offered to execute Plans conductive to those Ends, and, actuated by thele Motives, as well as in Consequence of divers Applications made to them in that Respect, Plans have been formed for'increasing the Accommodation, and for the more effectually securing the Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue of the Port of London, which, by the Aid and Authority of Parliament, they have Reason

to believe may be carried into. Execution without the Necessity of creating a new Corporation and other expensive Establishment, without such an Extent of Injury or Inconvenience to Individuals as the said . Bill must necessarily produce, and without unneceffaiily infringing on the ancient Rights and Privileges of the City of London, or burthening the Trade of the said Port in the Manner and to the Extent proposed by the said Bill, and the Petitioners assure themselves such Plans will be brought forward, and, if duly encouraged and sanctioned by the Legislature, carried into Execution j and that as, by carrying such a Plan into Execution, the Public at large would derive such Benefit and Accommodation as the Commerce of London at present moil urgently requires, at a moderate Expence, and perfectly confident with the Safety of its Shipping, and the Security of the Revenue, and as the Petitioners would not thereby take, or do they mean to take, any Emolument or Advantage to themselves, they rely on the Justice of the House that no new Corporation shall be established as proposed by the said Bill: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel,

Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, Agents, or Witnesses, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think 'fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for enabling Thomas Macklin to dispose of his Collection of Modern Paintings, as exhibited at his Gallery in Fleet Street, by Way of Chance, was read; whereby it is enacted, that the said Paintings should be disposed of by Way of Chance, and that the Number of Tickets should not exceed Two thousand Four hundred, to be numbered respectively One to Two thovfl'and Four hundred, at Five Pounds Five Shillings for each Ticket; and that Notice should be giveft in The London Gazette of , the Intention to dispose of the said Tickets; and that

the Whole of such Paintings should constitute Seventy-six Prizes only, to be determined by the First State Lottery to be. drawn after the passing of the said Act: And,

Mr. John Wakefield being examined, said. That he has conducted the Whole of the Business under the Authority of the said Act; and that the Petitioner hath not been able to fell more than Three Hundred and Forty, out of the Two Thousand Four Hundred Tickets limited by the said Act; and he added, That the Proceeding to the Drawing under the present Circumstances will be injurious to the Petitioner, and defeat the Object of the former Act, the Day appointed for the Drawing of the said Lottery by the said Act - being the 26th Day of this instant February.

Petitions from ' A Petition of the Manufacturers and Venders of Liverpool and Clocks and Watches, and of the Tools and Materials forrepelof concerned therein, resident in the Town and Neigh-the Clock and bourhood of Liverpool, in the County of Watch Duty wj10fe Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Trade of the Petitioners is very materially injured in Consequenceof an Act, passed in the last Session, for imposing certain Duties on Clocks and Watches; and that the Sale of every Description of those Articles is extremely reduced, and of Gold Watches for the Home Trade in particular is very nearly annihilated, whereby they are deprived of the most respectable as well as more profitable Branch of their Trade, and the Revenue mult in Consequence lose the Advantage of a considerable Amount of Duty which might be paid on Gold and Silver manufactured into WatchGafes; and that a very great Number of ingenious Artificers are deprived of Employ, and many of them, from the Habits produced by their Business, are incapable of applying themselves to other Kind of Labour: And therefore praying. That the said Act may be taken into the serious Consideration of the House, and that it may be repealed.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of, and Dealers in Clocks and Watches, resident within the City of Edinburgh and its Vicinity, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Tax imposed in the last Session on Clocks and Watches has not only affected and depressed the Manufacture in general, but has bore particularly hard ou the Workmen engaged in every Branch of the Trade, many of whom, who formerly supported themselves and Families in Credit and Comfort, are <now reduced, through Want of Employ, to the greatest Distress; and that most of the Petitioners, since the Commencement of the Tax, have experienced a Decrease fully of an Half, and others of Two Thirds, of their Trade, while, to the Dealers in Gold Watches, the Tax has operated almost to a Prohibition, and they are now loaded with an un-saleable Stock; the Consequences are, that many Journeymen have been discharged, others reduced short on Piece-working, and unless some Relief be granted, the Apprentices must soon be turned to other Occupations, a Set of ingenious Workmen, possessed of important and valuable Knowledge, driven from the Country, and the Petitioners cortipelled to relinquish their Business altogether: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and to reppal the said Act.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom it is referred to consider of the > several Petitions which have been presented to

the House in this Session of Parliament, praying for the Repeal of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for "granting to His Majesty certain Duties on " Clocks and Watches :" And they are to examine the Matters of these Petitions; and report the fame, as they shall appear to them, to the House.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following Were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 1. 1. 13. To leave out " is," and insert " may " be," instead thereof.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to enable His Majesty to order out a certain Proportion of the Supplementary Militia, and to provide for the necessary Augmentation of Men in the several Companies of Militia, by incQrporating the Supplementary Militia therewith.

Ordered, That Mr. Secretary Dundas do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Report on A<3 Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- Q Vne. ferred to consider of so much of an Act, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act more effectually to secure " the Performance of Quarantine, and for amending several Laws relating to the Revenue of Customs," as relates to the Performance of Quarantine, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to Re- port to the House; which he read in his Place;-and. afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to amend so much of an Act; made in the Twenty-eighth Year of, the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the Performance of Qua-, rantine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That Provision be made more effectually to prevent the fraudulent Importation of Glass into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient that Coffee and Cocoa, ware-housed on Importation, be permitted to be carried Goaftwife for the greater Convenience of Exportation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Commissioners of the Customs be authorized to return the Duties of Customs which shall have been paid on Goods imported, and which shall be lost or destroyed before the Landing thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to prevent Vessels, licensed by the Admiralty, from being engaged in any other Trade or Employment than such as shall be permitted by their Licences.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Provision be made, for iubjeding to Forfeiture all 'Goods prohibited or concealed, which shall be found in Packages landed by Bills at Sight or View.

The Five First Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question. severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time;

And the Question being put, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

It pasted in the Negative.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the Five First of the said Resolutions, and which have been agreed to by the House: And that Mr. Rose, Mr. Long; and Mr. Hobart, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.
