'fefident in the City of Carlisle and the Vicinity theredf, in the County of Cumberland, whose Names are there-tmto'subscrtbed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting foFth, That in consequence of the Act, passed in the last: Session, for granting to 'Mis Majesty certain Duties on Clocks and Watches, the Petitioners have sustained great Losses: That, should this Aftcoritinue in force, they will daily be exposed to still greater Hardships, and that, from the Eftefts already produced, they entertain the most alarming Apprehensions of the ©anger to which they will be subjected; and that, fmee the passing of the said Act, the Petitioners have, with Touch Anxiety, observed a gradual inereale in itsinju-tiotis'Operations, and that it appears from Experience that, prior to the Month of November last, a Diminution df -more than One -Half had ‘taken prlace in the Making of Clocks and Watches, and that the Manufacture and Sale thereof generally -has iirice 'deCreased, tend continues diminishing so rapidly, that thfe Home Trade must very soon be nearly annihilated; and that the Artificers in all the Branches of the Clock and Watch Manufactory, from the Causes before mentioned, tannot obtain Employment, and, if speedy and effect-tual Relief be not granted tottye Petitioners, they most seriously apprehend a great and continued Decrease, tend eventually an entire Destruction of their Trade: That the Home and Foreign Trades are particularly connected, so far as regards the instruction and Employment of the Workmen, because, the Foreign Trade being only periodical, the Manufacturers cannot, without the Home Trade, employ the Workmen at those Times when they are not getting up and executing the Orders for Foreign Markets; and that the Cotton and Woollen Manufactories are entirely indebted for the State of Perfection to which the Machinery used therein is now brought to the Clock and Watch Makers, great Numbers of whom have, for several Years past at Times, been employed in inventing and constructing as well as superintending such Machinery, and that those Persons, from their Want of Employment in the Clock and Watch Trades, will be induced to emigrate, and carry with them the important Knowledge; not only of improving and encouraging, but establishing Cotton and Woollen Manufactories Abroad, which the Petitioners submit will certainly be very prejudicial to the Commercial Interest of this Country; and that the Manufactory of Clocks and Watches must appear of great and 'peculiar National Importance when it is considered how many Thousands of Artificers are employed therein, and that, through the more productive Operation of their Labour, British Metals are rendered from Fifty to Five Hundred, and progressively in-many Instances more than One Thousand Times the original Value; and that, from these Considerations, the Petitioners are actuated, by Motives of Duty as well as Interest, to Jay the foregoing Statement of Fasts before the House,. and, at the same Time that they entreat its Interference by granting them Relief, to declare they are desirous to contribute their full pecuniary Proportion to the Exigencies of the State and the Constitution, but, unless the said Act be repealed, they will be totally unable so to do: And therefore praying, That the said Act may be repealed, and that the Petitioners may, if necessary, be heard, by themselves and Counsel, at the Bar of the House, in Support of this their Application.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee, to whom it is referred to consider of the several Petitions which have been presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, praying for the Repeal of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to " His Majesty certain Duties on Clocks and Watches:" And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

That, by an Act, passed in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were authorized to make a Navigable Canal from the River Kennet, at orr near the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near the City of Bath, and by an Act, passed in the Thirty-sixth Year of the Reign of His said present Majesty, the Petitioners were empowered to vary the Line of the said Canal in several Parts thereof; and that the Petitioners have made great Progress towards the executing the said Canal, but It appears, by. Surveys lately made, that if the Line of the said Canal was varied in certain Parts, in the County of Wilts, from the Course originally intended for it, namely, from, and out of, a Piece of Arable Land, in the Parish of Bishops Cannings, in the County of lately belonging to Thomas Rigge, Esquire, deceased, to a Piece of Meadow Ground, in the said Parish, belonging to R. E. Drax Grosvenor, Esquire, and from the Turnpike Gate at the West End of Devizes, in the said County, to a Close of Meadow Ground belonging to ‘

Henry Penruddocke Wyndham, Esquire, in the Parish of Rowde, in the said County, the Line of the said Canal would be considerably shortened and improved; and that, if the Line of the said Canal, instead of being carried into the River Avon at Bath Easton Mill, in the County of Somerset, as directed by the said Acts, was varied, and carried from a Close of Land, in the Parish of Bathampton, in the said County, lately belonging to Mr. Robert Fisher, into the River Avon at or near Dole Mead, in the Parish of Lyncomb and Widcombe, in the said County, the Communication of the said Canal with the City of Bath would be much more conveniently effected, and the Navigation less liable to be impeded and obstructed by Floods; and that it would tend to thd better carrying the Purposes of the said Act into Execution if some of the Powers and Provisions thereof were altered and extended: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize the Petitioners to make the said Variations, and to make such other Amendments in the said Acts as to the House shall appear necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Charles Dundas, Mr. Goddard, &c.; And they are to meet upon Monday Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Perl'ons, Papers, and Records.

The House was moved, That the Resolutions which were Yesterday reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, and were then agreed to by the House, might be read.

And the larfle were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as followeth;

" Resolved, That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand " Five hundred and Eighty-seven Pounds Seventeen " Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to enable the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of an Act passed in the Thirty-fourth Year of the " Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " veiling certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and " Hereditaments, in Trustees, for the better securing " His Majesty's Batteries and other Works in the " Counties of Kent and Devon," to make Compensation to the Proprietors uf such Lands and Hereditaments as have been purchased for the Purposes of the " said Act."

" Resolved, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand " Nine hundred and Fifty-three Pounds Eleven Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, " to enable the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of " an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for revelling certain Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the County of Kent, in the former Proprietors thereof and for other Purposes " therein mentioned," to make Compensation for the " Loss or Damage sustained by the Owners or Occupiers of Lands in the County of Kent, in Consequence of an Act made in the Thirty-fourth Year of " the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for veiling certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and " Hereditaments, in Trustees, for the better securing " His Majesty's Batteries and other Works in the " Counties of Kent and Devon" '

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Mr. Singleton, and

Mr. Hobart, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Order of the Day being read, for receiving the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for rectifying Mistakes in the Names of several of the Commissioners, appointed by an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, to put in Exe-3

cution an Act, made in the same Session, intituled,

" An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land " Tax to be raised in Great Britain for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninetyseven," and for appointing other Commissioners, together with those named in the first-mentioned Act, to put in Execution an Act of this Session of Parliament , for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax to be raised in Great Britain for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-eight i and for indemnifying such Persons as have acted as Commissioners for executing the said Act for granting an Aid. to His Majesty by a Land Tax to be raised in Great Britain for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-seven, was committed;

Ordered, That the said Report be received upon ThursdayMorning next.

A Bill to give further Time to comply with the Rp- ST gulations of an Act, passed in the last Session of Par- for obtaintof liament, intituled, "An Act to indemnify such Per- certain Certifons as have omitted to obtain their Certificates of kted.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Bill to amend so much of an Act, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the Performance of Quarantine; to prevent the fraudulent Importation of Glass into this Kingdom; for permitting the Removal of Coffee and Cocoa Coastwise for the greater Convenience of Exportation; to authorize the Commissioners of the Customs to return the Duties paid on Goods imported, which shall be lost or destroyed before the Landing thereof; and to prevent Vessels licensed by the Ad- miralty from being engaged in any Trade or Employment not permitted by their Licences, be read a Second Time Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Petition for amending Tynemouth Moor Inclo-fuxe Act,

Jjetth Har-iour,&c. Petitions

Ordered, That the said Accounts do He upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

A Petition of several of the Owners and Proprietors of the Allotments of the Lands set out by virtue of an Act; of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, a certain Common Moor, or Tract of Waste Land, called 'Tynemouth Moor, Shire Moor, Billy Moor, or Billy Mill Moor, within the Manor of Tynemouth, otherwise Tynemouth Shire, otherwise Tynemouth with Tynemouth Shire, in the County of Northumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Commissioners, thereby appointed, divided and allotted the said Tract of Waste Land, arid have set out several Roads through or over the fame; but they were not, by the said Act, authorized to ascertain or determine what Parts of the said Roads Were to be amended, and kept in Repair, by the respective Townlhjps, wherein the said Moor or Waste Land was situate, or to which Allotments of the said Lands were set out, and therefore Doubts and Disputes have arisen, touching the fame, and the said Act is, in other Respects, defective: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaining and settling in what Manner, and by whom, the different Parts and Proportions of the said Roads are to be amended, and kept in Repair, in future, and for otherwise amending the said Act, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pur-fiiant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Burdoti and Mr. Beaumont do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinbfor themselves, and on Behalf of the Community of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging and improving the Harbour of Lfor making a new Ba-son. Quays, Wharfs, or Docks, for building Ware-fcoufes, for making new Roads, and widening others, leading to and from the said Harbour, Power was given to the Petitioners to levy and collect the several Rates and Duties therein mentioned on all Ships or Vessels brought irito or using the new Bason or Dock to be made at the Port of Leith, His Majesty's Ships of War and Yachts only excepted, and Power was also given to borrow a Sum, not exceeding £. 30,000 Sterling j and that the Petitioners have, at a considerable Expence, opened a new Street to the Harbour, repaired the Quays, and erected a Draw-bridge across the Harbour, between South and North Leith, instead of an old Bridge, now taken away, and have also deepened the Harbour, and widened a great Part of the Quays; and that, in order to complete a commodious Bason or Wet Dock, it will be necessary to authorize the Petitioners to borrow a further Sum of Money, and to levy certain Rates and Duties on all Ships or Vessels brought into the Harbour of Leith, even although they shall not be brought into the said intended Bason or Wet Dock, excepting always His Majesty's Ships of War or Yachts: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effectuating those Purposes, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. William Dundasftlr. McDow-all, &c: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Vo l. S3-

Mr. William Dundas reported from the Committee, Edinburgh to whom the Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, &-ot°piuJn, and Council of the City of Edinburgh, for themselves, reported, and on Behalf of the Community of the said City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had dire (fled- him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it'in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition it appeared, That, by an Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in the Year 1693, a Duty of Two Pennies Scots was granted to the Community of tire City of Edinburgh, and to the Magistrates and Town Council of the fame, and their Successfors in Office, for the Ul'es therein specified, upon every Pint of Ale and Beer, either brewed, brought in, tapped, and fold, within the said City and Suburbs, and Liberties thereof, for the '

Space of Fifteen Years, and further, not exceeding the Space of Thirty Years, commencing from the ift of July 1693; and by several 1'ubsequent Acts, the Term of the before-mentioned Act- has been continued, and the Powers thereof altered and enlarged: And,

London, Esquire, on Behalf of themselves and the other Proprietors of the Manufactory and Property of the late Governor and Company of the British Call Plate Glass Manufacturers, was presented to the House, 'and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, to incorporate certain Persons therein named, and their Successors, with proper Powers for establishing one or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the more effectually supporting and conducting the same upon an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner calculated for calling of large Plate Glass, certain Persons therein named were incorporated by the Name and Stile of " The Governor and Company of the British Call Plate Glass Manufacturers," and were empowered to raise a Capital Joint Stock, to be applied for carrying on the said Manufacture, not exceeding £.40,000, and, in case the same should be found insufficient, to raise an additional Sum of £.20,000 in the Manner therein mentioned; and that the said Manufactory was established in the Year 1773, and wras conducted by the said Governor and Company in Conformity to the Terms of the said Act, first with a Capital Stock of £. 40,000, and afterwards with the extended Capital of £. 60,000, aided by Loans negotiated by the Company with Individuals to a large Amount, until the Year 1794, when the said Governor and Company were under the Necessity of felling the Whole of their Property for Payment of their Debts, and Thomas Oakes, Esquire, became the Purchaser thereof at the Sum of £. 105,600, on Behalf of himself and several other Persons, who from thenceforth carried on the said Manufactory, under the Authority, and according to the Regulations of the said Act, until the Expiration of the Term thereby limited for the Continuance thereof, which expired at the End of the Session of Parliament of the Year 1795, and from that Period the Proprietors of the said Manufactory have carried on the same on their joint Account as a Private Company; and that, by virtue of the said Purchaseby the said Thomas Oakes, and of subsequent Transfers of SliarfA the said Manufactory, and the Estates and Effects-belonging thereto, are now become the Property of the Petitioners, and of those on whose Behalf they petition; and that the Method of making Plate Glass hath been greatly improved by the Establishment of the said Manufactory, and the Public Revenue, arising from the Duties laid on Plate Glass, hath in consequence been considerably increased, and is likely to be Hill further increased by a Continuance of the said Manufactory, but, in as much as the same cannot be carried on to Advantage without a larger Capital than is at present employed therein, and as the Contributors to such Capital will be numerous, and as all the Proprietor or Co-partners in a Private Company must be named in all Actions, Suits, and legal Proceedings, by or against them, which will be attended with great Inconvenience, and as they may also be liable to have Commissions of Bankrupt ifl'ued against them as Traders, which will deter many Persons from engaging in the Concern, it is very desirable that the Proprietors of the said Manufactory should be incorporated, with proper Powers for carrying on the same: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for eftectuating the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Petition «-Poor, and several of the principal Inhabitants, of the tafn Raw'of Parish of Saint Peter, in the Borough and Liberty of Saint the Parish of Alban, in the County of Hertford hoit Names are there- Alban.',) unto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That in the Years 1786, 1787, and 1788, the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the fp.id Parish did, with the Consent of the principal Inhabitants, at Vestries legally assembled, borrow of different Persons the Sum of £. 2,790 upon Annuities, for the Purpose of repairing the Church belonging to the said Parish, which was then in a very ruinous and dangerous State, and the said Money was duly laid out and expended''in such Repairs; and that, for securing the Payment of such Annuities, the said Churchwardens and Overseers, together with several of the principal Inhabitants of the said Parish, did, in pursuance of several Orders of Vestry, enter into Bonds, to the Persons who had advanced the above Sum of Money, for Payment to them, during their respective Lives, out of the Annual Assessments which should be made on the Inhabitants of the said Parish, such Yearly Annuities upon the Sums respectively advanced as were agreed upon at such Vestries; and that in consequence thereof, the Churchwardens and Overseers Rave paid to the several Annuitants, out of the Church Rates which have been made and assessed upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, their Annuities as they became due, until on or about the Year 1795, but since that Time they hav,e not been able to raiie and pay the same without advancing a Part thereof out of their own private Monies; to prevent Actions being brought against them, owing to some of the Inhabitants having refused to pay their Quota to such Rates, alledging that the same were made from the Poors' Rates, against which they had appealed, as being illegal, and contrary to Law; and that, by Reason of such Refusal, the present Churchwardens and Overseers are involved in great Difficulty and Distress, being wholly unable to pay the Annuities, granted by their Predecessors in Office, as they become due, and, unless Power is given to enable the Petitioners to satisfy the Claims of those Annuitants who are now living, as their Annuities become due, and all Arrears thereof, either by making and collecting Rates sufficient for that Purpose, or by such other Ways and Means as the House shall think right, it will . be attended with great Injury and Expence to the Petitioners, and all those who are engaged in the said Bonds, as well as be the Means of producing much Mischief and Disorder in managing the Affairs of the said Parish:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes before-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem just and equitable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to tire Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Bucknell, Mr. Baker, 8{C.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

That Sir John Parker , and those under whom he claims, as Lords of the Manor of Manchester, have for Eighty Years last past used and exercised the Right of taking and raising Water, by Means of Pumps, from and out of the River Medlock, within the Parish of Manchester and County of Lancaster, and throwing into arid preserving the same in Reservoirs, and thereby, and with Pipes therefrom, have supplied the Inhabitants of the Manor and Town of Manchester with Water, which Pipes have been and

who have paid yearly Rents or Sums for the Use thereof; and that the said Waterworks have been for many Years, and are now, very much out of Repair, and will require a very considerable Sum of Money to put them into proper Repair, and to keep up and support suitable Reservoirs for Water, which, as the Petitioner is only Tenant for Life, with Remainder to his First and other Sons in Tail, and hath a numerous Family, he cannot, with Justice to the younger Branches thereof, perform; and that the Petitioners,- the said Sir John Parker Mojley, and John Dickenson and Charles White, his Trustees, have contracted and agreed with the other Petitioners, on Behalf of themselves and others, for a Demise or Lease of the said Waterworks, with the Rights, Liberties, Privileges, and Advantages, thereunto belonging, and for his and their Right and Privilege of supplying the said Inhabitants with Water, and also of a Plot of Land in Manchester aforesaid, for Reservoirs for Water, for a Term of Nine hundred and Ninety-nine Years, under and subject to the Payment of a certain Yearly Rent, and the Covenants and Agreements in such Contract mentioned; and that the said Contract, so entered into by the said Sir John Parker Mojley and the said John Dickenson and Charles , will not only be greatly for the Benefit of the Persons entitled to the said Waterworks and Privileges, Plot or Parcel of Land, in Remainder after the Death of the said Sir John PaYker Mojley, as the Rent thereby re-

served is a full, fair, and ample Rent, and a much greater Income than the said Sir John Parker Mojley hath ever been able to receive for the fame, and that the said Contract, when carried into Effect, will also be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Manor, and Town of Manchester, not only by affording a constant Supply of Water for their necessary and common Occasions, but also by affording an immediate Supply of Water in Cafes of Fire, to which the Manufactories of Manchester are particularly liable; and that the said Contract cannot be effectually carried into Execution, nor the said Waterworks carried on and conducted to Advantage, either to the Purchasers or to the Inhabitants of the Manor and Town of Manchester, without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize and enable the said Sir John Parker Mojley, Baronet, and his Issue, and his and their Trustees, to ratify and confirm the said Contract, and also to enable the Purchasers thereof to alter, improve, and extend, the said Waterworks within the said Manor and Town of Manchester, for the better supplying the Inhabitants thereof with Water, and to recover the Rents and other the Confident ions, which shall be agreed to be paid by any of such Inhabitants, and also to enable the said Sir John Parker Mojley to charge the Persons in Remainder, as aforesaid, with the Payment of the Expences which he shall be put unto, in and about the obtaining the said Act, he, the said Sir John Parker Mojley, keeping down the Interest of such Money during his Life, and also to incorporate the Purchasers of the said Waterworks, and for such further and other Powers, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Company of Merchants of the City of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Merchants of Edinburgh, Importers or Sellers of Cloaths, Stuff's, or other Merchandize for the Apparel of Men and Women within the City of Edinburgh, were, by Charter, or Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of Scotland, dated the 29th of October i68r, created a Body Corporate by the Name and Stile of " The Company of Merchants of the City " of Edinburgh,"and invested with certain Powers for the Management and Regulation of their Affairs, particularly with Power to make certain Exactions, in Name of Entry Money, from Persons becoming Members of their Body — to apply the Money arising therefrom, and from such other Funds as might be acquired by the Corporation, towards the Support of their Poor Members, and also towards the Support of their Widows, and Orphans of Members, dying in indigent Circumstances: The Charter conferred a Right to prevent Persons, not entered of the Corporation, from exercising the said Trades, until they were admitted Members of it, and authorized them to exact certain Sums from those who became Apprentices to Members; and that the above-mentioned Royal Charter was confirmed by an Act of Parliament of Scotland on the 15th June 1693; and that, from the Funds of the Corporation arising from Entry Monies, the Petitioners are enabled to afford final 1 Pensions yearly to their Poor, and, from Contributions of Members, and Grants made them for the Purpose of supporting and educating the Children of distressed Members, the Petitioners are also enabled to support nearly Eighty Female and Sixty Male Children: But, while the Children are liberally provided for, the Poor of the Corporation and their Widows do not receive an adequate Assistance from the Corporation, although, by a Royal Charter obtained on the 26th September 1777, the Petitioners were empowered to demand, and have accordingly demanded, from Persons becoming Members of the Corporation, £. 6 Sterling of Admission Money, and, annually thereafter, 6s. Sterling, in Place of ftnaller Fees formerly paid; and that, in order to make a proper and adequate Provision for the Poor of the Corporation and their Widows, it becomes necefiafy, that the Charter 1681, and the A«ft of 1693 ratifying the fame, should be confirmed, as also the Charter 1777, that the Admission Money and Annual Contributions should be considerably enlarged, and that the Corporation should be veiled with the necessary Powers for carrying so laudable an Intention into Execution, and for making, from Time to Time, such Rules and Regulations as are most likely to insure its Success: And therefore praying. And he moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Papers be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The said Papers are preferred amongst the other Papers of this Session,

Veneris 2 30 die Februarii;

Anno 38 Georgii III. K Regis, 1798. Prayers.

A MESSAGE from the Lords, by Mr. Popham

and Mr. Smith:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to give further Time for putting in Execution an Act, made in this present Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to enable His Majesty to order out " a certain Proportion of the Supplementary Militia, " and to provide for the necessary Augmentation of " Men in the several Companies of Militia, by incorporating the Supplementary Militia therewith ;" without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Henry Ferdinand Pelerin; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

And the said Bill from the Lords was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. John Pitt reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Neath Canal Navigation was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of His present Majesty, for making a Canal Navigation from or near a certain Place called Abernant, in the County of to

and through a certain Place called The Brickfield, near Mjelin-crythan Pill, into the River of Neath, near the Town of Neath, in the said County, was read: And, Mr. John Wood, Senior, being examined, said. That the said Company have completed the said Navigation: That it appears, by Surveys lately taken, that the said Canal may be extended from the present Termination thereof near Melin-crythan Pill to or near to a Place called Giants Grave Pill, in the Parish of Briton Ferry, in the said County; and that such Extension of Canal will be attended with considerable Advantage to the Neighbourhood, and be of Public Utility, as thereby the very inconvenient Navigation of Part of the River of Neath will be avoided; and the Witness further laid, that the Company are willing and desirous, at their own Costs and Charges, to make, complete, and maintain, the said Extension.

And being further examined, he said. That the said Art requires to be amended, and that some of the Powers thereof should be altered and enlarged.

Mr. John Wood, Junior, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for extending the Neath Canal Navigation, and for amend-

ing an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal: And Vot. 53.

that Mr. John Pitt and Mr. Gore Langton do prepare; and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several of the Trustees for putting in Execution an Art, made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for building a Bridge over the River OuJ'e at Newhaven, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have proceeded in the Execution of the said Art, and have caused the said Bridge to be built, and a Road to be made thereto, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act; and that the Petitioners find the Exemptions, allowed by the said Act, have been the Means of many Persons evading the Payment of the Tolls thereby granted; and that, to enable the Petitioners effectually to carry the Purposes of the said Art into Execution, it is necessary the same should be explained, altered, and amended: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain, alter, and amend, the said Art, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Hobart, Mr. See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

An ingrossed Bill for naturalizing John Frederick -tin and Daniel Eckenfiein, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for naturalizing John Frederick Ifilin and Daniel Eckenfiein.

Ordered, That Mr. Hobart do carry the Bid to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

The House being informed that the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council af>. femb.led.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That the Price of Flour and Bread in the City of London and Parts adjacent is frequently much higher than the Price of Grain at the same Time warrants, and that the unnecell'ary high Price of Flour and Bread is a very great Grievance and Hardship on the Inhabitants of the Metropolis and Parts adjacent, and is most severely felt by the lower Orders of the People; and that the said Grievance is, as-the Petitioners apprehend and believe, occasioned in a great Degree by the Decrease which has of late Years taken place in the Number of Mills in the Vicinity of the Metropolis, and likewise, by the Supplies of Flour, which used formerly to come to the London Market, being diverted through various Channels to other Parts of the Kingdom; and that the most effectual Mode of reducing the Price of Bread, within the Limits aforesaid, would be by encouraging the erecting of Mills on the Banks of the "Thames in the Vicinity of London, capable of furnishing regularly an adequate Proportion of the usual Consumption of Flour for the Supply of the Metropolis, and taking Measures towards providing a constant Supply of Wheat, the Whole under the Management, Superintendance, and Controul, of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the above-mentioned Purposes, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That considerable Diladvantages and Impediments to the Trade of the Port of London arise from the circuitous Course of the River Thames round the Isle of Dogs, Ships and Vessels being sometimes loft, or greatly damaged, and their Cargoes injured, in attempting the Passage round it, or detained below it, for several Days together, waiting for a Change of Wind; which Loifes and Inconveniences rrlight be avoided, and the Delay rendered unnecessary, if a Passage between Black-wall and The Pool could be effected without such circuitous Course; and that, from the very great "and progressive increase of the Number and Size of Ships, and other Vessels, trading to the Port of , the

River Thames, in and near the said Port, is, in general, so much crowded with Shipping, Lighters, and other Craft, that the Navigation of a considerable Part of the said River is thereby rendered tedious and dangerous, and there is great Want of Room in the said Port for the safe and convenient Mooring of Vessels, and constant Access to them; and that great Inconveniences are also experienced in the said Port, from the Want of Regulations concerning the navigating and removing of Vessels in and near the fame, and the Want of a proper Arrangement of Ships, and other Vessels, in their several Moorings, with respect to their Dimensions, the Nature of their Cargoes, and their relative

Intercourse with the Custom House; and that great Delays, Accidents, Damages, Loifes, and Expences, are almost continually sustained from the last mentioned Causes, to the Hindrance and Discouragement of Commerce, and the great Injury of the public Revenue; and that the said Evils might, in a great Degree, be remedied, if the Petitioners were enabled to make and maintain a Navigable Canal or Passage, sufficient for Ships and other Vessels, across the said Isle of Dogs, between Blackball and LimehouseHole, so as to avoid, when necessary, the circuitous Course aforesaid, and to purchase the Mooring Chains iir the River,

from London Bridge to the King's Moorings at Deptford, and to appoint Harbour Mailers to regulate the navigating and mooring of Ships and Vessels in and near the said Port, which Improvements would give Accommodation and Encouragement to Commerce, and be of great Public Utility; and that, by Plans and Surveys lately made, it appears that such Cut or Canal as before-mentioned may be made, and the Petitioners are willing and desirous to undertake the making and maintaining thereof; and that the Petitioners appre- i hend and believe, if good and sufficient Wet Docks and Basons, with proper Cuts, Sluices, and Outlets, were made and established in lonie Part or Parts of the Isle of Dogs, with Quays, Wharfs, and Warehouses, attached thereto where necessary, for the Reception and Discharge of Ships and Vessels employed in the West India Trade, the same would be extremely beneficial to the said Trade, and advantageous to the general Commerce of the Port of London, by the Room and Accommodation which would necessarily arise from the Removal of the Ships and Vessels employed in the West India Trade out of the River, and such Removal would also tend greatly to the increase and Security of the Public Revenue; and that, by Plans and Surveys lately made, it appears that such Wet Docks, Basons, and other Requisites, may be made and constructed in the Isle of Dogs, which will afford ample and complete Relief and Accommodation to the Port: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Mayor of London, Mr. Mainwaring, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Message by Sir Francis , Gentleman Ulher

of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendence of this Honourable House in the . House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills and One Private Bill therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Arch-bishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Earl of Chesterfield, and the Earl Spencer, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

That the Petitioner,. William Beckford is ieifed, or entitled in Fee Simple, of, or to Four several Woods, or Wood Grounds, called Old Coppice, The Old Hills, Landmore, and Deadmonfey Woods, in the said Parish, containing together 222 Acres, or thereabouts; and that the Owners and Occupiers of certain Messuages, Lands, and Tenements, in the said Parish, have used and enjoyed a Right of Common of Pasture for Sheep, Hogs, Cows, and other Cat-i tie, in or upon Three of the said Four Woods, or Wood Grounds, at a Time, and it hath been customary for the Petitioner the said William Beckford, and the former Owners of the said Woods, or Wood Grounds, to inclose the same in Rotation, one at a Time, for the Space of Eighteen Years, for the Preservation thereof, from the Bite or Spoil of Cattle; and that the said Right of Common of Pasture, in or upon the said Woods, or Wood Grounds, being very injurious to the Growth of Underwood and young Timber therein, the Petitioner the said William Beckford is desirous of inclosine and holding the fame, in Severalty, discharged of all Right of Common, and hath offered to charge the same with a perpetual Yearly Rent Charge of Thirty Pounds, clear of all Taxes and Reprizes, in lieu of, and as a Compensation for, all such Right of Common, and the Owners and Occupiers of the Messuages, Lands, and Tenements, entitled to such Right of Common, are 'willing to accept the fame, and to relinquish their respective Rights of Common in or upon the said Woods, or Wood Grounds, upon Condition that the said Yearly Rent Charge shall be vested in the Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, to be applied in Aid of the Poor Rates; but such Rights of Common cannot be extinguished, nor such -Yearly Rent Charge vested in the said Overseers, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effectuating the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall l'eern meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Parker Coke, Mr. Osborn, and Sir John Honywood, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Court of Assistants, of the Worshipful Company of Clock Makers of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in Consequence of an Act, passed in the last Session, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Clocks and Watches, the Petitioners, and the Trade of Clock and Watch Makers in general, have sustained great and heavy Losses, and, should this Act continue in Force, they will be exposed to Hill greater Hardships, and, from the Effects already produced, they entertain the moll alarming Apprehen-fion of the Dangers to which they will be subjected; and that a great Number of Persons have disposed of their Clocks and Watches, and the Market has become so much overstocked, and the Value of the Article so much reduced, as almost to suspend the Manufacture; and that Multitudes of industrious Workmen, either directly or indirectly engaged in making Tools, Chains, Trinkets, and other Articles, have been thrown out of Employment, and reduced, with their Families, to the utmost Indigence and Distress, the Number of which is daily incfeafing: And therefore praying. That the said Act may be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom it is referred to consider of the several Petitions which have been presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, praying for the Repeal of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Clocks and " Watches:" And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of the Trustees of The British Mufetm, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

' Setting forth. That, in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the Sum, allowed them for the Establishment and Support of the said Mufeuni, was reduced to a Capital of £ 30,000, Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £.900, was, notwithstanding their utmost Attention to the forming their Establishment with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose; upon which Representation they have, at sundry Times, obtained from the House various Sums to supply the Deficiency of their Income, which Sums, together with the Salary allotted to the King's Librarian, yearly amounting to about £.250, have proved insufficient to defray the necessary Expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the Hands of the Trustees is not sufficient to carry on the Purposes of the Trust:, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House, to grant them such farther Support, towards enabling them to carry on the Execution of the Trust reposed 8

in them by Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Called in, and examined.

How long have you been in Business?

Ten Years on, my own Account, and 9 or Years before I took the Business upon myself.

State to the Committee what Effect the Act, which passed in the last Session, for granting certain Duties on Clocks and Watches, has had upon the Trade?

I have been in the Habit of making from 3 to 4,000 Watches Annually; but since the Act took place I have experienced a Diminution as follows:

--The Witness further said. That his Trade is altogether in the Home Trade, and that he exports none.

Are your Watches fold for Exportation or for the Home Trade?

The Home Trade almost exclusively — don't know that 100 Watches of mine go out of the Kingdom.

In what particular Branches of the Business are you

concerned?

Manufacturer of Watches; which is completing the m.

Is there any Diminution of the Orders for Watches since the passing of the Act?

The Diminution is much greater — there is not an Eighth of the Orders that there \vere prior to the Act.

Are the Description of the Watches you make chiefly of the Higher or Lower Value?

'They are chiefly Silver Watches — The Proportion will be about from 2 to 300 Gold, and the Remainder in Silver and Metal; but the greater Proportion in Sil-yer — about a 12th Part Gold. '

In your present diminished Orders, does the same Proportion in the Sale of Gold and Silver Watches flail continue?

The Diminution in the Gold Trade is greater — I do not recollect to have had an Order for a Gold Watch since the Act took place, and have only fold Five since passing the Act to the present-Time.

Do you consider that Decrease in the Sale of Gold Watci ies to be owing to the additional Duty on Gold used ip Watches imposed this Year, or to the Annual 'fax?

To the Annual Tax,

Vol, 53. .

What Number of Workmen did you usually employ previous to the Tax taking place?

Upwards of One hundred.

How many have you been accustomed to pay Weekly Wages to since that Period?

I believe I have not been able to employ Twenty.

Do you not . conceive that the Diminution in the Demand for Watches, during the lad Four Months, may have been occasioned in Part by a Number of Watches offered for Sale, which have been returned ip order to be sold by Persons who have been unwilling to wear them on account of the Burthen imposed upon them by the Annual Tax?

It does not fall under my knowledge to know of a single Return of a Watch.

In the Course of your Enquiries, do you find this Complaint of the Decrease of the Trade general?

Yes.

Have you any particular Means of informing yourself from Time to Time on that Subject?

Yes — by travelling myself, Twice a Year, through England.

Js your Stock of Watches in Hand now as great or larger than it was in February 1797, or is it in Proportion to the Numbers made?

My Stock of complete Watches is larger, in con sequence of endeavouring to employ some few of my befl Workmen, rather than turn them away.

Can you continue to employ your present reduced Number of Hands, without still increasing our Stock, pnless the Annual Tax be taken off?

Jt would be impossible to do so.

I »

528 27 Q Februarii.A. 1798.

Have you, in the Course of your Trade, received Gold Watch Cafes in Part of Payment, since the passing of the Act?

I cannot Hate the exact Number, or the Amount, but I have bought more than 200 Pair of Cafes.

Previous to the passing of the Act, did you frequently buy Gold Cafes?

I believe those 200 Pair of Cafes are more than I ever received in the whole Course of my Trade; and in speaking of that Number, I am very much within Bounds. When they fell their Cafes, they usually fend up their Movements to be put in Silver or Metal Cafes; and I have had more Business of that Nature, than for many Years before.

Do you know any Instance of any Manufacturer in your Trade having, since the passing of the Act, delayed to execute, or refuie, any Orders given them?

I know of no such Instance.

Do you know of any Combination among the Manu-fasturers to make the State of the Trade appear worse than it really is?

I know of no such Instance. I believe that all the Manufacturers, in Humanity to their Servants, have given them Employ without any Prospect of the Sale of their Goods. .>

0

Are there any other Hardships, besides those you have already stated, which you are likely to suffer by, from the Continuance of this Act?

My Dealings are with the Trade, and consequently I am likely to fuller, in as much as the Whole of my Property is in the Hands of Country Watch Makers; and I find, finet;the passing of the Act, Persons who before paid their Accounts regularly, are unable to pay, in consequence of the Decrease of their Trade.

' What were your Weekly Payments to your Workmen before the Tax took place?

From £. 100 to £. 150 Weekly.

What are they now?

For many Weeks past under £. 20.

When you paid the larger Sum, how many Hands do you imagine you employed?

One Hundred.

To what other Branch of Business have those discharged Artificers been able to apply themselves?

Many of them have been compelled to apply to their several Parishes for Relief — many of them have also been obliged to pawn the principal Part of their Goods for their Support; and others have gone for Soldiers and Sailors.

Are there many now totally out of Employment i

Yes — a vast Number.

What do you conceive may be the whole Annual Amount of Watches made for Home Consumption?

I think, and I believe it is the general Opinion of the Trade, they amounted to about 50,000, before the Act took place; the Export Trade being about 70,000.

Do you conceive, that the Diminution of Sale for the Home Trade, is in Proportion to the Diminution experienced in your own particular Trade?

1 believe the principal Manufacturers for the Home Trade, are affected much in the same Proportion with myself. The present general Appearance of the Trade gives us Reason to think it will still gradually 'decrease.

Withdrew.

Called in, and examined.

Have been in Business for myself, and myself and my Father, Forty Years.

What Diminution has taken place in your Trade since the late Act?

About Half; — as will appear by a Paper

What Number of Workmen did you usually pay Weekly Wages to, previous to the Act taking place?

I cannot state the exact Number — but we paid about £. i2o or , 130'a Week.

What Sum do you pay Weekly now?

It is now reduced to, from £. 20 to .£. 25 a Week.

Previous to the passing of the Act, did you frequently buy Gold Cafes of Watches, or receive them in Exchange for other Watches.

Sometimes we did — but seldom.

Have you had much Employment of that Nature since the passing of the Act, in changing Gold Cafes for Silver or Metal, or receiving them in Part of Payment?

Very frequently; but I cannot ascertain the Number.

Have you any further Information to Hate to the Committee, respecting the Effect of the Taxon the Trade?

The Loss of Trade our Customers in the Country have experienced, has rendered our Book Debts precarious, and our Customers declare their Inability to pay, on Account of the Decrease of their Trade.

Is your Stock of Watches now on Hand, as great or larger than it was in February 1797?

I suppose it to be rather lei's; on this Account, that finding a Decay in the Trade from last, we have been more cautious in putting Watches forward.

Is your Stock less ini Proportion to your Number of Hands than it was at the Time of passing the Act?

More in Proportion to the Number of Hands employed.

Can you continue to employ your present reduced Number of Hands, without increasing your Stock on Hand, if the Tax continues?

No — we cannot. We have made many Watches to keep our Hands on, in Hopes of the Trade mending.

Have the Workmen discharged by you since the Tax, been enabled to find Employment elsewhere?

Many of them have not — to my Sorrow I fee their Distress: 1 believe many of them to be beholden to their Parishes for their Support.

Withdrew.

Mr. John Carr, Watch Manufacturer;

Called in, and examined.

Are you engaged in the Watch Manufactory at Coventry?

Yes — as a Principal Five Years.

Are you concerned chiefly in the Home or Foreign Trade?

In the Home.

State to the Committee', whether the Watch Manufactory was in a thriving State previous to the Tax taking place?

Yes — it had been so for several Years.

What Effect has the Annual Tax had on the Trade?

Since the Act has taken place, more than One Half of our Orders have been withdrawn.

What Number of Watches did you make in the Half Year previous to the Annual Tax, from 1796 to Midsummer 1797, and what Number in the

subsequent Year?

From 1 ft January to ift July 1,990 Watches; from l ft July to 1 ft January 1,829 Watches.

Were the Watches manufactured in the last Haif Year made for Orders, or in the Hope of felling them in the common Course of Trade?

In the Hope "of felling the m.

Have you disposed of them with the same Facility as before the passing of the ACb?

We have not.

Is your Stock upon Hand larger or smaller, in Proportion to the Number of Hands employed, than it was in February last?

Much larger.

Were your Workmen fully employed before the Tax took place?

They were.

Are those you still keep fully employed?

They are not.

Do you manufacture chiefly by Apprentices or Journeymen?

By both — the greatest Part by journeymen. What Men we have, we can only give them Three Days Work in a Week, as we have had no Sale for these Two or Three Months past.

7

1798.

Can you continue to supply them even with that Proportion of Work, unless there be some Improvement in the Trade?

We cannot.

Are there any other Branches of Mechanics at Coventry, in which these discharged Men can be employed?

None that I know of.

To what Cause do you ascribe the Reduction of the Manufacture?

From the Annual Tax.

Do you ascribe the Reduction solely to the additional Tax, or to the Effect of the Duty on Gold and Silver ? To the Annual Tax solely.

Do you, in Person or by your Riders, go through the Country upon your Business?

Myself once a Year.

Can you state what Alterations have taken place in the Course of the Trade since the Tax?

[The Witness delivered in the following Statement:]

Do you believe that the Loss of your Orders arises from Watches being returned upon the Hands of the Retail Sellers, or in cortsequence of the Tax?

In consequence of the Tax.

Do you know of Any Combination, on the Part of the Manufacturers, to make the Trade appear worse than it really is?

I do not.

Do you believe that there is any such Thing in Existence?

I verily believe there is not — if there had been, I certainly should have known it.

Have you any Assurance from your Correspondents of further Orders, in case the Tax should be taken off?

I have.

Do you believe that the Watch Manufactory would revive if the Tax be taken off?

I do think so.

Do you think any thing ftiort of Repeal would answer that Purpose?

I myself think it would not.

In what Situation are your Book Debts, in consequence of the present State of the Trade?

Very casual — Ilook upon our Property in Trade to be reduced One Half by it; that is, 10 in the Pound.

Withdrew.

Mr. John Carry again called in, and examined,

Do you deal in Ornaments for Watches j and what Effect has the Annual Tax had upon the Birmingham Seal and Chain Trade?

I have been in the Habit of felling them for Twenty Years, and from my own Returns the Sale has been reduced Three Parts out of Four since the impof ing of the Tax.

Would this Branch of the Trader be restored, provid ed the Tax was repealed?

In my Opinion it would.

Is it a Manufacture of Conference?

Three or 4,000 People are employed in it — .-Chain, Seal, and K.ey Makers, are Three distinct Branches of Trade — there are some who do manufacture the Whole, but not many.

Mr. Edward Bin}, of;

Called in, and examined.

Are you engaged in the Clock and Watch Business? Yes — for above Twelve Years;

Can you state the different Effect it has had on the Clock and Watch-making Business?

The Effect has been much the fame; but in the rough Material considerably more.

Are the Persons employed in the Business in , Manufacturers or Venders only?

In the Watch Trade Venders only-r-there were a great many Clocks manufactured in Bristol before the Tax, and the Business in the raw Material was more considerable than in making Clocks complete.

Have you observed any Diminution in the Sale of Clocks and Watches since the Imposition of the late Duty?

Yes.

Yo what Amount?

Equal to Three Fourths in my own Business.

Have you observed its ElTects upon the Business of others concerned in the same Trade?

Yes — I have made it my Business to esquire; the Result has been a Diminution of Three Fourths, some Five Sixths, and none less than Halt.

Do you know the Number of Persons employed in the Watch and Clock Trade at Bristol?

About 150 to 20c; Matters and Workmen.

Have any been thrown out of Employ in consequence of the Tax?

A considerable Number.

Has any Alteration taken place in your own Journeymen or Apprentices?

At present I have no more Work than what I can do myself and my Apprentice, and I have before employed Two Apprentices, and sometimes a Journeyman besides.

Have you been engaged in felling Ornaments for Watches?.

Yes.

Have the same Effects attended that Btanch of the Trade? '

It has very materially diminished it.

Has there be'en a Manufacture for rough Materials for the Trade carried on at Bristol?

There has, for Clock Work; in one House a Diminution has taken place of Cwt. a Week in rough Brass for Clocks, and nearly in the same Proportion with others.

In what Degree Has your Trade of Clock Maker been reduced since the Tax?

As a Clock Maker I may say it has been totally annihilated, for I have only fold One Clock since: I used to fell about Six in Six Months.

What has been the Diminution in Watches ? Three Fourths.

Withdrew.

Mr. Charles Penny, of;

Called in, and examined.

What Branch of Business have you carried on?

A Vender of Watches.

Has your Sale experienced any Diminution since the Duty has been laid on Watches?

Considerably more than' One Half.

Can you state what the Effect has been upon the Trade in general, at Bristol, since the Tax?

I have made it my Business to inform myself; and it has decrcafed One Half, and in many Cafes considerably more.

Has the same Effect happened with respect to the Manufacture of rough Materials for Clocks?

That Branch of the Business which used to supply the Clock Makers in the Western Counties, and Wales, is now almost annihilated.

Having stated to the Committee, upon your former Examination, that there was a great Decreale in your Manufactory, how do you account for the Statement delivered in, shewing that Decreale not to be considerable?

Orders that were had before the Tax was laid on, which Orders we lent out to the Watch Makers, although not One in Six were really fold.

Is that Nurnper of Watches given actually fold?

They are not — they are lent to different Correspondents in the Country, with their Names on them, and then they are paid for when fold — and I know they are not fold, because I have just come off that journey,

Withdrew',

Mr. William Bradshaw, again called in, and examined.

Can you state the Number of Watches made by you in the Half Year previous to the Annual Tax, and like-wife in the Half Year subsequent?

Before the Tax I might manufacture between Forty and Fifty per Week; and since, not Half: And before the Tax I always had Orders in the House for more than I could get made. As soon as the Tax took place I had daily Countermands of Orders, dating, that they should never fell them, or be able to pay for them. I have been making a few even since. I have such a Stock now in Hand, that unless the Demand for Watches is increased, I dread the Consequence; and I am certain that nothing but the Repeal of the Tax will cause the Sale of them. We are obliged to do some Work for the Sake of employing our Apprentices, which is now a Loss to us, and whole Indentures cannot be thrown up.

Withdrew.

Has been in the Business Fourteen or Fifteen Years.

Has your Business suffered considerably since the passing of the Tax?

Since the 6th of December last to about the 14th Instant, I did not fell a single Watch — Before the Tax,

I was in the Habit of felling One Watch a Week.

Have you any particular Means of ascertaining the Distresses of the Clock and Watch Makers in your Part of the Country?

Oh the Call of the Committee in , a Meet-

ing of the Clock and Watch Makers was called in our County, and an Enquiry made respecting the Business j when it seemed, on the Average, that Half the Trade was loft since the Tax commenced, and that some have loft near Three Fourths. I was Chairman of the Committee; and the Tax has had the same Effect upon others in the Trade at Leicester, as upon myself. Previous to the Tax, I was in the Habit of felling Forty Clocks in the Year; and since, I have only fold Two, One of which was ordered before. Since the Tax, I have bought many Watches merely for the Price of the Gold and Silver, and more Gold ones than others.

Mr. John Chapman, Clock Maker, at -Loughborough;

Called in, and examined.

Has been in the Habits of felling Clocks Twenty-three Years.

What Effect has the Tax had upon your Trade ? Nearly destroyed it — I have not fold One Clock during the last Three Months — previous, I usually fold about Seven in Three Months.

What Effect has it had on your Situation in Life?

I have been affected in the same Proportion with respect to the Sale of Watches.

Has it had the same Effect upon the rest of the Trade in Leicester?

Yes.

Withdrew.

In what Situation are they now as to Employment?

I have had more Applications for Work since the Tax, than I ever had-at any former Time — and Two of my Journeymen are lately gone Abroad.

Are the rest of the Trade in a better Situation than yourself?

Much worse.

Do you believe the Reduction in the Sale of your Clocks and Watches to arise wholly from the Annual Tax?

' I felt the Decline of my Business from the Moment the Tax took place.

Do you think any Measure can restore your Trade except the Repeal of the Tax?

Nothing less than that.

Are there many Hands employed in Scotland in repairing Clocks and Watches?

Yes, a great many.

Called in, and examined.

Has been in the Business about Thirty-three Years.

Has any, and what Alteration taken place, in your Business since the Act?

In Clocks, since the Act, by taking the same Time in preceding Years, there is a Difference in my Trade of nearly Two Thirds Decrease — In Watches a Decrease of about Half. The Clocks and Watches I make are of the best Quality — none of the common Sort.

Have you been under the Necessity of discharging some of your Workmen in consequence of the Act?

I do not employ so many as I did.

Will the Decline of the Watch Trade diminish the Supply of Mechanics capable of constructing the Machinery used in Astronomical and other Observations?

Doubtless it is likely to do lb.

Are you of Opinion, That, in consequence of the Tax, any considerable Emigration will take place, and any valuable Secrets be thereby communicated, to Foreign Countries, to the Prejudice of the Manufacturers in this?

Yes, it certainly mull.

Do you consider the English Watches to be fhperior to those of any other Country?

Certainly they are. — Sometimes a Watch fold for 150 Guineas is intrinsically, with respect to the Materials, not worth 20r. — -The Materials areincreased ip value, in many Instances, by Labour, a Thousand Times. We thought, before the passing of the Act, that the higher Watches and Time Pieces which I make would not be affected by the Tax; but we find it otherwise.

Withdrew.

Mr. Whitfield Grtcnwell, Watch Finilher;

Called in, and examined.

Do you know any Thing of the present State of the Trade?

With respect to the Trade, it is in extreme Distress — the Parish Work-houses are daily filling with the Poor of the Trade.

Has it affected your particular Branch?

My Branch is in the Repeating Line, and the very best Kind of Work.

Have you done much Business before the Tax-took place?

Yes.

Has any Alteration taken place since?

Yes; so much so that I have not had One \Vatch to finish.

Do you know any particular Circumstances respeCfc-ing the Workmen employed in the Trade?

I am one of the Committee of Workmen; and know that they did resolve, that in case the Act was not repealed to petition for Leave to depart from this Kingdom, with their Families.

How many Persons were Parties to that Resolution?

The Committee at that Time might perhaps represent 5,000 Persons, and it was then the general Intention of the Workmen in the Trade to make that Application.

Mr. Charles Smith, Watch Manufacturer in the

Home and Foreign Trade, Bunhill Row,;

Called in, and examined.

Are the Home and Foreign Trades connected, with respect to the Instruction and Employment of the Workmen?

They are — the Foreign Trade is chiefly confined to certain Parts of the Year; and, if it was not for the Home Trade we should experience great Difficulty how to employ the Men at Times when we are not getting up those Foreign Orders.

What Effect has the Act had upon the Trade generally?

With respect to my, own Trade, within Six Months there has been a Deficiency of 1,071 Watches; and I believe the Decrease in the Trade generally has in many Cafes been much higher.

2 70 Februarii.

Do you knovy whether, in consequence of the Clock and Watch Manufacturers being out of Employ in the Parish of Clerkenwell, any and what Number of them have applied to the Parish for Relief?

Yes — We began to take an Account of them in November last, and Seventy-nine have applied to the Workhouse for Relief for themselves and Families. The Committee for relieving the Poor meet only Once a Fortnight to relieve the Poor. The Number of Applications since November has gradually increased. The Number of our Poor last Year in the House was 345, and out of it 140 were relieved Weekly. Besides the Seventy-nine Watch Makers who made Applications to the Workhouse for Relief, other Clock and Watch Makers have, since the Act, been relieved by the Churchwarden and Overseer; upwards of Forty by the Churchwarden, and as many by the Overseer, making together upwards of 150, all Watch and Clock Makers; none of whom had ever applied to the Parish before; :and that Number exceeds One Fourth of the whole -Number of the Poor.

Withdrew.

Mr John Gregson, Watch Maker, of London,

- Called in, and examined.

Are the Artizans of this Country in the Watch Trade, capable of performing the Workmanship in a superior Manner than Foreigners?

Y«s- — and particularly in the Jewelling of Watches, which cannot be done elsewhere. During the Thirty Years 1 refilled at Paris as a Watch Maker, I had always Keeourse to London for those Works, the Workmen in other Countries not being able to make them. I have resided in England Four Years, and my Business within the last Six Months has decreased more than One Half. My Work is chiefly of the most valuable Sort.

Do the Manufacturers of this Country derive any Advantage from Foreigners not knowing this Art?

Yes, certainly — by the Sale of those Articles to Foreigners, which cannot be had Abroad.

Very flourishing — we had more Orders than we could execute — since the Tax the Trade has diminiftied One Half.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Free- Potion holders, Justices of the Peace, Commissioners of Supply, and Heretors, of the County of Banff, specially «np the low convened by public Advertisement at Banff, the 15th PnceofConi» of February 1798, to take into their Confederation the present low Prices of Grain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, while Agriculture is acknowledged an Object of the first National Importance, the Means of improving and extending it must be considered highly deserving the Attention and Support of the Legislature; and that the Petitioners cannot contemplate with Indifference the Distresses which the Farmer suffers from, the present low Prices, and great Stagnation in the Sale, of Grain, and are of Opinion the Evil of which they complain originates principally from the Opening of the Ports for the Introduction and Sale of Foreign Grain: By the Corn Laws, the Importation of Grain has been prohibited in certain Circumstances, and Exportation encouraged by a Bounty, and, from a Review of those Laws, and the State of Agriculture for a Century past, they cannot help expressing their Fears that, unless the Importation of Grain from Foreign Countries be immediately prohibited, the Industry of the People will be turned from the railing of Corn to Objects of less Importance to the Prosperity of the Kingdom; and that the present low Prices of Grain may be attributed to another Cause operating with the former, namely, the late heavy additional Duties laid on the small Scots Stills, and the avowed Intentions of His Majesty's Ministers farther to depress them; and that, while the Petitioners highly applaud the Policy which enjoins the Suspension of Distilling in Times of Scarcity, they contend that the Discouragement or Suppression of the Distilleries inordinary Seasons of Plenty is highly prejudicial to the Interests of Agriculture — the Farmer is deprived of a certain Market for his Grain — the Price which, he receives bears no Proportion to the Rent he pays, and is totally inadequate to support the Expence of Labour, and the Maintenance of his Family; and that the Petitioners are well warranted in afierting, that, since the Discouragement of the legal Stills, the Smuggler has re-commenced his illicit and pernicious Traffic of both Foreign and Home-made Spirits; tempted by the low Prices of Grain, and, having little Property to lose, these Adventurers are daily becoming Vo numerous, and so expect, that it is almost impossible to frame -Laws which could reach and punjlh them — and that, though the Distilleries are charged with corrupting the Morals of the People, the Petitioners assert that the lower Ranks of Society, in all the Northern Counties of Scotland, are as loyal, sober, and pure in their Morals, as any of the same Denomination in Europe, and the Interests of Virtue are much more in Danger from the Trade of Foreign Smuggling, and the Prevalence of unlicensed Distilleries at Home: For these and other Reasons which might be specified, the Petitioners respectfully beseech the House to restore them to the Benefit of the Act of 1784, or to adopt such Measures as to them may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. George Meffiter being examined, said. That a Progress hath been made in repairing the said Roads, in the doing of which a considerable Debt hath been contrafted on the Credit of the Tolls by the said Acts granted, which cannot be paid off, and the said Roads be effectually amended, widened, turned, and kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers of the said Acts be enlarged, and some additional Tolls granted.

That the Road leading from Zeals Green to the Parish of Maiden Bradley, through or into the several Parishes and Places of Stourton, in the County of Wilts, and mington and Norton Ferris, in the County of Somerset, and also the Road leading from the present Road, opposite the Porter's Lodges at Zeals aforesaid, through the said Parishes or Mere and Stourton, to join the last mentioned Road at the North End of Lane, are much out of Repair, narrow, and incommodious, and that it would be beneficial to the Neighbourhood, and of Public Utility, if the same were put under the Care and Management of the Trustees for executing the said Acts.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to make Provision, in the said Bill, for extending the Provisions of the said Act to the said United Provinces, and to the Persons exercising the Powers of Government therein, and also to the Persons, Territories, and Places, under their Government.

MR. John Pitt presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill to continue the Term, and enlarge the Powers, of Two several Acts, passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty

A Petition of the Subscribers, Brewers in the City of Petition of Edinburgh and its Environs, was presented to the House, agIiuftEdin-and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for enlarging the burgh Two Term granted by an Act, of the Twenty-fifth Year of j mes 540(4 the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for continuing the Duty of Two Pennies Scots upon every Pint of Ale and Beer sold in the City of Edinburgh, for the Purposes therein mentioned, and for explaining

38 Geo. ill- Martil 357

plaining and amending the said Act; and Setting forth. That the Duty under which the Brewers of Edinburgh and its Environs have so long laboured, and which is fought to be renewed by the present Bill, is a most intolerable Grievance, unjust and oppressive in its Principle, and most injurious to the Public Revenue and Agriculture of the Country, and to the Community at large; and that, while the House and the Country fee the Necessity of giving every Encouragement to the Consumption of Porter, Ale, and other Malt Liquors, as elsential to the Morals and Health of the People, the present Bill is counteracting ever)' such Measure in the Metropolis of Scotland and its Environs, by laying ' Burthens on the Manufacture which put it out of the Power of the Brewer to make his Liquors of such Quality as to induce the general Use of them; and that the Petitioners cannot admit that the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council, of the City of Edinburgh, are entitled to a Renewal of the Duties which they now apply for, the Debt, said by the Bill to be due, not having been properly contracted, considerable Part of it having arisen from Misapplication of the Money arising from the Duty, and a great Loss having been occasioned by the partial and improper Conduct of the said Lord Provost and Magistrates, and those employed in the Collection of it; and that there is no Ground for renewing this odious Imposition upon ' them, but, if it is necessary to provide a Fund for liquidating the Debt contracted upon the Faith of the' Adh before recited, much better Means may be devised than renewing the Imports fought for by the present Bill, which lo materially affects the Petitioners, their Manufacture, and the Public, and particularly, that a general Duty affecting the Inhabitants at large of the City of Edinburgh, and its Environs, would be much more advisable: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to allow the 1 Petitioners to be heard, by themselves, or their Coun-' fel, against the aforesaid Bill, and to reject the fame, or to give to the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.
