of Hill Street, Berkeley Square, in the said County, Esquire, Henry Grant, of Portman Square, in the said County, Esquire, William Mills,. of BiJlern, in the County of Hants, Esquire, Robert Sherbourne, of Raven-head, in the County of Lancaster, Esquire, James Affleck, Esquire, a Lieutenant Colonel in His Majesty's Army, and Alexander Aubert, of Aujliti London, Esquire, on Behalf of themselves and the other Proprietors of the Manufactory and Property of the late Governor and Company of the British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, to incorporate certain Persons therein named, and their Success'ors, with proper Powers for the Purpose of establishing one or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the more effectually supporting and conducting the same upon an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner, calculated for calling of large Plate Glass, read: And,

Mr. Alexander, Black being.examined, said. That the said Manufactory was established in the Year 1773, and was conducted by the Governor and Company, in conformity to the Terms of the said Act, first with a. Capital Stock of £. 40,000, and afterwards with an -extended Capital of £. 60,000, aided by Loans negotiated by the Company to a large Amount, until the Year 1794, when the said Company yvere under the Necessity of felling the Whole of their Property for Payment of their Debts, and Thomas Oakes, Esquire, became the Purchaser thereof, at the Sum of 105,600, on Behalf of himself and others, who, from thenceforth, carried on the said Manufactory under the Authority and according to the Regulations of the said Act, until the Expiration of the Term thereby limited for the Continuance thereof, which expired at the End of the Session of the Year 1705; and from that Period' the Proprietors of the said Manufactory have carried on the same on their joint Account as a private Company.

And the Witness further said, That by virtue of the said Purchase by the said Thomas Oakes, and of subsequent Transfers of Shares, the said Manufactory, and the Estates and EffeC'ts belonging thereto, are now become the Property of the Petitioners, and of those on whose Behalf they petition.

And being further examined, the Witness said, That the Method of making Plate Glass hath been greatly improved by the said Manufactory, and the Public Revenue arising from the Duties laid on Plate Glass hath in consequence been confulerably increased, and is likely to be so, by a Continuance of the said Manufactory; but inalmuch as the same cannot be carried on to Advantage without a larger Capital than is at present employed therein, and as the Contributors to such Capital will be numerous, and as all the Proprietors or Co-partners in a private Company mud be named in all Actions, Suits, and legal Proceedings by or against them, which will be attended with great Inconvenience, and as they may also be liable to have Commissions of Bankrupt issued against them as Traders, which will deter many Persons from engaging in the Concern, it is very desirable that the Proprietors of the said Manufactory should be incorporated, with proper Powers for carrying on the fame.

Mr. Tucker Steward reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Joseph , of in

the County of Middlesex, Engineer, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed hint to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, His Majesty's Letters Patent, bearing Date the 23d Day of April 1784, granting to the said Joseph Bramah, for the Term of Fourteen Years from the Date thereof, for that Part of Great Britain called , and the Town

of Berwick-upon-Tweed, the Sole Use, Benefit, and Advantage, of his Indention of a new Sort of Lock for Doors, Drawers, Cabinets, and every other Purpose for which secure Fastenings are required, was read: And,

Mr. William Redgt ive, Book-keeper to Mr.

being examined, produced to your Committee a Statement of Disbursements and Receipts in the Lock Trade of Mr. Bramah; and said, That Mr. Bramah has progressively lowered the Price of his Locks, so as to fell them at Two-thirds less Price than what he was able to do at the Commencement of the Business: Then,

Mr. William Nicholsonbeing examined, was a iked,

Whether, amongst the various Objects that have occupied his Studies, he had ever considered the Nature and Offices of secure Fastenings, commonly called Locks, and their Importance in Society? he said. He had. And being asked, Whether he ever had Occasion to consider the Nature and Principles on which this Instrument has in general been constructed prior to the Petitioner's Patent, and whether, in consequence of such Confide-ration, he had been led to any Conclusions on the Merits or Demerits of Locks so constructed, or to judge on the Sufficiency or Insufficiency of them to the Purposes. for which they were intended ? he said, That the Locks commonly to be bought are insecure in a great many Respects. And being asked, Whether he had ever endeavoured to trace the Causes which render Locks, on the common Construction, deficient in Point of Security ? he said. It would be difficult to enumerate the Causes specified in general, but it may be stated that a Depredator has Access to the Bolt by Means of Pick Locks, and can besides, with Ease, procure Keys. And being asked, Whether he had ever examined and considered the Principle laid down in the Petitioner's Patent for the Fabrication of Locks, so as to draw any Conclusions on the Competence or Incompetence of the Invention to the Object of perfect and inviolable Security, considered with Regard to Principle only ? he said. When the Patentee published a Pamphlet on this Subject, he read it with Attention, and understood the Principle from his Description, previous to having seen the Lock; afterwards, on seeing the Implements, he endeavoured to investigate its Powers, to determine what might be its Defects, and from much Meditation he is disposed to think himself considerably Master of both. And being asked, Whether he ever considered the Petitioner's Principle as truly scientific, and derived from a real mathematical Original, and capable of the endless Variation he sets forth in his Cafe? he said, Vot. 53.

Yes, in Theory and Practice he conceived the Advantages to exceed, not fall short. And being asked, Whe-r ther he conceives that (provided Duplication is avoided in manufacturing the Petitioner's Locks) perfect Security is attainable, and maintainable through any distant Periods of Time, as set forth in his Cafe? he said, Yes. And being asked, W hether he believes that it is likely this Duplication will be the Consequence of a random Fabrication, or a Want of that systematic Order observed by the Petitioner in carrying on this. Work, or whether it can be avoided by any other Means than that he prescribes in his same ? he said. That he has inspected the Machinery of the Petitioner by Means of which he avoids the Operation of Hand Work in constructing his Locks; that if the Lock9 were constructed by a less curious and well-contrived Machinery, or by Hand, he has no Doubt but many Duplicates mud infallibly be produced; with respect to the other Means of avoiding Duplicates in manufacturing, he mud decline speaking to, as it includes too large a Field of Investigation. And being asked, Whether he has examined the State of Perfection to which the Petitioner has matured his Invention, and whether he has considered it as a Work both laborious and costly ? he said, That he has seen the Works, and is convinced that the bringing them to the Perfection they are now in, mud have been attended with much Labour and great Expence. And being asked. Whether the Accomplishment of the Objects of the Petitioner has been attended with much Study and Invention; or whether the Principle requires that Degree of Accuracy said to be attained unto by him, in order to produce and perpetuate the main Objects of the Invention? he said. The Organization of the Principle of these Locks mud have been attended with much Study and Invention, as mull likewise have been every particular subordinate Detail in the manufacturing. And being asked. Whether he has examined the Machines, Tools, and Implements, said to be invented and rected by the Petitioner for the sole Purpose of acquiring Speed and Exactness in this Business, and whether such Machines, Tools, and Implements are voluminous, ingenious, and costly, and if they will be of great Use or not in any other Branch of the Petitioner's Works should he not have Employment for them in the Lock Way ? he said. That the Machinery is voluminous, ingenious, and costly, and as he (the Wit/iefs) conceives icarcely, applicable to any other Purposes than those to which it was originally directed. And,

Mr. Alexander Palmer, Cutler, being examined, said. That he carries on the Trade of a Locksmith. And being asked. Whether he ever examined the Locks made by the Petitioner? he said. Yes, and that in his Opinion, with Regard to the Security of those Locks, the Bit of the Key being now fixed on the internal Part of the Lock, which was formerly fixed to the Key, and the Accuracy with which they are constructed, they are inviolable. And,

Mr. Samuel Rehe, Mathematical Instrument and Watch Maker, being examined, said, That Mr. mah' % Works-are exceedingly extensive; that he (the Witness) has in the Course of his Trade made many Machines and Contrivances for making Instruments of many Sorts for Silk throwing and spinning of Cotton; that he knows Mr. Bramah's Machinery are original Inventions, and mult have been made at a great Expence, and are the Result of great Labour and Ingenuity, and that his Locks are brought to a high Degree of Perfec- , tion, and as he conceives are fold cheap in proportion' to the Coil of the Materials of which they are made. . His Doubts concerning the practical Application of the Principle, when he first perused Mr. Bramah's Pamphlet, w'ere entirely directed to Particulars of a practical Nature; that he is convinced that the Locks would be rendered more accessible and less Valuable, if construded in any less perfect Manner, and that his Doubts were removed by Inspection of the Patentee's Works. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Freeholders of the Parish of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, on Behalf of themselves arid other Freeholders of the said Parish, and also of other Inhabitants, assessed and paying the Poor Rates of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the several Commons and Waste Lands lying within the Manor and Parish of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick', and Setting forth, That the Expences of maintaining the Poor within the said Parish have rapidly increased, and now amount to the enormous Sum of £. 25,000 per Annum, whereas Twenty Years ago they were little more than One Fourth Part of this Sum; and that, from Tim? to Time, the Parish have had it in Contemplation to eale the Poors Rates by agreeing with the Freeholders for Part of the said Waste Lands, for the general Benefit of the Poor of the said Parish, there being a Clause in the Guardian Act enabling the Guardians and Overseers of the Poor'to purchase One hundred Acres of Land, for the general Advantage of the Parish Poor; and that it appears to be highly expedient that the general Sense of the Freeholders and Inhabitants should betaken on this Measure before an Act of Inclosure takes place; and that the present Application for an Act of Inclosure has been made by a few Individuals, without the Concurrence of the Petitioners, the Freeholders, and Inhabitants at large, and there is Reason to apprelund these few expect to divide the Whole among themselves; and that the Inclosure of 380 Acres of Waste Land, being the Whole thereof, lying near or adjoining to so populous a Town as Birmingham, is a Matter of great Importance, and requires much previous deliberate Confederation: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law this Session, but that further Time may be allowed for Deliberation, and for investigating the Claims of the Freeholders at large, and the general Advantage of the Parish, in order that, if it should be thought advilable to inclose the said Waste Land, the general Interest of the Town and Parish, and the private Interests of Individuals, may be more accurately known and determined.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

The Lord Mayor of London reported frotn the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for improving any City or Town, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House 5 and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for widening and improving the Entrance into the City of London, near Temple; for making a more commodious Street or Passage at Snow Hill, and for railing, on the Credit of the Orphans Fund, a Sum of Money for those Purposes, was read: And,

Mr. William Montagu being examined, said. That a considerable Progress hath been made in putting the said Act in Execution, and it hath been discovered that the Powers thereof require to be altered, amended, enlarged, and rendered more effectual, in order to enable the Petitioners to complete the several Works by the said Act authorized and directed to be done: That tVie taking down of the Church of Saint Clement Danes, as authorized by the said Act, will be attended with great unhecessary Expence, as well as Inconvenience to the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and that, by Plans and Surveys lately made, it appears that a commodious and sufficient Enlargement of the Street from Saint ment's Church Yard to Temple Bar, may be made without removing the said Church, and at a much less Expence, by taking down certain Houses on the South Side of the Strand, and at the West End of Saint Clement's Church Yard; whereby the Communication between the Cities of London and will be

greatly improved:

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and enlarge, the Powers of an Act, passed in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for widening and improving the Entrance into the City of London near " Temple Bar; for making a more commodious Street " or Passage at Snow Hill-, and for railing; on the Credit of the Orphans Fund, a Sum of Money for those " Purposes:" And that the Lord Mayor of London and Mr. Alderman Combe do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for and upon every Carriage with less than Four Wheels, to be drawn by One Horse, Mare, or Gelding, kept to be used in the Affairs of Husbandry by any Person occupying a Farm, and making a Livelihood solely thereby, or kept for the Purpose of carrying Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, from Place to Place, in the Way of Trade, by any Person carrying on any Trade, and making a Livelihood solely thereby (although the same may occasionally be used by such Person, or his or her Servants, for other Purposes) which shall be built and constructed wholly of Wood and iron, without any Covering other than a tilted Covering, and without any.Lining or Springs, or any Ornament whatever other than Paint of a dark Colour, for the Preservation of the Wood or Iron only, and which shall have the Words " a Taxed Cart," and also the Owner's Name and Place of Abode, thereon, and the Price of which (Repairs excepted) shall not have exceeded, or the Value whereof shall not at any Time exceed the Sum of Twelve Pounds Sterling, there shall be charged ✓ the Annual Sum of One Pound and Four Shillings.

Extract of a Letter from Captain Cotes to the Commissioners for conducting His Majesty's Transport Service, and taking Charge of Prisoners of War, dated 13th March, 1798.

And the Title of the said Paper was read.

Ordered, That the said Paper be referred to the Com-hiittee, to whom it is referred to consider of the several Papers which, upon Wednesday last, were presented to the House, by Mr. Whitehead, from the Transport Board, and by Mr. Stewart, from the Commissioners for Sick and Wounded Seamen, respecting the Treatment of Prisoners of War.

The said Paper is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

An ingrossed Bill for dividing and inclosing the Heaths, Fen Grounds, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parish of Reydon, in the County of Suffolk, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act for dividing and inclosing the Heaths, Fen Grounds, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parish of Reydon, in the County of Suffolk.

Ordered, That Sir Charles Runbwry do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

An ingrossed Bill for dividing and inclosing the Heaths, Fen Grounds, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parishes of Gijleham and Pakefield, in the County of Suffolk, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act for dividing ajid inclosing the Heaths, Fen Grounds, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parishes of Gijleham and Pakefield, in the County of Suffolk.

Ordered, That Sir Charles Bunbury do carry the Bill ,to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, -to consider further of the several Reports which, in the last Session of Parliament, were made from the Select Committee, who were appointed to examine and state the Total Amount of the Public Debts, and other Matters relating to the Public Revenue and Expenditure; .

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday, the 17th Day of April next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty;

- - Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

- RefJved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The House was rrjoved, That the Order, made upon the 2.8th Day of February last, for taking into further Consideration, Tomorrow, the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to explain

and amend an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King William the Third, Intituled, " An Act for preventing Charge and Expence in Elections of Members " to serve in Parliament,' was committed, might be read.

And the said Oi'der being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Th'urfday, the 19th Day of April next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Walker and Mr. Spranger:

Petition for 'A Petition of the several Persons thereunto fub-Leave to pre- feribing, Owners and Occupiers of Land adjoining, forre-imHd-11 and hear to, the River Tweed, in the Neighbourhood of in" Kelib Kelso, in the County of Roxburgh, was presented to Bruige. . tjle House, and read; Setting forth. That about Forty Years ago a Bridge, chiefly by Voluntary Subscription, was built across the Rivet Tzveed, below its Junction with the Tiviot, near Kelso, at an Expence of between if. 7,000 and £.8,000; and that the said Bridge has been of great Advantage to that Part of the Country, but, by the very high Floods of the Tweed and Tiviot, in the Month of Qflober last, the same was thrown down, whereby the Communication to and from the Northern and Southern Parts of the County of Roxburgh, as well as the neighbouring Counties of Berwick and Northumberland, has been greatly impeded, the Fords on the said River being dangerous, and often impafiable; and that, as it would be of the greatest Advantage to the Public to have the said Bridge rebuilt," the Petitioners have been employed in taking the necessary Information, as well with regard to the Scite and Strudlure of the Bridge, and the Materials which, ought to be employed, as to the Expence of executing the Work; but, as during the Winter Season, owing to Floods and otherwise, the Bed of the River could not be explored with Advantage, much Time has necessarily elapsed before the Petitioners could come to any Degree of Certainty with respect to those Particulars, fq as to know whether there was a Probability of again erecting the Bridge by Voluntary Subscription, and without the Necessity of levying any Toll or Pontage; and that it is now evident the Expence of re-building the said Bridge will be so great, that it cannot be done without the Authority of Parliament for that Purpose, and for. levying a Pontage on the said Bridge; and that the Time limited for presenting Petitions for Private Bills is now elapsed, and it would be attended with great Loss and Inconveniehce to the Town of Kelso, and the whole Country around, were the Application to lie over till next Session of Parliament: And therefore praying. Sir George Douglas reported from the Committee, to Kelso Bridge whom the Petition of the several Persons thereunto sub- tg£n> re" feribing. Owners and Occupiers of Land adjoining, and near to, the River Tweed, in t,he Neighbourhood of Kelso, in the County of Roxburgh, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for building Bridges, had not been complied with, the Bridge in the Petition mentioned having been thrown down by the very high Floods of the River Tweed sib late as the 22d of OBoherlaft; and that the Commit- > tee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House;'and he re&d the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth > viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed your Committee, That about Forty Years ago a Bridge was built, chiefly by voluntary Subscription, across the River Twee below its Junction with the Tiviot, near Kelso, at an Expence of between Seven and Eight Thousand Pounds, which Bridge has been of great Advantage to that Part of the Country:

That by the very high Floods of the Tweed and Tiviot, in the M<pnth of Octoberlaft, the said Bridge was thrown down, whereby the Communication to and from the Northern and Southern Parts of the County of as well as the neighbouring Counties of Berwick and Northumberland, has been greatly impeded, the Fords on the said River being dangerous and often impassable; and that it would be of the greatest Advantage to the Public to have the said Bridge rebuilt, but as it will cost a very considerable Sum to rebuild the fame, and make the necessary Avenues thereto, and as there are no Funds for Payment thereof, the same cannot be effected without the Authority of Parliament, for building the fame, and levying a Toll or Pontage thereon, or near thereto.

A Petition of the Religious Society of Friends, commonly called Quakers, was presented to the House, and VoL -53-

read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners; although they have continually lamented the Miseries occasioned to the Natives of Africa by the Slave Merchants of England, and the Want of Success even of the Measures which have been attempted in, the House for their Relief, have not, until lately, believed it their Duty again to solicit the Attention of the House to the extreme Injustice of the Traffic, and to the Injury which it produces to the Morals of the People, and to the Welfare of the Nation; for, however trite may be the Assertion, it remains a-Truth that Righteousness exalts a Nation, and, therefore, that the Public Sanction of Injustice, so flagrant as a Trade in the Persons of Men, is among the Causes which induce National Calamity; and it is to be deplored, that it should be necessary to urge the Extirpation of this cruel Trade by any other Motive than its own inherent Evil, but in these Times, pregnant with Alarms, it surely becomes us, if there be any Truth in our Professions of Trust in the Providence of the Almighty, to endeavour to recommend ourselves to His Protection, by forbearing to blast the Comforts ' of so large a Part of His rational Creation; and that the Petitioners trust they are adverting to an incontrovertible Truth, when they request the House of Commons to recollect that, compared with Divine Protection, all human Efiorts are as a Thing of nought; and that the Almighty can protest with equal Ease in the Hour of extreme Perplexity as in the Time of less impending Danger; and that the Evil of the Slave Trade is not now unknown and obscure, it has been proved at the Bar of the House, and has been con. demned by their Voice: 'Still, nevertheless itfubfifts; and fubfilcs with unabated Rapacity: The Petitioners, therefore, once more earnestly bclcech the House to take such Steps for its immediate Abolition as may warrant and animate the Hope of a Continuance of Divine Favour to this our Country, by the Reflection that our Country at Length ceales to spread Desolation over the Regions of Africa.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A MESS AGE by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by 'virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. James Daly, a Surveyor and Builder, being examined, said, That the said Parish Church was. in a very ruinous and dangerous State, and that the said Money was duly laid out and expended in repairing the said Church: Then,

Mr. Thomas Cumber being further examined, said. That for securing the Payment of such Annuities, the said Churchwardens and Overseers, together with several of the principal Inhabitants of the said Parish, did, in pursuance of several Orders of Vestry, enter into Bonds to the Persons who had advanced the above Sum of Money, for Payment to them, during their respective Lives, out of the Annual Assessments which should be made on the Inhabitants of the said Parish, such Yearly Annuities upon the Sums respectively advanced as were agreed upon at such Vestries: And,

John Cowper, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Churchwardens and Overseers have paid to the several Annuitants, out of the Church Rates which have been made and assessed upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, their Annuities as they became due, until on or about the Year 1795? but since that Time they have not been able to raise and pay the same, without advancing a Part thereof out of their own private Monies, to prevent Actions being brought against them, owing to some of the Inhabitants having refused to pay their Quota to such Rates, alledging that the same were made from the Poor's Rates, against which they had appealed as being illegal and contrary toLaw: That by reason of fu'ch Refusal, the present Churchwardens and Overseers are involved in great Difficulty and Distress, being wholly unable to pay the Annuities granted by their Predecessors in Office as they become due, and that unless Power is given to enable the Petitioners to satisfy the Claims of those Annuitants who are now living, as their Annuities become due, and all Arrears thereof, either by making and collecting Rates sufficient for that Purpose, or by some other Means, it will be attended with great Injury and Expence to the Petitioners, and all those who are engaged in the Bonds, as well as be the Means of producing much Mischief and Disorder in managing the Affairs of the said Parish.

A PETITION of the Master, Wardens, Searchers, Petition of and Assistants, of the Company of Cutlers, within Hallamshire, in the County of York, and of the against Ship

Merchants, Manufacturers, and Tradesmen, residing at Owners Bill. Sheffield, and employing Owners and Masters of Ships and Vessels in the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize, -was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Masters of Ships; and Setting forth, That the same will, if passed into a Law, materially injure their Interests, and( the Commercial Interests of this Kingdom, inasmuch as it will, First, completely destroy that Part of the Common Law of the Land which charges Carriers by Water with Responsibility to the Shippers of Merchandize for Loss or Damage happening to such Merchandize whilst in the Custody, and under the Care of such Carriers; Secondly, release all Owners and Masters of Ships and Vessels usually employed in Navigation on the High Seas from Responsibility for any Loss or Damage which hath, already arisen, or shall or may hereafter arise, to any Goods or Merchandize which have been or shall be shipped, taken in, or put on Board of any such Ships or Vessels, by Reason or Means of any Accident whatsoever, unless the same shall have happened by or through Robbery, Embezzlement, or the making away with, or by or through the wilful Neglect of the Owner, Master, or Mariners, of the Ship or Vessel; which will, besides opening a wide Field for Fraud, Thirdly, charge the Petitioners and others.

Shippers of Goods, with Losses, which in most probable Cafes may, by due Care, be foreseen and prevented by the Carriers and their Servants, and which the Shippers of Goods cannot have the Power of preventing, and may not be able to insure against, but which the Ship Owners may insure against by railing their Freight in Proportion to the Risque; Lastly, that, if such Losses happen by Robbery, -Embezzlement, secreting, or making away with, or by or through the wilful Neglect of the Carriers or their Servants, the Shippers of Goods will have no Remedy but by proving such Robbery, Embezzlement, secreting, or wilful Neglect, the Difficulty whereof will be apparent to the House, inasmuch as the Master and Mariners of Vessels are the Persons who are likely to be able to prove, and be guilty of the fame: And therefore praying the House wholly to reject the said Bill, and not suffer the same to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do Ire upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Report from

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred Land to consider of an Act, made in this present Session of Act, Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting an Aid to " His Majesty by a Land Tax to be raised in Great " tain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven " hundred-and Ninety-eight," the llefolutic-ns whicliL the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several and respective Sums of Money, charged by virtue of an Act of the present Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty,

" by a Land Tax, for the Service of the Year One " thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-eight," on the respective Counties and Places in Britain, in re-

speft of the Premilles, in the said Act mentioned, lying within the same Counties and Places respectively, to be raised, levied, and paid unto His Majesty within the Space of One Year, from the Twenty-fifth Day of One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-eight, shall, from and after the Expiration of the said Term, continue, and be raised, levied, and paid Yearly to His Majesty, His Heirs and Succefi'ors, from and after the Twenty-fifth Day of March in every Year, for ever; subject nevertheless to the Rules, Regulations, Restrictions, and Conditions of Redemption, to be prescribed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it shall be lawful for Commissioners, to be appointed, for that Purpose, to contract and agree with all and every Persons or Person, Bodies Politic and Corporate, having or holding any Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, for the Redemption of the Land fax charged upon their respective Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, according to the Assessment and Pound V.ate to be made in pursuance of the said Act; and t hat the Consideration to be given for such Redempt ion shall be so much Capital Stock of Public Annuities, transferrable at the Bank of England, bearing an Interest after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centura per Annum, commonly called The ‘Three Pounds pet Centum Consolidated Annuities and The Three Pounds pet Centum Reduced Annuities, as will yield an Annuity or Dividend, exceeding the Amount of the Land Tax so to be redeemed by One Fifth Part thereof; such Capital Stock to be transferred to the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt, within the Period of Five Years from the Time of entering into such Contraft, by Four Instalments in every Year; videlicet, on the First Day of May; the First Day of; the First Day of November; and the First Day of,

in each Year; the First Instalment to be made on such of the said Days as shall next enlue after the entering into such Coptraft; but with Liberty to any Person to stipulate with the said Commissioners for the Transfer of v the Whole of the said Capital Stock at one Time, or at different Times, within a less Period than Five Years} so that the same be made by even Instalments, at equal Intervals, within the Period agreed upon, and by not less than Four Instalments in each Year of the said Period.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Bodies Politic, Corporate, or Collegiate, Corporations Aggregate or Sole, and all Guilds, Mysteries, Fraternities, or'Brotherhoods, and all Trustees or Feoffees in Trull for Charities or other Public Purposes, having any Estate or Interest in any such Manors, Messuages, or Tenements (whatever may be their Estate therein, other than Tenants at Rack Rent) and all Committees of Lunatics or Idiots, and Guardians of infants, and all Executors and Administrators, and all other Trustees whatsoever, may contract with the said Commissionere

missioners to be appointed for the said Purposes: And that Persons in the actual Possession, or beneficially entitled to the Rents and Profits of any Manors, Messuages; or Tenements (except Tenants at Rack Rent) shall be preferred, in the Purchase of such Land Tax, to Persons in Remainder, Reversion, or Expectancy, provided they offer to contract for the Redemption of such Land Tax on or before a Day to be specified; but that the Persons in Remainder, Reversion, or Expectancy, shall be entitled to redeem such Land Tax in Preference to any other Persons having no Estate or Interest therein, according to the Priority of such their respective Estates or Interests, and in the Order in which they will be respectively entitled to succeed to the said Manors, Messuages, or Tenements: And that in Cafes of Demise at Rack Rent, the Persons beneficially entitled to the Rentrelerved shall (notwithstanding any Covenant) be considered as being in the actual Possession of such Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, for the Purpose of claiming such Benefit of Preference, with Power to add the Amount of the Land Tax fopurchased to the Rent reserved, and to use the same Powers for the Recovery thereof as for the Recovery of Rent in Arrear: And that, ' on the Completion of any Contract, by the Person having such Title to Preference, or by any other on his Behalf, and Payment of the First Instalment thereof, the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, comprized in such Contract, shall thenceforth be wholly freed and exonerated from the Land Tax charged thereon, and from all further Assessments thereof, unless the Person con-trading for such Land Tax shall, at the Time of entering into the Contract for the fame, declare his Option to be considered on the same Footing as a Third Person purchasing the Land Tax: And that upon every Contract to be so entered into, upon which the Transfer of S(ock shall be made by Instalments, there shall be paid, at' the Time of making the Second Instalment upon such Contract, and so of every fubl'e-quest Instalment upon such Contract, into the Hands of the Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England (whose Receipt shall be a sufficient Discharge) to the Use of His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, a Sum of Money, by Way of Interest, to be computed from the Period of the First: Instalment, equal to Five Sixth Parts of the Amount of what would have been the Produce up to the Time of making such Payment of the Whole of the Stock to be transferred upon such Contriad, deducting therefrom the Amount of the Produce of such Part of the Stock as shall then have been transferred: And in ever}' such Case, the Persons beneficially entitled to any Estate in Remainder, Reversion, or Expedancy, in the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, whereof such Land Tax shall have been so contracted for, shall, at at any Time or Times after such Estate shall veil in Possession by Reason of the Determination, of the next preceding Estate or Interest, be entitled unto an Alignment of such Contract, upon transferring to such original Contradors the like Amount of the Three Pounds per Centum Bank Annuities, as was transferred by such original Contradors, as the Consideration for the Redemption of such Land Tax; or upon paying to such original Contradors (at their Option) such a Sum as shall be of equal Value therewith, at the Time of such Conveyance; and to the same Option to be «on-lidered on the Footing of a Third Person, with respect to such Land Tax, as the Person or Persons first redeeming the same might have.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Bodies Politic or Corporate, and other Persons, being in the actual Possession, or entitled beneficially to the Rents and Profits of any Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, may fell any Part or Parts thereof for the Purpose of redeeming or purchasing such Land Tax, or charge the said Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, with such Sum or Sums of Money as shall be sufficient

to redeem or purchase the Land Tax charged thereon; and, for securing the Re-payment of such Sum or Sums of Money, with Interest, may convey, surrender, or demise the same by Way of Mortgage; or may grant, limit, or appoint, any Yearly Sum or Sums of Money, by Way of a perpetual Rent Charge, nod exceeding the Amount of the Land Tax charged upon the said Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, to be issuing out of, and charged upon, such Manors, Messuages, or Tenements: And every such Sale, Conveyance, Mortgage or Grant of any Rent Charge, shall, after the lame'shall be duly enrolled, be good, valid, and effectual in the Law', to all Intents, nutw'ithstanding any Defect of Title in any of the Parties thereto; and the respective Persons to whom any such Sale or Mortgage shall be made, or any such Rent Charge shall be granted, shall respectively hold the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, or the said Rent Charges, freed and absolutely discharged from ill former Titles, Charges, and Incumbrances whatsoever: And that wherever there shall be any Surplus, after paying so much as shall be sufficient for the Purchase of Three Pounds per Centum Annuities, to be transferred as the Consideration for such Land Tax, the said Surplus shall be paid into, or placed in, the Bank of in the Name, and with the Privity, of the Accountant General of the Court of Chancery, to the Intent that such Surplus Money may be inverted, as focn as conveniently may be, under the Direction, and with the Approbation, of the said Court, in the Purchase of other Estates, to be conveyed to the like Uses, and in the same Manner as the same flood settled, and in the mean Time such Surplus to be inverted in Government or other Public Securities, in the ‘Name of the said Accountant General, and the Dividends and Annual Produce thereof shall, from Time to Time, belong to the Person who would, for the Time being, have been entitled to the Rents and Profits of the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, purchased.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if, within a Time to be named, no Contract shall be entered into with the Commissioners to be appointed for the Redemption or Purchase of the Land Tax, or any Part or Parcel thereof, charged in any Parish or Place, by any Person entitled to ?he Benefit of Preference, or by any Person substituted in that Behalf, the Commissioners may then put up to Sale, either by Public Auction or otherwise, as the Commissioners of the Treasury for the Time being shall direct, the Whole or any Part or Parcel of the said Land Tax, charged in any County, or Division of any County, or in any Parish or Place, or any specific Share or Shares thereof; or any Land Tax charged on any particular Estate or Estates, or any Part or Parcel thereof, which shall not be redeemed or purchased within the said Period, and to contract and agree with any Persons for the Sale of the fame, subject to a Proviso for the Redemption of such Land Tax at the Time, and in the Manner to be provided: And the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, whereon the Land Tax purchased is charged, shall be subject to a new Assessment from Year to Year, by an equal Pound Rate, according to the Value thereof, in common with all other Estates in the same Parish, which shall remain chargeable to the Land Tax; and the Consideration shall be the Transfer of Stock in the Three Pounds per Centum Annuities, transferable at the Bank of England as aforesaid, of the like Amount, as is hereinbefore directed, unto the Commissioners appointed for the Reduction of the National Debt, to be made within the Period of One Year from the Time of entering into such Contract, by Four Instalments, of not left than One Fourth Part of the whole Amount of the Stock to be so transferred as aforesaid, at Intervals of three Months from each other, the Transfer of such Stock for the First Instalment to be made at the End of Three Months

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Receiver General of each County, Riding, or Place, where any such Land Tax shall remain chargeable as aforesaid, after the same shall have been purchased, not as a specific Charge on any Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, in such Parish or Place, or his Deputy or Deputies, shall, before such Land Tax shall have become due and payable, on the Twentieth Day of -Septemberfor the Half Year ending on the Twenty-ninth Day of September, and on the Sixteenth Day of March for the Half Year ending on the Twenty-fifth Day of March, in every Year, upon Demand, pay, or cause to be paid, to the Purchaser or Purchasers thereof, or the Heirs, Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, of such Purchaser or Purchasers respectively, the full Amount of the Land Tax so purchased, free of all Charges and Deductions whatever, without Fee or Reward, out of any Public Monies in his Hands, in the Manner to be provided: And that where any Purchase shall be made of any Land Tax, as a specific Charge on any Manors, Mdfuages, or Tenements, or where any Person entitled to Preference shall have made his Option to be considered on the Footing of a Third Person purchasing the Land Tax, and any Abatement shall afterwards take place in the Sum so charged, the Receiver General shall, upon the Production of the Certificate of such Abatement, pay the full Amount thereof, free of all Charges and Deductions whatever, and without Fee or Reward, to such Person or Persons as aforesaid, in like Manner, and out of such Monies, and at such Times of Payment, as is directed for the Payment of the Whole of the Land Tax purchased; and that, in Default of such Payment by the Receiver General or his Deputy, the Purchaser, or the Heirs, Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, of such Purchaser, may cause Notice of such Default to be given to the Occupier of the Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, on which the Land Tax so purchased shall be charged; and such Occupier shall be obliged to pay the same upon Demand, unless he shall havepreviously paid the fame, for Want of such Notice, to the Collector of the Parish, or unless the Yearly Value of the Estate Whereon such Land Tax shall have been charged (estimating such Value by the Rack Rents, and the highest Improvements made thereof) shall be reduced, so that the Estate shall be charged with a higher Rate than Four Shillings in the Pound on such Value, in which same the Occupier shall not be liable to the Payment of any greater Sum than after the Rate of Four Shillings in the Pound on such Value; or unless the Land Tax charged shall, by any Abatement thereof, be reduced to a Sum less than the Sum charged on the same Manors, Messuages, or Tenements', at the Time of the Purchase, in which same such Occupier shall not be

liable to the Payment of any greater Sum than the Sum actually charged on such Manors, Messuages, or Tenements at the Time of the Demand, with the like Remedies for the Recovery as Landlords may by Law have for the Recovery ot Rent in Arrear; anjd that, in case of any Diminution of the Sum to be paid to the Purchaser of any Land Tax, by reason of any Reduc- , tion in the Value of the Estate charged therewith, the Purchaser shall have the Option of continuing to receive a Sum, necessary to complete, in each Year, the whole Annual Amount of the Sum originally purchased by him; or to demand of and from the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt, a Transfer of so much Capita] Stock in the Three Pounds per Centum Bank Annuities, as shall yield an Interest exceeding the Amount of such Abatement by One Fifth Part thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if the Receiver General of any County, where any Land Tax shall be purchased, not as a specific Charge upon any particular Manors, Messuages, or Tenements, in any Parish or Place, but a Charge upon such Pari fit or Place at large, or upon such Part thereof as shall continue chargeable, shall neglect to pay, to the Purchaser of any Land Tax, the full Amount of the Land Tax so purchased,' the Purchaser may cause. Notice of such Default to be given to the Collector of the said Land Tax, and of his Intention to receive the Land Tax in future from such Collector; and on such Notice, every such Purchaser shall be entitled to receive the Amount of such Land Tax from such Collector accordingly: Or if such Receiver General, where any Land Tax shall be purchased as a specific Charge on any particular Estate or Estates, or where any Land Tax shall be redeemed by the Person entitled to Preference, who shall have made his Option to be considered on the Footing of a Third Person purchasing the Land Tax, and any Abatement shall afterwards take pl.ace in the Sums so charged, shall neglect to pay to the Person entitled to such Land Tax the full Amount of such Abatement, such Purchaser may cause the like Notice to be given to the Collector, to entitle such Purchaser to the Land Tax so purchased from such Collector in the Manner before directed; and that every such Collector, on the Production of the Contract of Purchase, shall, from Time to Time, pay, or cause to be paid, to such Purchaser, the foil Amount of the Land Tax purchased, free of all Charges 'and Deductions whatever, and without Fee or Reward, out of any Monies in the Hands of such Collector, arising from the Produce of the Land Tax in such Parish or Place, unless such Collector shall, for Want of such Notice as aforesaid, have paid the Whole of the Land Tax, charged in such Parish or Place, to the Receiver General of the County.

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That g-jf owners the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is now depending, declaring that no Owner dr Mailer of any Ship or Vessel usually employed, or about to be employed, in the Navigation of the High Seas, should be liable for any Loss which should happen in the Cargoes of such Ships or Vessels, except in certain Cafes,

Whether such Loss should happen on the High Seas, or In the Tideway of any River, on in any other Place whatever; and that the Sloops and Vessels of the Petitioners, notwithstanding thfc utmost Care of the Mailer and Crew, are, as well as Ships, liable to many Accidents be-fid£s those occasioned by the Act of God„ and the King's Enemies; and that the Petitioners apprehend, although they are subject to the like Responsibility for Losses as the Owners and Mailers of Ships, yet they will not, as the Bill now Hands, be entitled to any Protection from Losses which shall happen to the Cargoes on Board their Vessels, notwithstanding such-Losses shall happen from the very same Cause as shall occasion any Loss in the Cargo of any Ship, and even in the same Place, and at the same Time: And the Petitioners therefore, conceiving that such a Distinction would be unjust, pray. That the Benefits, intended by the said Bill to the Owners and Mailers of Ships, may be extended to the Petitioners, and that they may not be answerable for any Loss which shall happen to the Cargoes of Sloops and Vd-fels while such Sloops and Vessels shall be in any Place frequented by Ships navigating the High Seas, and where the Owners and Mailers of such Ships would not be liable to Loss; and that such other Relief may be granted to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth;

GEORGE VL.

His Majesty thinks it proper to acquaint the House of Commons, that, from various Advices received by His Majesty, it appears that the Preparations for the Embarkation of Troops and Warlike Stores are now carried on with cQnsiderable and increasing Activity in the Ports of France, Flanders, and Holland, with the avowed Design of attempting the invasion of His Majesty Dominions; and that in this Design the Enemy is encouraged by the Correspondence and Communication of Traitorous and Disaffected Persons and Societies of these Kingdoms.

His Majesty places the firmest Reliance, under the Divine Providence, on the Bravery of His Fleets and Armies, and on the Zeal, Public Spirit, and unshaken Courage, of His Faithful People, already manifested in the voluntary Exertions of all Ranks of His Majesty's Subjects, for the General Defence, and more than ever necessary, at a Moment when they are called upon to contend for the Preservation of all that is dear to them.

His Majesty, in pursuance of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for raising a Provisional Force of Cavalry, has thought it right to give Directions that the said Cavalry should be drawn out, and embodied: And it is also His Majesty's Intention to order the Part, not yet embodied, of the Augmentation made to the Militia, under the Acts of the last Session, to be forthwith drawn Out and embodied, in pursuance of His Majesty's Communication already made to the House of Commons on this Subject.

His Majesty feels it incumbent on Him to make the lulled Ule of the extensive Means already provided by the Wisdom of Parliament for the National Defence; but He feels it at the same Time, under the Circumstances which He has dated, indispensably necessary to recommend it to the House of Commons to consider, without Delay, of such f urther Measures as may-enable

His Majesty to defeat the wicked Machinations of dif-affected Persons within these Realms, and to guard against the Designs of the Enemy cither Abroad or at Home. G. R.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That an humble AJ>irefs Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His 1 ltrcui, on' Majesty the humble Thanks of this House for His most gracious Message; and to allure His Majesty that this House, will, without Delay, proceed to the Confederation of the interesting Subjects, therein mentioned, with all the Attention which their Importance to the Safety of these Kingdoms require.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council.

His Majesty's Letters Patent, bearing Date the 2d of June 1795, for the Term of Fourteen Years, from the Date thereof, for the sole Use and Benefit of his Discovery or Invention of Tanning Leather with Elm Bark; and, in pursuance of a Proviso in that Behalf, contained in the said Letters Patent, caused a particular Specification and Description of his Method and Materials used for tanning to be inrolled in the High Court of Chancery on the 27th Day of 1795, and did, for a valuable Consideration, assign to the Petitioner all his Right and Title to, and Interest in, the said Letters Patent, and the same are now veiled absolutely in the Petitioner; and that, prior to such Assignment, and in consequence of an Intercourse between the Petitioner and certain Persons of Eminence in the Tanning Trade, numerous Experiments were made, with the Consent, and under the Direction, of the Petitioner, to enable them to determine, with Certainty, how far Elm Bark might prove a Substitute for Oak Bark; and that, from the Result of the said Experiments, the said Persons, being convinced of the great Utility of the said Invention, convened a General Meeting of the Tanners, and submitted Parts of the Leather so tanned, with a particular Account of the Experiments, to their Examination, and Rated it to be> their Opinion,-that the Leather, so tanned with Elm Bark, was nearly equal in Goodness to what was theretofore tanned with Oak Bark, and farther Rated, that Elm Bark would prove a Substitute for Oak Bark, afiiR the Manufacturer, be the Means of preserving Oak Timber, and of increasing the Public Revenue; and that the Tanners, assembled at the said Meeting, were satisfied that the Leather tanned with Elm Bark was firm, durable, and good, and that the Advantages above-mentioned;would accrue to the Public from the Use thereof being generally introduced, and accordingly agreed, unanimously, that a Memorial should be presented, to that Effect, to the Lords of the Committee of Privy Council for Trade and Foreign Plantations, from which Memorial, and from the Answers given to the Questions proposed by their Lordships, it appears that the Tanners in general are desirous of having the Use of Elm Bark legalized, and the Advantages to arise from the said Patent secured to the Petitioner; and that the Petitioner hath employed great Part of the lafi Three Years in prosecuting and bringing to Perfection this Discovery, in which he hath incurred a very considerable Expence, without deriving the leaR Advantage therefrom; and that the Petitioner hath seen a Bill depending in the House for legalizing the Use of Elm Bark, by taking off the ReRridtions of an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of King James the FirR, intituled, "An Act " concerning Tanners, Curriers, Shoemakers, and other " Artificers, occupying the Cutting of Leather," which he conceives is introduced at the Request of the Tanners, upon the avowed Ground that Elm Bark may be used in the Tanning of Leather greatly to the Advantage of the Public, and the Petitioner is apprehen-five, if the said Bill should pass into a Law as it now Rands, it would be highly injurious to the Petitioner, by depriving him of the Advantage secured to him by the said Letters Patent: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill for l'ecuring to him all the Rights, Privileges, and Advantages, granted by the said Letters Patent, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. , Mr. Gore

ton,&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Fishcurers are not upon an Equality with the British Fishcurers in regard to Bounties, and the Petitioner is authorized by them to say, that, should the Parliament of Great Britain think it expedient, in the present Times, toabolish the Herring Bounties altogether, they Would not complain; that all they alk is to be put on the same Footing with the British Fishcurers (whether Bounties be granted or not) so that they may go to Market on equal Terms; and that the Petitioner, being sensible of the Reasonableness of these Requests, feels' it his Duty, not only as Governor of the Isle of Mann, but as otherwise deeply interested in, and connected with, the Prosperity of the said Isle, to lay these Matters before the House, more especially, as he understands a Bill is at present pending in the House, for the further Encouragement of the British Fisheries: And therefore

Pfctltion from A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Shfr> Shippers, of Goods, and others interested in the Exports Owner Bill, and Imports of the Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Mailers of Ships; and Setting forth, That the same would, if passed into a Law, greatly reduce the Responfi-bility of the Owners and Mailers of Ships, at the Rilk, and highly to the Prejudice, of the Shippers of Goods on Freight, and thereby deprive such Shippers of that Security which is foeffential to the Protection of Trade, and which manifellly results from proper Care being heceflarily taken of their Goods, and from the efficient Equipment of freighted Ships, and the due Navigation thereof; and that by the Law, as it now Hands, the Shippers of Goods can protect themselves, by Insurance, against all Rilks which their Goods are exposed to in a Sea Voyage, and for which the Owners of Ships are not responsible, whereas, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, they would be exposed to Rilks against which they cannot insure, in consequence of the present Re-fponfibility of the Ship Owners being removed, or greatly reduced; and such Increase of Rilk would tend to deter Manufacturers, and other Persons who have been aCCustomed to export Goods on their own Account, from engaging in these Adventures, and thereby greatly injure the Export Trade of this Kingdom; and that the said Bill purports to exonerate Owners of Ships from Refpolifibilities to which they are now liable, upon Contracts already entered into, and thereby to operate as an ex post facto Law, which the Petitioners submit Vvould be highly unjust: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against such Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

" and for other Purposes and also an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year- of the Reign of His present Majesty, to explain and amend the said Act, lo far as the same relates to the continuing and granting an additional Term of Five Years to Acts made for amending Turnpike Roads; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to thife House; That the Committee had confideted the said Acts, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Traffic upon the Roads in the Neighbourhood of London is exposed to considerable Inconveniences by the present Limitation of Weights.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That. Carts, having the Fellies of the Wheels Six Inches in Breadth, and the Tire perfectly flat and cylindrical,

should be allowed an additional Weight of Ten Hundred to the respective Weights now allowed in Summer and.

Winter, on paying an Addition of £.Centum upon

the Tolls now paid at the respective Turnpike Gates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Waggons, having the Fellies of the Wheels Six Inches in Breadth, and the Tire perfectly flat and cylindrical, should be allowed an additional Weight of Thirteen Hundred to the respective Weights now allowed in Summer and Winter, on paying an Addition of£.50 per Centum upon the Tolls now paid at the respective Turnpike Gates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, as Weighing Engines are intended to prevent c'xccffive Weights, and not to increase the Revenues of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Weighing Engines should be inspected by, and under the Regulation of, the inspectors of Weights and Balances, or of l'uch Persons as the Magistrates of the County shall appoint.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,' That the Roads in the Neighbourhood of London, suffer materially from the conical Shape of the Sixteen Inch Wheels, and from the projecting middle Tire and the improper Form of Nine Inch Wheels now in use.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Wheels of all Waggons and Carts of the Breadth of Six or Nine Inches, should be perfectly flat and cylindrical.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Weights now allowed to Waggons with Sixteen Inch Wheels are injurious to the Roads.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the proposed experimental Regulations, with re-fpect to the Weights to be carried in Carts and Waggons, should be limited to a Distance within Twenty-tive Miles of the Metropolis, and to continue for a limited Time.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty recommends it to the House of Commons, to consider of enabling His Majesty to make Remittances, from Time to Time, to be applied to His Service in Ireland, in such Manner as shall be approved by the Parliament of that Kingdom, to an Amount not exceeding Two Millions, on Provision being made, by the Parliament of Ireland, for defraying the interest and Charges of a Loan to that Amount. q

Ordered, That His Majesty's laid most Gracious Mef-sage be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to prevent, during the War, Persons residing or being in Great Britain from advancing Money or Efiefts for the Purchase, or on. the Credit, of Debts owing to any of the Governments in Switzerland, or any Bodies Politic or Corporate, or any Persons therein, without Licence for that Purpose; for extending the Provisions of an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, more effectually to prevent, during the present War between Great Britain and France, all Traitorous Correspondence with, or Aid

or Assistance being given to, His Majesty's Enemies, to Switzerland and to the Persons exercising the Powers of Government therein, and all'o to the Persons, Territories, and Places, under their Government; and for preventing the Transfer of Stock, by virtue of any Power of Attorney, from Persons residing in,

The llnited Provinces, or Switzerland, or any of the Territories belonging to, or dependent on, either of them, without Licence from one of His Majesty's principal Secretaries of State, be now read.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Fortnight, the 8th Day of May next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the several Reports which, in the last Session of Parliament, were made from the Select Committee, who were appointed to examine and state the total Amount of the Public Debts, and other Matters relating to the Public Revenue and Expenditure.

Ordered, That the ingrossed Bill for repealing the Duties upon Male Servants, Carriages, Horses, Mules, and Dogs, and for granting to His Majesty other Duties thereon in lieu thereof, be read the Third Time upon Thursday Morning next.

Ordered, That the ingrossed Bill for repealing the Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights, on Inhabited Houses, and on Clocks and Watches, and for granting to His Majesty other Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights, and on Inhabited Houses, in lieu thereof, be read the Third Time upon F Morning next.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for better dividing the Militia into Regiments, Battalions, and Companies, for augmenting the Number of Field Officers and other Officers of Militia, and for making other Provisions concerning the Militia and Supplementary Militia.

Ordered, That the Bill for incorporating the Commissioners appointed for erecting certain Lighthouses in the Northern Parts of Great Britain, be read a Second Time upon Monday Morning next.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-eight.

Ordered, That the Proceeding upon the Third Reading of the ingrossed Bill to abolish certain Offices, and to regulate certain other Offices, in the Customs; and for applying the Fees which have been received from vacant Offices towards a Superannuation Fund, be further adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Taylor, Esquire, Deputy Clerk of the 'Peace for the County of Lancaster, being examined, said. That he has, fine t January 1772, officiated as Deputy Clerk of

the Peace for the said County; that in the County there are Six Hundreds, Lonsdale,

Blackburn, West Derby, Lay land, and Salford-, that the

Four Quarterly Sessions held Annually, open at Lancaster for the Hundred of Lonsdale, that they adjourn from thence to Preston, to transact the Business for Amounderness and Blackburn Hundreds, and from thence to Ormskirk, for the Two Summer Quarters, and to

Wigan for the Two Winter Quarters, for the Hundreds of West Derby and Lay land, and from those Places to Manchester, for tranlacling the Bulinei's of Salford; and frequent Adjournments have been made from Manchester to different Parts of the County, for transaCling special Business; that Lancaster Sessions occupy One Day; Preston Sessions Two Days; and Wigan

Two Day$: That the Justices have exercised a concurrent Jurisdiction for the whole County; that the whole Magistrates of the County (except Lonsdale Hundred) have, for many Years pall, found their Time Occupied at the Quarterly Sessions fd very much, and the general Business of the County respecting the Rates so much increased, that they thought, as Guardians and Trullees of the Public Purse, it was impossible that they could discharge their Duty during the Times of their holding the Quarterly Sessions, and they have individually and collectively deemed the Business of the County of so much Importance, and of 1b much Magnitude, as to require a Special Meet- ing for the Purpose, and they have thought that Preston (being the moll central Place in the County) was the bell calculated for that Purpose; that the Rates of the County have in his Knowledge increased from £. 1,000 per Annum to £. 12,000 per Annum, and for the Three lall Years a Sum of 12,000 for each Year has been-raised to serve the Exigencies of the County, and in the laffc Year it exceeded that Sum; that the Items in which the Money is usually expended, are as follow: Conveying of Vagrants;

Coroners Bills; Prosecution of Felons; conveying Baggage for His Majesty's Use; in the Amendments of Gaols, and building of Houses of Correction; conducting Offenders to Gaol; in the Business of the Navy; in the Business of the Militia; and in County (not Hundred) Bridges; that these are the principal Articles, but there are other Purposes in which the County Money is expended; that the Expences of all these Articles have for several Years been gradually increasing, and are likely to increase; that the Improvements of the Gaol of Lancaster have already coll the County upwards of £.26,000, and are likely -to coll a considerable Sum more; that those Accounts are Hill unl ttled; that the new Bridge at Lancaster Coll the County upwards of £.1; that the Business of the Vagrants some Years ago amounted to

only 3 or £.400 a Year, but in a short Time it m-crealed to £. 1,800 a Year; that by the Exertion of the Magistrates of the County, they were feme Years ago reduced from . 1,800 a Year to the former Sum; that they are now got to ppwards of £. 1,300 a Year;

that the Petitioners are one and all of Opinion, that a large Reduction will be made from ill 1 or most of the above Items, if a Conference can be Annually had among the Magistrates of the County at large, and a Session held for that Purpose; and they are of Opinion, that without such a Measure they cannot be effectual; and it is impossible for any select Number of Magistrates in the County, without so communing together with the Body at large, to form a true Idea of the several Items contained in such Accounts.

And the Witness further said, That the Adjournment Session is adjourned from Manchester to; that

there are acting Magistrates in Hundred, .

Seven on the North Side of the Sands, and Five on the South Side, and Fifty-five acting Magistrates in the rest of the County; that the Magistrates having appointed at such adjourned Session, a Treasurer to serve the County, and the Quarterly Session at Lan-casler having afterwards dismissed him, without the Concurrence of the other Magistrates of the County, was, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, one Instance of its being infringed upon; that another Instance was, that it was in pursuance of a Recommendation at the March Affixes in 1784, by the Sheriff and Grand Jury, that a Committee should be appointed for the Purpose of conducting the Improvements of Lancaster Castle, to consist of Three Justices out of each Hundred in the County; that the same were accordingly appointed at a General Annual Sessions at Preston in July 1787, and that the Quarterly Sessions at Lancaster held in January 1794, nominated all the Twelve Magistrates in Lotifdale Hundred to be added to that Committee, without the Concurrence of the rest of the Magistrates of the County.

The Witness delivered in to the Committee a Copy of the Appointment, which is annexed in the Appendix, N° 2.

And being further examined, lie said. That this General Annual Session, is a Measure that meets the general Approbation of the County (except as aforesaid); and as a Proof of that, he delivered in to the Committee Two Resolutions signed by the Grand Jury in the Years 1795 and 1797, which are annexed in the Appendix, N01 3 and 4.

And the Witness being asked. Whether he did not, in the Course of the last Year, bring forward a Bill for the same Purpose ? he said. He did. Being asked. Whether the House of Commons rejected the bringing in of that Bill ? he said, What he understood of the Matter was, that the Bill was received, and read a Second Time, and committed; that in the Committee, that fat upon that Occasion, the Petitioners against the Bill were called upon to be heard by their Counsel, but none were produced to support it. That the Counsel , in support of the Petition for the Bill, claimed to be heard, upon which a Motion was instantly made and carried. That the Proceedings should be postponed for Six Months. That it was afterwards moved in the House for the Committee to be revived, which was negatived. Being asked, Whether there was any, and what Difference, between the Bill now proposed, and that which was thrown out last Sessions ? he said. The Objcdts of the Bill are to be the fame. Being asked. Whether he knew the Distance from the furthermost Part of Lotifdale Hundred, to Lancaster,. over the Sands ? he said. He did not. That the Jurors attending caster General Quarter Sessions, frequently come there in a Morning, and return the same Evening. Being asked. When he mentioned, that the Jurors frequently come and go the same Day, Whether he was aware, that there is a considerable Distance of the Road, Sand, which can be passed only at certain Times, owing to the VOL. 53.

Reflux of the Sea ? he laid, He was perfectly aware; that the Time of their returning must depend upon the Flux and Reflux of the Tide, and as the Tides serve, tl\e Courts at Lancaster have uniformly consulted the Convenience of such Juryffien, that they might return in the same Time. Being asked, What was the greatest Distance any Juryman had to go ? he said, From Manchester, Fifty-five Miles. Being asked, Whether there are any Jurors or Suitors attend the General Annual Session ? he said, There are no Jurors required to attend;

If the Question means, that if any Persons over the Sands, or any other Persons in the County, have any Business relating to the County at large, and by which the Rates of the County are afiedted, such Persons will either attend, or rely upon such Justices who may attend, to do their Business. Being asked, Whether he meant to include in his Statement of the 'Increase of the Rates from £.1,000 to £.12,that the £.26,000 for the building of the Castle, and the £.16,000 for building the Bridge, are already paid, and principally account for the Increase of such Rates ? he said, The £.16,000 for the Bridge, constituteS no Part of the £. 12,000; that the £.26,000 constitutes a Part. Being asked. Whether he was not aware, that the Quota of the County Rates, which the Hundred of Lotifdale pays, although Twelve Justices are found sufficient for the Business of the Hundred, was as great, if not greater, than the Quota paid by the great and populous Town of Manchester, and the Hundred of Salford, in which the Town of Manchester Hands ? he said, The Hundred of Lonsdale pays, when £.1,000 is raised, £.160; the Hundred of Salford£.140; I Hundred £.2 40;

Layland Hundred £.90; AmoundHundred £.190; and Blackburn Hundred £.180. Being asked. Whether he was, or was not aware, that a Letter was written to the Duchy Office by those Justices who displaced Mr. Myers ? he said. He never heard of such a Letter. Being asked. Whether such Annual Sessions, as are prayed for in the Petition, for the Transaction of all such Matters wherein the Rates of the County are affected, will not take away from the Magistrates assembled at the.General Quarter Sessions, as by Law established, every Power that adds Dignity, or indicates Confidence ? he said, He conceived it took away no more from the Justices acting for Lancaster, than it docs from the Justices acting for the whole County, as it only fixes that Confidence, and that Business which is appointed to the Magistrates at large, which is now trans-adtedbyafew. Being asked, Whether any Attempts, and by whom, were ever made, or called in question, the Legality of such Adjourned Sessions, or what Doubts upon the Subject have ever been entertained, and by whom ? he said. He conceived he had already stated Two Instances, and should wish to decline repeating any Declarations that have been made by the Chairman of the Quarter Sessions at Lancaster as to such Legality; the Petitioners are advised they cannot be established without the Aid of Parliament. Being asked. Whether the Justices of the Hundred of Lonsdale, ever interfered with the building of the House of Correction at Prefon, or with the Bridge over the River Kibble, and what did they both cost? he said, In both Instances the Magistrates of the County at large had Notice, and were requested to attend at Preston, to take those Matters into Consideration, and he did not believe any of the Lotifdale Gentlemen attended; that the Bridge at Kibble cost about £.4,000, and the House of Correction about £.16,000. Being asked. Whether, though the Amount of the Rates being increased, the Proportions of which they are paid, do not remain the lame, and what was the Rule of Payment ? he said, They are the fame. Being asked. Whether he knew what are the Proportions paid by the different Townships in the County ? he said. Yes; all of them.
