Preston Sessions, 8th February 1787. 14 Justices.

Upon reading the several Orders made at this Session, and particularly the Order made at Lancaster, appointing George Poftlethwaite, Gentleman, to l'ucceed to the Office ot Treasurer for the said County, now vacant by the Death of tire late Treasurer, and all'o die Rolls signed at the said Sessions, for railing One thousand Pounds upon the County, made payable to the said George Poftlethwaite, as Treasurer, and this Bench being nowafl'em-bled in consequence of Notice given to Magistrates of the County, signifying that this Session would be holden at this Time and Place, for the Purpol'e (amongst other Things) of taking this Business into Consideration:

It is ordered, declared, and adjudged by this Court, That the said Proceedings at Lancaster, in this Matter, are irregular, for Want of having been previously communicated to, and laid before the Magistrates of the County at large, as has heretofore been the Custom in all Businesses relating to the whole County; and therefore this Court doth refeind, annihilate, and make void, the said Order, appointing Mr. Poftlethwaite Treasurer as aforesaid, and also the said Rolls lb ligned as aforesaid, and doth direct that the same shall not be ifl'ued, nor the said One thousand Pounds be raised, collected, levied, or paid, as therein mentioned; and the said. George PojUethwaiteis accordingly, by this Court, re-

moved and discharged from the said Office and Trufi of Treasurer.

in Trust for the Use of the said County, and the Rectitude of the said Accounts having been verified upon Oath by William Fftier, Gentleman; This Court, in pursuance of the Statute in such same made, doth discharge the legal Representatives of the said William Butterfield from the said Trust of the said Office, and from the Money so paid as aforesaid; and doth order, that the Bond, given by the said William Butterfield for the faithful discharging of his Duty, shall be surrendered and given up.

It is the unanimous Sentiments of this Court, That a General Court of Quarter Sessions shall, in future, be holden in and for the County of Lancaster, and that an Adjournment of the Rafter Session shall Yearly be made to Preston(a central Fiace in the said County) there to be holden on the Full Wednesday in July, at Eleven o'Clock in the Morning, for the special Purpose of transacting all Business relating to the County at large.

Lancaster Sessions, 29th April 1794. 5 Justices.

Upon hearing the Orders and Resolutions of the Adjourned Sessions, held at Preston, on tire Twenty-third Day of April instant, read by the Clerk of the Peace, This Court, apprehensive of the dangerous Tendency of Innovation under the specious Pretext of Reform, cannot avoid repeating its Dislent to the Propriety of reluming the recently adopted, and afterwards discontinued Annual Adjournments of the Quarter Sessions recommended therein; it being the Opinion of this Court, that the same would be injurious even if not illegal; and that all Measures necessary for the general Good of the County ought as heretofore to originate in the Sessions first holden, pursuant to Royal Patent and judicial Confirmation, at Lancaster, and to be from thence circulated through the other Parts of the County, by Reference to the usual Adjourned Courts, holden within the other Hundreds; and that if a General Annual or Quarterly Meeting of the Magistrates resident within the different Hundreds of the County should seem expedient, the same may be best . effected by their appearing at the Opening Sessions at Lancaster, to which this Court does accordingly invite them; this Court at the same Time doth certify its Opinion, that lpccial Adjournments of the Quarter Sessions may with Propriety take place pursuant to ancient Practice, when and as often as the Necessity for them shall occur, of which the Purport ought to be explicitly stated and published in the London or Provincial Newspapers.

Taylor, Dep. See.

Wigan Sessions, 18th May 1795. 22justices.

Th is Court having read and taken into Consideration the Proceedings of the General Court of Quarter Sessions held at Lancaster, in and for the County Palatine of Lancaster, in April lad, respecting the Difmilfal of Mr. ers from his Office of Treasurer of the said County, and the Appointment of Mr. Johnson, as his Successor, is unanimously of Opinion, and adjudge, order, and resolve, as follows; to wit;

That upon having Recourse to the Records of the Court of Quarter Sessions, kept at the Office of the Clerk of the Peace in and for the said County, it will appear, that in ancient Times, and down to a very late Period, the Magistrates of the County have been accustomed to aflemtye at the General Session of Assize held at Lancaster, at a Meeting convened by the Sheriff, called the Sheriff's Board, for the special Purpose of communing together, and transafling all Business relating to the County at large, and particularly that of nominating Public Officers, and where, with the Advice and Assistance of the Gentlemen of the Grand Jqry, and others of the County, they have almost invariably been nominated, so long as such Meetings continued to be held;

That from the Increase of the Business of the Assizes, and of the Affairs of the County, it some Years ago became difficult, during the Hurry of an Assizes, to apportion sufficient Time to the above Purposes, and the Sheriff's Board was very ill attended, and at last so totally neglected, that it has for some Years been discontinued:

That in consequence of the several Acts of Parliament made, requiring the Amendments of the Gaols, Houses of Correction, and Penitentiary Houses, with the heavy Burthen of several large County Bridges, and other incidental Circumstances, the Rates of the County advanced so considerably, and the Business concerning the same became so great and important, it was found impossible to inveliigate the same during the Time of transacting the Business of the General Quarter Sessions, and expedient and necessary for the Magistrates of the County to alienable together, at some convenient Time of the Year, in a central Part of the County, for the special Purpose of hearing, investigating, arranging, and settling, all Accounts, Matters, and Things, concerning the County at large, and to give Efficacy to such Proceedings, that the General Court of Quarter Sef-4

lions should be adjourned for the Purpose; and it was accordingly, at a very large general public Meeting of the Magistrates, moved and agreed, that the Epiphany Sessions should Annually be adjourned to V rest on, a central Place in the County, and-Notice given in the public Provincial Papers of the Time and Place of holding the said Adjourned Sessions for those Purposes, that all the Magistrates of the County and Persons interested might assemble, and the same have been held accordingly:

That the said Adjourned General Court of Quarter Sessions, so Annually holden at Preston aforesaid, for the Purposes aforesaid, with a very few Exceptions, hath met with the unanimous Approbation of the Magistrates, Gentlemen, and Inhabitants of the County, and by their communing together, the County hath derived many Advantages which they mull otherwise have been deprived of:

That the Treasurer of the County being resident in a central Part of the County is a great Convenience to Persons who have Occasion to apply to his Office, and the Business of the County is transacted with much greater Facility than it otherwise would be:

That the Concerns of the Inhabitants dependant on the County Rates are become considerable, and of the utmost Importance to their Estates and interests, and the Office of Treasurer moll responsible:

That it is acknowledged that the ordinary Business of the General Court of Quarter Sessions, held in and for the County at large, at the Four usual Feasts and Times of the Year, at the several Places following; (that is to say) at Lancaster, Preston, in the Summer in the

Winter Wigan, and at Mancheftfor the Purposes of accommodating the several Hundreds or Divisions, is attended with great Convenience, and Justice is by this Means distributed with more Facility and better than it could be by any other Mode; and whatever may be the Authority of any of the Courts of Adjournments to interfere with the Judgment of the Court at,

or one Adjournment with that of another, it would be highly improper, big with much Mischief, and in such Cases has not been done; but in respeifl of the Business of nominating Public Officers, of auditing the Treasurer's Accounts, and of transatling all other Matters concerning the Inhabitants of the County at large, it is infilled upon, the same is better done at a General Annual Assembly of the Magistrates, holden at a central Place, for the special Purposes, where they commune together for the general Good of the Whole, than it can be at any other Time:

That the Appointment of a Treasurer in an opulent County like the County of Lancaster, is of such general Concern to its Inhabitants, that it ought always to have the Approbation of the Magistrates of the whole County:

That it is the unanimous Opinion of the Magistrates, That the Appointment of Mr. Johnson at the lall Quarter Sessions at Lancaster, under all the Circumstances of the Cafe, without any previous Examination of the late Treasurer, Mr. Myers, or Communication with the rest of the Magistrates of the County, was highly improper, and its Legality also questionable, and not pursuant to the true Intent and Meaning of the Statute made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second; nevertheless, that the Magistrates present think it most prudent and conciliatory to defer the rei'einding the Appointment of Mr. Johnson to the Office of Treasurer, until the Sentiments of Lord Hand Lord Kenyon. on this Subject shall be known:

That it is the Opinion of this Court, founded in Experience, that the Annual General Court of Quarter Session has been of great Public Utility within the County, that it every Day becomes more necessary, and has in its Consequences such beneficial Advantages

to

\ .

38 GEO. III. 25 Aprilis,501

to the Inh&bit&hts of the County, that it ought to be Continued, and if the Laws for this Purpose are inadequate to effect the desirable Purposes of it, that Application ought to be made to Parliament for proper Relief:

That they have to lament, that the Anntial General Quarter Setfion herein mentioned does not meet with the Approbation of all the Magistrates of the County, but is opposed by some of the Magistrates in the Hundred of Lonsdale only: And it is believed from none of the others throughout the County.

It is ordered by the Court, That a same be stated by the Deputy Clerk of the Peace, of the Proceedings had respecting the Dismissal of Mr. the Treasurer of the County, and the Appointment of Mr.

Johnson, and that he lay the same before the Attorney General of the County; and for so doing this shall be the said Deputy Clerk of the Peace's Authority.

Preston Sessions, o.zd February 1797. 10 Justices.

This Court having recognized the several Proceedings heretofore had concerning the holding an Annual General Session of the Peace in and for the said County, for the Purpose of transacting all Matters of Business relating to the Concerns of the County at large, declare, That in the Judgment of this Court, the same has been productive of many Advantages to this County, but as they are likely to be disturbed, it is become necessary to have the same sanctioned by Parliament, and if an Act is obtained for these Purposes, it will be attended with Public Utility.

Taylor, Dep. &c.

Lattcaster Sessions, 13th January, 24th . 1784.

It appears to this Court, That the Business respecting. Page 3. the State of the Gaols, Houses of Correction, and Prisons, within the County Palatine of Lancaster, is of such Magnitude and Importance to the Inhabitants of the: said'County, that no Measures should be takeh regarding the fame, without the fullest Investigation and Enquiry into the State and Condition thereof, and until the Senl'e of the County has been taken; therefore, being satisfied that, however great the Necessity of a speedy Remedy may be with Regard to the Houses of Correction, it is evident no Steps should be taken without the general Approbation (as none can be effectual without the actual Concurrence) of the Persons of principal landed Property in the same County, and therefore it is the unanimous Opinion and Wilh of this Court, that the same Steps which were taken in consequence of the Fourth Resolution of the Grand Jury, at the last Gloucester Assizes, should be takeil in this County; to wit; That the High Sheriff of the said County of Lancaster shall be requested to call a Meeting of the Nobility, Gentry, and Clergy, of the same County, to take the above Business into Consideration, and to adopt the most effectual Means for putting the said Gaols, Houses of Correction, and Prisons, into proper State and Condition: And this Court is of Opinion, that such Meeting will be belt attended if it is appointed to be had at an Assizes at Lancaster.

Taylor, Dep. &c.

It is therefore ordered. That Application shall be made to the Right honourable the Lord Chancellor and Council of the Duchy of Lancaster, and they be requested to prepare and bring a Bill into Parliament, for the Purpose of authorizing the Justices of the Peace of the County to hold an Annual General Court of Session of the Peace in and for the said County, at such Time, and at some convenient central Place, for the Purpose of appointing all Officers in the County in the Nomination of the said Justices of the Peace, and who are paid out of the County Rates, and for the transacting all Matters of Business concerning the County at large, at such Session only, and hot elsewhere: The Court recommends Preston as a central convenient Place to be appointed for holding the said Sessions, and submit that the last Thursday in June would be a proper and seasonable Time.

Taylor, Dep. &c.

The Court with great Deference recommends to the Consideration of his Lord ship and the Council, the several Proceedings upon this Subject, heretofore transmitted to them by the Sessions, which the Court fub-mits, furnishes abundant Matter of Ground for the intended Application to Parliamen t.

Upon reading the following Order made last Lancaster 4. Sessions, held the 13th Day of this Instant; to wit- —

[vide last mentioned Order.]

This Court doth hereby signify its Concurrence and 4» Approbation of the Measures recommended by the above Order; and having taken into Consideration the present State of the Gaols and Houses of Correction within the said County, and having in Contemplation the Insufficiency thereof (particularly the Houses of Correction) which are now crowded with very great Numbers of unhappy Wretches, many of whom are dan-#gerously lick of a Putrid Fever, of which the late Gaoler of Lancaster, and several Prisoners, have lately died; which Circumstances prove the great Necessity of an immediate Enquiry into this Business, in order that the most speedy and effectual Means may be taken to effectuate the laudable Purposes of making the said Gaols and Houses of Correction complete for every Purpose of humane Confinement, wife Correction, ana exemplary Punishment, and that they may be construdied so as to prevent the dreadful Public Calamities which may be occasioned by the Increase of the said Distemper among the poor Prisoners, and from them spreading itself abroad; This Court doth hereby order,

That the Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the said County, shall represent their Proceedings to the High Sheriff of the said County, and requell him to call a Meeting agreeable to the above Order, and the Resolution therein mentioned; and this Court doth earnestly request the Attention, Attendance, and Assistance, of the Nobility, Gentry, and Clergy, of the said County on this Occasion; and it is ordered, that the said De-» puty Clerk of the Peace shall publish this Order Three Times in the Liverpool and Manchester Papers, and circulate the same in Hand Bills.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Benjamin West, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Art t»f Sculpture, which is confcfledly the Foundation of every Thing elegant and ornamental in Arts and Manufactures, has not hitherto experienced from the Legislature of this Country that Protection to which it is so eminently entitled; that the ingenious Artists, who have applied themselves to the Study of Sculpture, have, to their great Mortification and Injury, found that their Works have been pirated, whereby the Fruits of their Labours have been loft to themselves and their Families, and the Art itself has been degraded, and many have been thereby discouraged from Attempts, to which their Genius may have prompted them, and others have been afraid to put forth the Works which they may have executed.

And the Witness further said. That the Art of Engraving has been manifestly advanced to its present State

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, Petitlonsfrom of the Town of Lancaster, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Taking tices, &c.of Notice of the Bill for obviating and1 removing Doubts respe«5ling the holding of the Adjournments of the effter Session General Court of Quarter Sessions of the Peace in and Bill, for the County Palatine of Lancaster, and for authorizing the Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the said County, to hold an Annual General Sessions, and also a Special Sessions, for the Purposes therein mentioned; and Setting forth, That the same would, if passed into a Law, invalidate and destroy several valuable and ancient Grants, Charters, Immunities, and Privileges, made, given, and confirmed, to the Petitioners, by several of the Monarchs of this Kingdom; and that the Four General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, for the said County, have, in consequence and by virtue of a Charter of King Edward the Third, originated at Lancaster for upwards of Four Centuries past, and have been adjourned from thence to IVigan, Or ms-

kirk, and Manchester, for the general Ease and Conve-

nience of the County at large; and that, by Reason of the Quarter Sessions having been held at Lancaster aforesaid, from such a remote Period of Time, great Emoluments have accrued to the Petitioners, and the other Owners of Property in the Town and Vicinity of Lancaster, which will be greatly diminished, should the said Bill pass into a Law; and that, in the Preamble of the said Bill, it is alledged that the Legality of the said Adjournment hath been attempted to be called in question, which Allegation the Petitioners contend to be unfounded; and that the Mode of holding the Sessions, and transacting the Business of the County, as proposed by the said Bill, is confused, expensive, and lo novel, as to be without a Precedent, and the Petitioners are confident it is a Measure not called for by any existing Cix-cumstances, and likely to produce much Mischief and Inconvenience: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel, against the fame, at the Bar of the House.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being respectively Justices of the Peace in and for the County Palatine of Gentlemen, Clergymen, or Freeholders, within the said County Palatine, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Laws now in Force authorize and direct the Justices of the Peace to hold all such Courts of Session as are necessary or expedient to be holden within the said County Palatine; and that, in confe-' quence of a Charter granted by King Edward the Third,

at

513 37 Aprilis.A. 1798.

at the Request of the then Duke of Lancaster, and afterwards confirmed by Eight succeeding Sovereigns, by the Usage of more than Four Centuries, and by a solemn legal Decision, the Town of Lancaster has been,

' and is, the Place appointed for holding such Courts, and at Lancaster Four Courts of Quarter Sessions, being Courts of General Session for the County, are regularly holden pursuant to the said Laws, and in conformity to the said Charter, which last mentioned Courts are, and long have been, for the greater Convenience' and Accommodation of all Parts of the County, adjourned to Preston, Ormskirk, Wigan, and; and that

the taking away any of the Powers and Authorities vested in the said Courts of Quarter Sessions, and the Substitution at Prejlonor any other supposed central Place within the Palatinate, of a novel and unprecedented Court of Annual Sessions, would not only be an Innovation upon ancient Laws, Rights, and Usages, under which the County has prospered, but be highly inconvenient to many of the Magistrates, and detrimental to the greater Part of the Inhabitants of the County, and particularly so to Persons residing North of ter Sands, who, if such Annual Sessions were established

at Preston, would thereby be virtually excluded from any Participation in the general Affairs of the County, whilst called upon to contribute very largely to case the Burthens of it; and that many other Objects of the Bill would, if the same were carried into Effect, be highly prejudicial to l y far the greater Part of the Inhabitants of the said County, without affording any material Benefit or Accommodation to any particular Place or Persons: And therefore praying. That, they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a . Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then

heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if , they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

A Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Sloops and Vessels navigated in the Tideway of the Rivers,

5 Trent, and Ouze, to and from the Port of was

' presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is now depending the rein, declaring, that no Owner or Mailer of any Ship or Vessel usually employed, of about to be employed,' in the Navigation of the High Seas should be liable for any Loss which should happen in the Cargoes of such Ships or Vessels, except in certain Cafes, whether such Loss should happen on the High Seas, or in the Tideway of any River, or in any other Place whatever; and that the Sloops and Vessels of the Petitioners, notwithstanding the utmost Care of the Mailer and Crew are, as well as Ships, liable to many Accidents besides those occasioned by the Act of God, and the King's Enemies; and that the Petitioners apprehend, although they are subject to the like Responsibility for Losses as the Owners and Mailers of Ships, yet they will not, as the Bill now Hands, be entitled to any Protection from Losses which shall happen to the Cargoes on Board their Vessels, notwithstanding such Losses shall happen from the very same Caule as shall occkfion any Loss in the Cargo of any Ship, and even in the same Place, and at the same Time: And therefore praying. That the Benefits, intended by the said Bill to the Owners and Mailers of Ships, may be extended to the Petitioners, and that they may not be answerable for any Loss which shall happen to the Cargoes of Sloops and Vessels while such Sloops and Vessels shall be in any Place frequented by Ships navigating the High Seas, and where the Owners and Mailers of such Ships would not be liable to Loss, and that such other Relief may be granted to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Mailers of Ships is committed.

A Petition of the Owners and Masters of Sloops and Vessels navigating in the Tideway of the Rivers Humber, 'Trent, Ouze, and Dunn, to and from the City of,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, declaring that no Owner or Master of any Ship or Vessel usually employed, or about to be employed, in the Navigation' of the High Seas, should be liable for any Lois which should happen in the Cargoes of such Ships or Vessels, except in certain Cafes, whether such Loss should happen on the High, Seas or in the Tideway of any River, or in any other Place whatever; and that the Sloops and Vessels of the Petitioners, notwithstanding the utmost Care of the Master and Crew, are, as well as Ships, liable to many Accidents besides those occasioned by the Act of God and the King's Enemies; and the Petitioners apprehend, although they are subject to the like Responsibility fdr Lolfes as the Owners and Mailers of Ships, yet they will not, as the said Bill now Hands, be entitled to any Protection from Lolfes which shall happen to the Cargoes on Board their Vessels, notwithstanding such Lolfes shall happen from the very same Caule as shall occasion any Lois in the Cargo of any Ship, and in the same Place; And that the Petitioners, conceiving such Distinction would be unjust, therefore pray. That the Benefits intended by the said Bill to the Owners and Mailers of Ships may be extended to the Petitioners, and that they may not be answerable for any Lois which shall happen to the Cargoes of Sloops and Vessels, while such Sloops and Vessels shall be in any Place frequented by Ships navigating the High Seas, and where the Owners and Mailers of such Ships would not be liable to Loss, and that such other Relief may be granted to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committ.ee, to whom the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Mailers of Ships is committed.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Petition from Rochdale Canal, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That, in 1793, a Number of Persons panyfor

associated together, and entered into a Subscription,

for the Purpose of making a Navigable Canal from the tion.

Colder Navigation, near Halifax, in the County of York, to the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal near Matt-chester, in the County of Lancaster, and thereby effect ing a Navigable Communication between the East and West Seas, which it was conceived would be a Work of great Public Utility, and would prove an important National' Advantage; and that previous to applying to Parliament for an Act for granting the necessary Powers for carrying the said Design into Execution, the said Subscribers, in order to obviate the Opposition which might otherwise have been made thereto, on Account of the private Interests of the Individuals whose Lands were intended to be cut through, caused Treaties to be entered into with several of such Proprietors of Lands for the Purchase of the Lands which would be required to be taken, and that, amongst others, Application was made to Robert Parker, late-of Halifax aforesaid, Gentleman (since deceased), the Owner of an Estate through which the Canal was intended to pass, who was unwilling to fell such Part . of his Land as was wanted for the making of the said Canal, but, to accommodate the Concern, he consented to fell the whole Estate, and, as it was apprehended that the said Robert Parker's Opposition would be materially detrimental to the Undertaking, it was judged expedient on the Part of the Subscribers to accede to his Proposals, and a Contraft was accordingly entered into for the Purchase of the whole Estate, it being intended to fell again such Part thereof, as would not be wanted for the Purposes of making the said Canal; and that, in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, an Act was passed, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the-Calder Navigation, at or near Sozverby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County v of York, to join the Canal of the Duke of in the Parish of Manchester, in the County Palatine of

38 Geo. III. 2° Mali. c2

Lancaster, and also certain Cuts from the said intended Canal, whereby it was eha&ed, that certain Persons therein named, and others, who should thereafter be possessed of Shares in the said Navigation, should be united into a Company, for the Purpose of making the said Canal and Cuts according to the Directions therein mentioned, and should be and becorpe a Body Corporate, by the Name of " The Company of Proprietors of " the Rochdale Canal," and by that Name should have perpetual Succession, and should have a Common Seal, and by that Name should sue and be sued, and ihpuld have Power and Authority to purchase Lands, and other Hereditaments, to them, their Supcessors, and Assigns, for making the said Canal and Cuts, and the several Works thereby authorized to be made, without incurring any of the Penalties or forfeitures of the Statutes of Mortmain, and divers Powers and Authorities were thereby given to the Petitioners for effecting the Purposes aforesaid; and that they have undertaken the Execution of the Powers and Authorities vested in them by the said Act, and have made great Progress in the making of the said Canal; and that the Petitioners considered it incumbent on them to fulfil the ContraCl made with the said Robert , for the Purchase of the said Estate, and caused the stipulated Purchase Money to be paid to him; and, because they doubted the Propriety of taking a Conveyance, to tjhemselves as a Corporate Body, it was judged proper, that the Conveyance should be made to Two of their Members on their Behalf; and that accordingly, by Indentures of Lease and Release, bearing Date respectively the 24th and 25th Days of June 1795, the Release made between the said Robert Parker and Mary his Wife (also since deceased) of the one Part, and the Reverend George Travis, Archdeacon of the Archdeaconry of the Diocese of Chester, and John Hamer, of Rochdale aforesaid. Gen-

tleman, of the other Part, the said Robert , in consideration of the Sum of £. 7,035 to him therein mentioned to be paid by the said George Travis and John Hamer, granted and released to the said George Travis and John Hamer, their Heirs and Assigns, the Capital Messuage and Tenement, called Upper Rrearly Hall, ©therwife Bryerly Hall, and sundry other Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, therein particularly mentioned, situate in the Parish of Halifax aforesaid, with the Appurtenances thereunto belonging, to hold the same unto the said George Travis and John Hamer, their Heirs and Assigns, to the only proper- Ule and Behoof of the kid'George Travis and John Hamer, their Heirs and Assigns, for ever, and that the said Sum of £. 7 035, the Consideration Money paid for the said Purchase, was the 'proper Money of the Petitioners, and the said Conveyance was made to the said George and John Hamer, as Trustees for, and on Behalf ofy 1 the Petitioners, although such Trull was not declared; and that the said George Travis. is since dead; and that it never was the Intention of the Petitioners to keep the Whole of the Ellate, so purchased of the said Robert Parker, but only to take so much thereof as was required for making the said Canal, and thenecessary Works and Conveniences thereof, in and through the said Estate, and to sell and dispose of the Remainder, to the Intent that the Money arising thereby might be applied towards -the completing of the said Canal, and that the said Canal hath nearly been made through the said Estate, and the Petitioners are now desirous of felling such Part of the said Estate as hath not, and shall not, be used or appropriated for the Purposes aforesaid, but Doubts have arisen, whether such Part of the said Estate as was not necessary for the making of the said Canal, and other Works and Conveniences authorized by the said ASt to be made, is not now become forfeited to the Crown by virtue of the Statutes or Laws of Mortmain; and that His Majesty has been graciously pleased to signify His Intention of waving all Benefit of the said Forfeiture, and all Claims in respect thereof, but it is Vot. 53.

doubted whether this can be effectually done, and whe-. ther such, and so much, of the said Lands and Hereditaments so purchased and conveyed as aforesaid as have, or hath not, been used, or shall not be used or appropriated for the Purposes aforesaid, can be fold and disposed of without the Aid and Authority of Parliament; and that the Petitioners are aware that the Time limited for presenting Petitions for bringing in Bills of a private Nature is elapsed, but that, the Matters Hated by the Petitioners having been for some Time under the Consideration of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Petitioners have been thereby prevented from complying with the Rules of the House with respect to the Time of presenting of Petitions of the Nature aforesaid; and that the Petitioners would incur great Loss, and be put to great Inconvenience, were their Application to the House to be deferred till the next Session: And therefore praying. That, on, Account of the special Circumstances of the Cafe, Leave may be given to the Petitioners now to present a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for veiling the said Lands and Hereditaments in the Parish of Halifax, in the County of York, in Trustees, and their Heirs, upon certain Trulls therein to be declared, discharged from all Claims of the Crown, in respect of any Forfeiture incurred under, or by virtue of, the Statutes of Mortmain, or the Laws relating to Mortmain.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular , Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Company of Proprietors of the Rochdale Canal,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an additional Duty of Six Pence be charged upon every Gallon of Rum, or other Spirits, imported into the Island of Newfoundland, from any British Colony or Plantation on the Continent of America.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty of Six Pence be charged upon every Gallon of Rum, or other Spirits, imported into the said Island, from any British Colony or Plantation in the West Indies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Melasses, the Produce or Manufacture of any of the British Colonies or Plantations, be permitted to be imported into the said Island without Payment of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to amend an Act, made in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the Encouragement of the " Fisheries carried on from Great Britain, Ireland, and " the British Dominions in Europe, and for securing the " Return of the Fishermen, Sailors, and others, employed in the said Fisheries, to the Ports thereof, at " the End of the Fishing Season."

Mr. Dhkinson reported from the Committee, to whom Rc-commiN the Report Was re-committed, which was made from Mr. sSys°a the Committee, to whom the Petition of Edward Petition, r -Sealy, of Bridgewater, in the County of Pone<i *

Merchant, was referred; That the Committee had further examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Re-

£»rt in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the lerk's Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth} viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Patent granted to George Hawkes, of Long Fleet, in the County of Dorset, Tanner, bearing Date the 2d Day of June 1795, for the Term of Fourteen Years from the Date thereof, for the sole Use and Benefit of his Discovery or Invention of Tanning Leather with Elm Bark, and also the Specification and Description thereof, and also the Assignment thereof to the Petitioner, were severally produced, and read:

And,

Mr. Joseph Gutheridge being examined, said. That prior to such Assignment, and in consequence of an Intercourse between, the Petitioner and certain Persons of Eminence in the Tanning Trade, numerous Experiments were made, with the Consent and under the Direction of the Petitioner, to enable them to determine with Certainty how far Elm Bark might prove a Substitute for Oak Bark.

Mr. Samuel Beddome then confirmed the above Evidence of Mr. Gutheridge.

Mr. James Warne being then examined, said, That from the Result of the said Experiments, the Persons who made them convened a General Meeting of the Tanners, submitted Parts of the Leather so tanned, with a particular Account of the Experiments, to their , Examination, stated it to be their Opinion, that the Leather so tanned with Elm Bark was nearly, equal in Gobdness to what was theretofore tanned with Oak Bark} and further Rated, that Elm Bark would prove a Substitute for Oak Bark, assist the Manufacturer, be the Means of preserving Oak Timber, and of increasing the Public Revenue: That the Tanners assembled at

the said Meeting were satisfied that the Leather tanned with Elm Bark was firm, durable, and good, and that great Advantages would accrue to the Public from the general Use thereof.

Mr. Samuel Purkis, Mr. Peter Duncan, Mr. Robert Wyatt, and Mr. Samuel Beddome, confirmed the fore-

iing Evidence of Mr. Gutheridge.

Mr. Gutheridge being then further examined, he was aiked, Whether, in the Opinion he had given in Favour of Mr, Sealy's Discovery of the Use of Elm Bark in Tanning Leather, he was guided by Experiments he had made himself? he said. The Experiments were conducted under the Direction and Superintendence of Mr. Beddome and himself; in which Experiments Elm

Bark only was used, except that the first Woozes were prepared from Oak Bark, not from any Doubt of tho Success of Elm Bark in this Respect, but for Want of a sufficient Quantity: In Addition to these Experi-

ments, they tanned between Five and Six hundred Horse Hides wholly with Elm Bark, which Hides were good and serviceable Leather (a Specimen of which was produced to your Committee); but, convinced from former Experiments of the Advantages to be derived from the Use of Elm Bark, no particular Account was kept of the Weight of the Hides, or the Quantity of Bark used. Being asked. If he thought that the Use of Elm Bark will be of Advantage in Tanning ? he said. Elm Bark will be certainly advantageous in Tanning of Leather, as it will help to supply the Want of Oak Bark, which is become lcarce and dear; but he does not fey, that the Leather manufactured with Elm Bark will in every Respect be as good as that tanned with, Oak Bark; {rat it will be good, durable, and

marketable

v

544 7° Mali. A. 1798.

marketable Leather; and when, from longer Experience, its Nature and Properties will be better known, it is probable that the Leather will be further improved. Being asked. Is the Weight of the Leather, when tanned, a sufficient Criterion of its Goodness? lie laid, The Weight of the Sole Leather, when tanned, is, cruris paribus, a Criterion of its Solidity, and Solidity is the first Excellence of Sole Leather; with respect to Calf Skins, and all Upper Leather, it is an Argument in its Favour, but not to be wholly relied on. Being asked. If any Leather tanned with Elm Bark has been made into Boots or Shoes, or other Articles ? the Witness referred to Mr. and Mr:

Duncan; and Mr. IVyatt being present, produced some Leather tanned with Elm Bark, which he thinks as good as Leather wholly tanned with Oak Bark, and he should not have known whether it was so or not.

Mr. Duncan being also present, laid, That Shoemakers have, used it, and have declared that they thought it equal to that tanned with Oak Bark, and should not have known it had been tanned with Elm Bark if they had not been told of it.

Mr. Richard Norcott,a Mailer Shoemaker, who does his own Work, was asked. Whether he had worked up any of the Leather tanned with Him Bark? he said. Yes, he had made Six or Eight Pair of-Soles of it. Being asked, If it is nearly as good as that.tanned with Oak Bark ? he said. Yes, the only Fault he had found with Slices, of which the Soles were made of it, was, that the Upper Leathers, which were tanned with Oak, wore away before the Soles. Being asked. If he should have known the Difference ? he laid. No, it worked full as well. , -

Mr. Joseph Graves, also a Mailer Shoemaker, who does his own Work, was asked, Whether he had worked up any of the Leather tanned with Elm Bark? he laid, He had i'oled and heeled Shoes with it. Being asked; If it is nearly as good as that tanned with Oak Bark ? he said. Equally good. Being asked. If he should have known the Difference? he laid, Only by the Colour.

Then both the last mentioned Witnesses being lliewn a Piece of Sole Leather, tanned with Elm Bark, they were asked. Whether it was as good as it tanned with Oak Bark? to which they laid. Yes; they should never wish to work up better Leather.

Mr. Gutheridge then said. That he has tried some of the Leather tanned with Elm Bark in the W ear, and thinks it nearly equal to any other Leather; and that he having gone into his Warehouse to search for some Skins which had been tanned with Elm Bark, and which were mixed with Skins tanned with Oak, he found it impracticable to feleCl them without the Assistance of the Workman, by whom they had been marked with a private Mark.

Mr. Gutheridge being further examined, was asked. Whether he conceived the Use of Elm Bark would contribute either to lower the present Price of tanned Leather, or to prevent its rising? he said, Should the Use of Elm Bark become general, an additional Quantity of the Raw Material will be manufactured, which will probably tend to lower the.Price of Leather; the Trade can generally obtain a greater Quantity of the Raw Material than they can get Bark to manufacture. Being asked. Whether the Exportation of Leather tanned with Elm Bark might not hyrt the Reputation of the English Leather in Foreign Markets? he Paid, The Leather tanned with Elm Bark will be so nearly equal to the Leather tanned with Oak, that he conceives no Injury can arise therefrom. Being asked, What Ulc is now made of Elm Bark? he said. No Use is now made of it. Being asked, What has been the Average Price of Oak Bark for Six Years pad? he said. About 5 1 or. a Load of Match, or Two Tons and a Quarter in . W eight, delivered in London..; Being asked, ‘What Price he paid for the Elm Bark used in these, Experiments? lie said. Being asked, If he made use of Sait in tanning with Oak Bark, and if so, ip what Proportion? he laid, Salt is not used in tanning with Oak Bark. Being asked, Whether he made use of Salt in the Experiments with Elm Bark, and if so, in what Proportion ? he said. All the Experiments were made by the Direction of Mr. Sealy, the Proprietor of the Patent for tanring with Elm Bark; Two Pounds were used for every Hundred Weight of thin Leather, and Four Pounds for Sole Leather, and in One of the Experiments with Elm Bark, no Salt was used. Being asked, What Quantity of Bark is uled in tanning in England, on an Average, Annually ? he said, That is estimated from the Quantity o£Leather tanned; he imagines it to be about 70,000 Tons Annually. Being asked. What Quantity of Elm Bark does he imagine might be procured? he laid, When the Value of Elm Bark becomes generally known, and the Use of it authorized by a Repeal of the Clause in the ACk of the First of King-y wer the First, it is probable that Elm Timber will in future be cut, down at the Spring of the Year, when the Bark may be stripped:. It is difficult to say what Quantity may be procured; but as in many Counties of t Kim Timber is

much more abundant than the Oak, it will doubtless furnish a very considerable Supply. It has been lug-gefted, that ltripping the Bark from- Elm may be prejudicial to the Timber, but lie has Reason to believe that this Opinion is ill founded, or at lead can only apply to the lmaller Kind of 'limber, which is used for boring for Pumps and Pipes for W aterworks. Being asked? What Quantity of Leather may'be tanned with a Ton of Oak Bark, what Quantity with a Ton of Elm Bark, and what Quantity with a Mixture of both? he said, A Ton of Oak Bark will tau from Four to Ijive hundred Weight of Leather, according to the Quality of the Bark and the Species of Leather, and by an Experiment made with about Two Thirds of Elm Bark, it appears that a Ton of Elm Bark will produce nearly the same Weight of Leather, and, however mixed, the Relult will be proportionate. Being asked, What Proportion does the Value of Bark, according to the present Price, bear to the whole Expence of manufacturing Leather? he said. According to the present Price, the Value of the Bark used in tanning of Leather in general, is about Six Tenths of the whole Expence of manufacturing. Being asked. If Bark could be had in greater Abundance, could there be procured, and would there be tanned a greater Number of Hides and Skins? he said, Unquestionably a greater Quantity of the Raw Material would be imported and tanned. Being asked, Whether a greater Importation of Raw Hides and Skins would tend to lower the Price of Leather? lie laid. As it would increase the Supply without increasing the Demand, it is reasonable to conclude that the Price would thereby be' reduced. Being asked, Whether the general Use or Elm Bark will not benefit the Leather Manufacture in Ireland ?he said, The Use of Elm Bark in this Count ry will, independent of the Quantity which Ireland itself may afford, insure a greater Supply both of Oak and Elm Bark for the Irish Market, to which a considerable Quantity of our Bark is Annually exported. Duty free, and of course the Tanners in Ireland will partake of the same Advantages as the Tanners in England. Being asked, Whether there is any Quantity or Store of Oak Bark at present in the Kingdom, more than at any former Period ? he fjid, The great Demands for Oak-Timber for the Use of the Navy, during the last Three or Four Years, and the Exportation of Bark to the North of Ireland having last Year materially decreased, owing to the Disturbances in that Part of the Country,

have occasioned the Quantity of Bark now on Hand to be more considerable than it was a few Years ago, when Bark could scarcely be procured at any Price; yet it bears no Proportion to the Quantity formerly kept in Store by the Timber Merchant and the Manufacturer; and as the Fall of Timber this Year is expected to be rather.inconsiderable, the Stock of Bark now on Hand, together with the new Supply, will, it is feared, be inadequate to the Demand of the Manufacture. Being asked, Whether he has tried other Things besides Elm Bark ? he said. He has tried various Articles that might be used, but found nothing equal to Elm Bark. Being asked. Whether any Experiments have been made upon the Leather tanned with Elm Bark, in the common Purposes of Hamels, Saddles, or in general Wear? he laid, No Leather has been manufactured for the Purpose of Hamel's, the Experiments have only been Sole and Upper Leather.

And Mr. Duncan further said, That he is ready to give the same Price for Leather tanned with Elm Bark as with Oak Bark.

Mr. Gutheridge being further examined, was asked,

Whether the Tanning Trade in general will have any Reason to be dissatisfied with the Establishment of Mr. Hawkes's Patent? he said. If Parliament had thought fit to give the Patentee a Remuneration for introducing the Use of Elm Bark,'it appeared to him that this would have been the moll eligible Mode of Compensation, as the Use of the Article will, in his Judgment, prove of National Advantage, both as it respects the Revenue and the Public. Speaking for himself, nd for other Manufacturers, perhaps they might be justified in saying, " Give us a Benefit, and take nothing for it;' but, on the Ground of Equity, they think that no Manufacturer, who is inclined to use the Article, ought to object to paying to the Patentee a final 1 Compensation for a Licence. Being asked. What Security is there that the Patentee will grant such a Licence for a moderate Compensation ? he said, The belt of all Securities, the interest of the Patentee, which would lead him to grant a Licence for a small Sum, in order to induce a more general Use of the Article. Being asked. If the Patentee were obliged to grant a Licence for a Sum not less than One Guinea, nor more than Ten Guineas Annually, would the Security then be more complete and satisfactory to the Trade? he said, He apprehended it would. Being asked. If he thought that will afford a Prospect for a fair Remuneration to the Patentee? he said, This will depend on the Judgment the Public will form of it.

Mr. Beddome, Mr. Warm, and Mr. Purkis confirmed the above Evidence of Mr. Gutheridge.

Mr. Seafy, the Petitioner and Patentee, was then asked, For what Sum he should be willing to grant Annual Licences? he said, He should be willing to grant Licences at from One Guinea to Ten Guineas for each Licence; but he begged Leave to observe, that Three Years of the Term of the Patent is now expired, and he has'not as yet reaped any Advantage therefrom; and that, should it hereafter appear that the Advantages arising to the Public should be of great Importance, and that the Benefits derived to the Patentee should not amount to a reasonable Remuneration, he humbly hopes that the Circumstances of his then Situation will be favourably considered.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Town of Lancaster, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, ;yas presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for obviating and removing Doubts respecting the holding of the Adjournments of the General Court of Quarter Sessions of the Peace in and for the County Palatine of Lancaster, and for authorizing the Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the said County, to hold an Annual General Sessions, and also a Special Sessions, for the Purposes therein mentioned; and Setting forth. That, if the same should pass into a Law, it will invalidate and destroy several valuable and ancient Grants, Charters, Immunities, and Privileges, made, given, and confirmed to the Petitioners, by several Monarchs of this Kingdom; and that the Four General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the said County have originated at Lancaster for upwards of Four Centuries part, and have been adjourned from thence to Preston, Wigan, Ormskirk, and for the general Ease and Convenience of the County at large; and that, by reason of the Quarter Sessions having been held at Lancaster aforesaid from such a remote Period of Time, great Emoluments have accrued to the Petitioners, and the other Owners of Property in the Town and Vicinity of Lancaster, which will be greatly diminished should the said Bill pass into a Law; and that the Mode of holding the Sessions, and transacting the Business of the County, as proposed by the said Bill, is confused, expensive, and so novel as to be without a Precedent, and the Petitioners are confident it is a Measure not called for by any existing Circumstances,-and likely to produce much Mitchicf and Inconvenience: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Agents, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

ed it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr, John Roliinfon, Surveyor, being examined, said, That from Time immemorial there has been, and Hill is, a Common and Public Sewer on Little within the Tower Hamlets, in the County of Middlesex, called Tower Hill Sewer, and which receives the Waters from the City Sewers: That at the End of the Year 1794, the said Sewer was blown up, and that occasioned by a Defect that happened in the City Sewer, and by an additional Quantity of Waters turned therein; that the same was repaired, but very recently the like Accident has happened again; that upon Inspection, it appears from its Size, not sufficient to carry off the great Body of Water that has been recently turned therein, and which was formerly discharged in another Direction; and that a-netv Sewer is absolutely necessary to be made, sufficient for that Purpose.

And the Witness added, That it will be necessary to enable the Commissioners of Sewers to borrow a considerable Sum of Money for effecting the Purposes necessary for making the said new Sewer.

Mr. Wilbrahatn Bootle reported from the Committee, Report on «-to whom the Report was re-committed, which was committed made from the Committee, to whom the several Papers rdat-

which were presented to the House, upon the 21st ingtoPriibn-Day of March last, by Mr. Whitehead from the Trans- ers of War-port Board, and by Mr. Stewart from the Commissioners for Sick and Wounded Seamen, respecting the Treatment of Prisoners of War, were referred} and who were directed to examine the Matters thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had made some Alterations in the said Report, and some Additions thereto, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's

Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Reftlved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Charge of Cruelty towards French Prisoners of War, which has been brought against this Country, is utterly void of Foundation, and appears to have been fabricated, and industriously Supported by the Enemy, for the double Purpose of justifying their own ill Treatment of British Prisoners, and of irritating the Minds of their Countrymen against this Nation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the British Prisoners of War, confined in France, have been treated with a Degree of Rigour and Inhumanity

38 GEO.III. $ Maii.

555

humanity unwarranted by the Usages of War among civilized Nations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the British Government has always manifested a Delirc of entering upon a Cartel of Exchange on the mostfair and liberal Terms; that it has even offered to accede to any which could be adopted confidently with what is due to Individuals, and to the Nation; and that the Obstacles to a Negotiation have arisen from the extravagant and unprecedented Demands of and from the Refusal, on our Part, to abandon the customary and acknowledged Principle of the Law of Nations, which has been grossly violated in the Person of Sir Sidney Smith.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report, with the Appendix, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The said Report is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

N. B. A printed Copy is with the Original.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing the Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights, on Inhabited Houses, and on Clocks and Watches, and for granting to His Majesty other Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights, and on Inhabited Houses, in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And also.

would be necessary to complete a certain Branch from Taylor's Bam to Beat Bank, and the Petitioner therefore submits to the Justice of the House, that that Sum at the least ought to be specifically appropriated to the Completion thereof, and that proper and sufficiertt Clauses should be introduced, not only for that Purpose, but also to regulate the general Rates of Tonnage, so that no partial or particular Interests shall be preferred, to the Detriment of the Petitioner and other.

The Owners of Mines and Collieries in the said Navigations, and of the Public at large; and that a Clause is inserted in the said Bill to exonerate the said Company of Proprietors from the Repair and Amendment of any Part of the Roads over the Approaches to any of the Bridges over the said Canal, after such Roads shall have been first made and put into good Repair by the said Proprietors, titan which, the Petitioner submits nothing can be more unreasonable, since the Proprietors ought, on every Principle of Justice, to repair Roads which their own Schemes have rendered necessary: And therefore praying. That proper Provisions may be introduced in the said Bill to redress the Grievances complained of, and that the Petitioner may have such Relief in the Premises as the House shall deem reasonable, and that, for thfe Obtainment thereof he may be heard, by himself, or his Coua-fel. . Were severally presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Matters of Ships; and Setting forth, That, if the same should pass into a Law, it would reduce the Refpohfibility of the Owners and Matters of Ships, at the liilk, and greatly to the Prejudice, of the Shippers of Goods on Freight, and thereby deprive such Shippers of that Security for proper Care being taken of their Goods, and for the Sufficiency and efficient Equipment of freighted Ships, and their due Navigation, which are essential to the Protection and Encouragement of Trade; and that by the Law, as it now Hands, the Shippers of Goods can protect themselves, by Insurance, against all Rilks which their Goods hre exposed to in a Sea Voyage, and for which the Owners of Ships are not responsible, whereas, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, they would, in consequence of the present Respon-libility of the Ship Owners being removed, or greatly reduced, be jexposed to Rilks against which they cannot infpre; and such Increase of Risk would tend to deter Manufacturers, and other Persons who have been accustomed to export Goods on their own Account, from engaging in such Adventures, and thereby greatly injure the Export Trade of the Kingdom: That the said Bill purports to exonerate Owners of Ships from Responsibilities to which they are now liable, upon Contracts already entered into, and thereby to operate as an ex post faElo Law, which the Petitioners' submit would be highly unjust, and the more so, as the- Bill contains no such Provision with respect to the Owners of Vessels navigating the Tideway of Rivers; and that, pending the Discussion of the said Bill before a Committee of the House, a Clause has been introduced to extend the Relief, thereby proposed to be given to the Owners and Masters of Ships, to the Owners and Masters of all Vessels employed in the Navigation of the Tideway of any River, and not employed in the Navigation of the High Seas, with respect to any Loss or Damage hap-' pening below any Port or Place in such Tideway, where Ships, or other Vessels employed in the Coasting Trade, do or shall load or discharge by Entry or Sufferance; and that whatever Relief the Owners of Ships' or Vessels navigating the High Seas may be entitled to, so as to enable them to meet with Advantage Foreign Ships in open Competition in the carrying Trade, yet it would be extremely impolitic to allow the same Relief and Protection to Vessels navigating the Tideway of Rivers in this Kingdom, inasmuch as no Competition of Foreign Vessels can be opposed to them, and it.is com-, petent to the Owners to charge such a Rate of Freight as will be an adequate Compensation for the Rilks they are exposed to: In Addition to this Consideration, the Petitioners submit, that they cannot, without great Loss, protect themselves against the Rilks from which it is proposed to

relieve Owners of Vessels navigating th<? Tideway of Rivers, as the Commission and Duties upon Policies of Insurance, for the final left possible Space, is equal to that upon an Insurance for the longest Voyage, and would in Eftect amount to a l'uinouS Tax upon the Inland Navigation of the Country, whereas, the Owners of Vessels may, by an Annual Insurance upon Property,

Committed to their Care, at a very small Expence, protect themselves against the Riik they leek to be relieved from, and' may apportion such Premium amongst their Freighters; hitherto the Petitioners have not been accustomed to insure their Goods upon Inland Navigations, as the Risk did not amoiflat to One Filth Part of the Commission and Duty on Insurances, but, if the Risk usually borne by tire Owners of Vessels is taken away, the Petitioners mull either insure at a ruinous Expence, or leave their Property unprotected, under the Care ot Persons who will not be sufficiently interested in its Protection to induce them to pay adequate Attention thereto; and that, as the Bill now stands, the Owners of all Vessels, of every Size and Description, navigating the High Seas, os the Tideway of a River, would be entitled to the same Protection, without Regard to the Size or Construe-tion of such Vessels, or their Competency to carry the Goods they take on Board with Safety; an open Boat or Barge, however small, going from one Place to another, either at Sea or in a Tide River, will be placed in tho-fame Situation as a regular decked Vessel: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the fame.

A Petition of sundry Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, Subscribers to an Institution, called The Veterinary College, was presented to the House, and read; Set-

ting forth. That in pursuance of the Plan stated to the House in a Petition by them presented on the 6 th of February 1795, their Exertions have been continued to carry into Effect the several beneficial Purposes proposed to be derived from the Establishment of a College for the Study and Practice of Veterinary Science; that, for the general Benefit of the Proprietors of Horses and other valuable Cattle, they have Pleasure in dating that Forty-eight Pupils have palfed Examination at the said College, many of whom are now settled in different Towns of the Kingdom, and are practising the Knowledge they have acquired to the great Advantage of the Public; and it is with peculiar Satisfaction the Petitioners are enabled to state, that, the Importance of the In-ilitution having been taken into Consideration by his Royal Highnel's the Commander in Chief, the Propriety of appointing Persons educated at the College to be Veterinary Surgeons in the several Regiments of Cavalry has been determined on, in pursuance of a Report from a Board of General Officers, to whom the Subject had been referred; and that in consequence of such Decision, Twenty Pupils, whole Education has been completed, are engaged in the Service of the Army, and Twenty-seven other Pupils are now pursuing their Studies at the College, l'everal of them intending to fill similar Situations as loon as they shall be deemed duly qualified, each of them being subject to the same rigorous Examination of the Medical Committee, and to be certified in the same Manner, as has hitherto been praftif-ed in respect of the other Pupils of the College; and the Petitioners further state, that, desirous of rendering, to the utmost of their Power, their Institution advantageous to the Public Service, the Colonels of the different Cavalry Regiments have been invited to fend each a Farrier to the College, in order to his being taught the Structure, Economy, and different Diseases of the Horse's Foot, and instructed in a Mode of Shoeing, tending very materially to its Preservation, and that Army Farriers have been consequently admitted into the College for Instruction in that particular Part of Veterinary Knowledge; and that the College continues under the Direction of the Professor, Mr. , a

Gentleman of Talents and Skill, and who, by many useful and important Discoveries in the Science, has, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, fully justified the Expedations formed of its Improvement from his Exertions; and that the Petitioners have already stated to the House the Difficulties which have occurred in the Execution of their Plan, and particularly from the em-baraffed State of their Finances, and, though the Aid so liberally granted by Parliament has in a great Degree alleviated their Difficulties, it has yet proved inadequate to remove them entirely, notwithstanding the Petitioners have, with the utmost Frugality, reduced their Annual Expenditure much within the Estimate of the Committee of the House to whom their former Peti-. tion was referred, and within those Limits to which they are Still of Opinion it would be proper to extend it, in order that the Public may derive the full Benefit of such an Establishment, the Petitioners have again with Regret to state, that (under the heavy Pressure of Debt, of which an Account is before the House) without further Aid from Parliament, it will be impossible jto bring to Perfection an Establishment, which, from Vot- 53-

the Advantages accruing from the more skilful Care of so important a Branch of Public Property as the Horses of the Army, is become more than ever an Object of National Importance; and the Petitioners having been Unable, before the Time which was appointed for pro-Tenting private Petitions had expired, to obtain Information whether His Majesty's gracious Recommendation would be given to the said Petition, humbly hope-that the House will now be pleased to receive the same.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Leave given. Circumstances let forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Noble- men. Gentlemen, and others.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and Shippers of Goods for Exportation, resident in and near Huddersfield, whose Names are thereunto subscribed: And also,

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of the Town and Parish of Halifax, Shippers of Goods for Exportation;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the further Relief of Owners and Matters of Ships; and Setting forth. That the same will, if passed into a Law, reduce the llefponfibility of the Owners and Matters of Ships, at the Risk, and greatly . to the Prejudice, of the Shippers of Goods on Freight, and thereby deprive such Shippers of that Security for proper Care being taken of their Goods, and for the Sufficiency and efficient Equipment of freighted Ships, and the due Navigation thereof, which are essential to the Protection and Encouragement of Trade; and that by the Law, as it now Hands, the Shippers of Goods can protest themselves, by Jniurance, against all Risks which their Goods are exposed to in a Sea Voyage, and for which the Owners of Ships are not responsible, whereas, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, they would (in consequence of the present Responsibility of Ship Owners being removed, or greatly reduced) be exposed to Risks against which they cannot insure; and such Increase of Risk would tend to deter Manufacturers, and other Persons who have been accustomed to export Goods on their own Account, from engaging in such Adventures, and thereby greatly injure the Export Trade of the Kingdom; and that the said Bill purports to exonerate Owners of Ships from Responsibilities to which they are now liable, upon Contrafts already entered into, and thereby to operate as an ex pofi fatto Law, which the Petitioners submit would be highly unjust, and the more so, as the Bill contains no such Provision with respect to the Owners of Vessels navigating the Tideway of Rivers; and that, pending the Discussion of the said Bill before a Committee of the House, a Clause has been introduced to extend the Relief, thereby proposed to be given to the Owners and 7 E Matters

To prove the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Dance being further examined, laid, That the Want of Accommodation for the Landing and Shipping of Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes in the Port of London, has for some Years pad been experienced by all Persons trading to the said Port, and more especially the Persons concerned in the India Trade,

by reason of the confined and crowded State of the Legal Quays in, or belonging to, the said Port: That from the Nature and Value of the Cargoes imported from the West Indies, the Persons concerned in the West India Trade, fuller in a highly aggravated Degree from the heavy Losses occasioned by Plunder, and from the Delay and increased Expence arising from the above-mentioned Causes attending the Discharge of the Ships and Vessels employed in that Trade, and the Public Revenue is thereby materially dimini fired: That if good and sufficient Wet Docks and Basons, with proper Cuts, Sluices, and Outlets, were made and established in some Part or Parts of the Isle of Dogs, with Quays, Wharfs, and Warehouses, attached thereto, where necessary, for the Reception and Discharge of Ships and other Vessels employed in the India Trade, the same would not only be extremely beneficial to all Persons concerned in the said Trade, but advantageous to the Trade in general, frequenting the Port of London, by reason of the Room and Accommodation which would necessarily arise from the Removal of the Ships and Vessels employed in the' West India Trade out of the River: That by Plans and Surveys lately made, it appears that such Wet Docks, Basons, and other Requisites, may be made and constructed in the Isle of Dogs, and that the Petitioners are willing and desirous to make the same at their own Expence: That Application is making to this House by the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, for a Bill to enable them to make and maintain a

Navigable Cut or Canal, for the safe and convenient Passage of Ships and other Vessels across the said Isle of Dogs, which Cut or Canal will pass very near to the Place proposed for the Scite of the said intended Wet Docks and Basons; and that the making of the Wet Docks and Canal as above-mentioned, will be the Means of affording certain, adequate, and complete Relief and Accommodation, not only to the West India Trade, but also to all the rest of the Shipping now or hereafter frequenting the said Port of London, and to the general Trade thereof: Then, »

forth. That the same will, if pasted into a Law, entirely ruin the Trade; and that the Petitioners feel this the more severely, as it neither has been stated, nor can be proved, either by the Official Returns now before the House, or otherwise, that any Evil or Inconvenience whatever is experienced by the Negroes from their present Mode of Transportation; and that, by an Act, pasted in the last Setlion, the Height between Decks was fixed at Four Feet One Inch, conformably to which many Merchants have caused their Vest'els to be altered, at a very great Expence; and that, as several Ships lo altered, and all that Class of Vessels in which the Slaves are carried in the most perfect Health, and which it has been the uniform Rule of the Legislature to encourage, will be utterly excluded from the British CaTying Trade; and as the Reduction of the Number of Slaves to be carried in the large Ships will render it impossible to continue them in the Trade with any probable Prospect of Advantage; and, moreover, as the Vessels which will be so excluded from this Trade are so construded as not to be fit for any other, an enormous Loss will consequently be incurred by the Owners: An<f therefore praying. Mr. Rofc, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole. House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Duties payable on Salt, and who were instructyd to consider of an Act, made in this present Session of Parliament, intituled, " An " Act; for granting t(THis Majesty additional Duties on " Salt," the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

ReJ'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable on Foreign Salt imported into Great Britain, and on Salt brought from Scotland into England, and on Salt or Rock Salt made at any Sait Works, or raised or taken out of any Pits in Great Britain, and on Mineral Alkali, or Flux for Glass, made in Great Britain, and on Rock Salt exported from Great Britain, and the kveraT Drawbacks, Discounts, Allowances, and BoutUies, payable thereout, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel of Salt, not being the Product or Manufacture of Great Britain, that shall be imported into Great Britain, there be charged the Sum of Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, and so in proportion for any greater oriel's Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel of Salt, or Rock Salt, which shall be made at any Salt Work, or raised or taken out of any Salt Mine , or Salt Pit, in England or there be charged the Sum of Ten Shillings, and so in proportion lor ary greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel of Salt, or Rock Salt, which shall be made at any Salt Work, or raised or taken out of any Salt Mine or Salt Pit, in Scotland, there be charged the Sum of Six Shillings and Six Pence, and so in proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel ot all Salts, known or called by the Name of Glauber or Epsom Salts, which shall be made or produced at any Salt Work in Great there be charged the Sum of Ten Shillings, and so in proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Ton of Mineral Alkali, or Flux for Glass, which shall be made of any Rock Salt, or from any Brine or Sea Water, there be charged the Sum of Twenty Shillings, and lb in proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel of Rock Salt, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be charged the Sum of One Penny, and so in proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Bushel of Salt, or Rock Salt, which shall be imported from Scotland into England or Wales, having paid the Duty imposed on Sail made in Scotland, there be charged the Sum of Three Shillings and Six Pence, and lo in proportion for any greater or Id's Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for, every Bushel of Salt which shall be made in England ox Wales (li vck Salt excepted) for which all the Duties due and payable thereon shall be paid, or secured to be paid, and which Ilia!! be exported from thence to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Drawback of Ten Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Bushel of Salt which shall be made in Scotland (Rock Salt excepted) for which all the Duties due and payable thereon shall be paid, or secured to be paid, and which shall be exported from thence to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Drawback of Six Shillings and Six Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Bushel ot Salts, known or called by the Name of Glauber ox Epjlm Salts, which shall be made or produced at any Silt Work in Great Britain, for which all the Duties due and payable thereon shall be paid, or secured to be paid, and which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Drawback of Five Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every One Hundred Weight of dried Cod Fish, Ling, or Hake (commonly called Habcrdine) which shall contain in Length Fourteen Inches, or upwards, from the Bone in the Fin to the Third Joint in the Tail of every such Fish, and which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Three Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Wet "Cod Fish, Ling, or Hake, containing Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Two Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Salmon, containing Forty-two Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Four Shillings and Six Pence.

ReJ'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of White Herrings, containing Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Two Shillings and Eight Pence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of full Red Herrings, containing Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of One Shilling and Nine Pence.
