Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of clean Shotten Red Herrings, containing Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Last, confiding of Ten Thowfand dried Red Sprats, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Calk or Vessel of Pilchards or Seads, containing Fifty Gallons, which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Seven Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Beef or Pork, containing Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be salted in England or Wales with Salt which shall have paid all the Duties due and payable thereon, and which shall be exported from thence to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Five Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Barrel of Beef or Pork, of Thirty-two Gallons, which shall be salted in Scotland with Foreign Salt (without Mixture of Britishi or Irish Salt) which shall have paid all the Duties due and payable thereon, and which shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, there be allowed a Bounty of Five Shillings.,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person or Persons to whom any Salt shall be delivered, free of Duty, for the Purpose of curing and preserving Fish, shall be allowed a greater Quantity of Salt than Fifty Pounds Weight of Salt for every Hundred Weight of dried Cod, Ling, or Hake; Fifty-six Pounds Weight for every Barrel containing Thirty-two Gallons of Wet Cod, Ling, or Hake} Thirty-six Pounds height for every Barrel containing Forty-two Gallons of Salmon; One Hundred and Forty Pounds Weight for every Barrel containing Thirty-two Gallons of White Herrings; Sixty-five Pounds Weight for every Barrel containing Thirty-two Gallons of full Red Herrings; Fifty-six Pounds Weight for every Barrel containing Thirty-two Gallons of clean Shotten Red Her-ings; Twenty-five Pounds Weight for every Last confiding of Ten Thousand dried Red Sprats; and Two Hundred and Eighty Pounds Weight for every Calk containing Fifty Gallons of Pilchards or Seads; and so in proportion for any greater or less Quantity of such Fish respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty now payable on Licences for making of Mineral Alkali, or Flux for Glass, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon every Licence, authorizing any Person or Persons to make Mineral Alkali, or Flux for Glass, in Great Britain, there be charged a Duty of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that Compensation should be made to the Commissioners and Officers employed in England in the Collection and Management of the Duties on Salt, who shall or may be deprived of their Employments, and the Salaries and Emoluments arising therefrom.

' The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for transferring the Management of the Salt Duties to the Commissioners of Excise, That they do make Provision in the said Bill pursuant to the said Resolutions.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Leeds and Mr. Pepys:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Common, or Parcel of Waste Land, called Bleathwood mon, within the Parish of Little in the County of Hereford',without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing, for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, made in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of King 'George the Second, and the Nineteenth Yeah of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Dewsbury to Ealain the West Riding of the County of York; without any Amendment: And also,.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, Commonable Lands, and Waste Grounds, in the Phrtih of Wilbarfton', in the County of Northampton; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for extending the Neath Canal Navigation, and for amending an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign- of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill,' intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estates of Sir Robert Baronet, in the Counties of Stafford anti Warwick, in Trustees, and their Heirs, in Trust, for the said Sir Robert Lawley, to be sold, and for settling other Lands

and Hereditaments, in the County of of greater

Value, in lieu thereof; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estate of Guitton,

Esquire, deceased, in Trustees, to be conveyed pursuant to Articles entered into for the Sale thereof, and for laying out the Money arising therefrom in the Purchase of other Estates to be settled to the same Uses; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for dividing the Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob, in tire County of

Gloucester, and in the City and County of and for erecting a Church in the said new intended Parish, was read; whereby it appears, that the Inhabitants within the said new Parish should be divided from, and independent of, the Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob, and be exempt from bearing any Parish Offices or Charges, and from all Dependencies and Contributions for or in respect thereof, except such as are therein otherwise provided; and that all Rates and Levies to the Poor and for the Highways should be made, rated, levied, and assessed, upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob, and of the said new Parish, jointly and in common, without any Distinction of the Parishes intended by the said Act, and as they were before the making thereof; and that the Work -house then already built, and then Handing in the said Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob, should remain, continue, and be, for the joint Ule of the Poor of the said new Parish, and of the said Parish of Philip and Jacob-, and that all Orders of Justices of the Peace for removing of, dr relating to, the Poor, should be made and directed as before the making the said Act:

And, .

Mr. Daniel Pidding being examined, said, That he had been Overseer of the Poor of the Out Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob, and Saint George, for Six or Seven Years last pall; that a certain District of the said

Out Parish of Saint Philip and Jacob was divided therefrom, and formed into a separate Parish, being the said Parish of Saint George, and a new Church hath been erected thereon, conformable to the Directions of the said Act; that the Poor have greatly increased since the Division of the said Parish, and that they canhot be so well'provided for in their present State, as if they were separately maintained, and the Rates and Levies divided; that it would be a considerable Saving to each of the said Parishes, and the Highways' would be kept in better Repair, if the Expence of repairing them Was separated and made independent of each other: Then,

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estate of John ton, Esquire, deceased, in Trustees, to be conveyed pursuant, to Articles entered into for the Sale thereof, and for laying out the Money arising therefrom in the Purchase of other Ellatcs to be settled to the same Uses, was read the First Time.

A Petition of the Merchants and others concerned in the African Slave Trade from the Port of Live)-pool, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is now depending in the House for an Alteration of the Act for regulating the Trade in Negro Slaves to Africa, which, the Petitioners apprehend, will be very injurious to their Interests; and that the salutary Regulations lately enacted for the carrying on of this Trade have, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, removed the former Objections thereto, and secured all the Conveniences and Comforts so necessary for the Slaves on Board of the African Vessels: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the Alteration before-mentioned, and that the present existing Regulating Bill may be continued.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report, which was made from the Committee to whom the Bill for regulating the shipping and carrying of Slaves in British Vessels from the Coast of Africa was committed, be taken into further Consideration; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit. Then the said Petition was brought up; and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for enlarging the Term canted by an Act, of the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for continuing the Duty of Two Pennies Scots upon every Pint of Ale and Beer sold in the City of *

for the Purposes therein mentioned, and for explaining and amending the said Act; and Setting forth, That a Petition has been presented to the House, in Name of the now Petitioners, for Leave to be heard, by themselves and Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the Petitioners meant to shew that the Effects of the Bill would be attended with great Hardship on them in carrying on their Trade, and also that it would be not-only hurtful to the Morals of the People, but a Detriment to the Public Revenue of Excise to a much greater Extent than the whole Sum which would be received from it by the City of and that

Goverhment would be much benefited by granting a Substitute in Money for the said Duty; and that, so Conscious are the Petitioners of what they thus assert, they will withdraw their Petition against the Bill, if it shall contain a Clause granting Power to the Lords of the Treasury to apply a certain Annual Sum of Money, out of the Revenue of Excise in sufficient for answering and defraying the Purposes for which the Duty fought to be renewed was granted, for the Period of Three Years, with a discretionary Power to continue or discontinue it thereafter as they shall think proper and expedient, and that, during the Period of such Payment, the Two Pennies on the Pint of Ale and Beer within the City of Edinburgh and its Liberties should not be levied and collected: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill for the Purpose hereinbefore mentioned, in such Manner as the House shall think just and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

Your Committee, at the Close of the last Session, stated to the House, in their Fourteenth Report, That Time had been wanting to enable them to enter upon the Examinations of many Public Departments, not reported upon by the Commissioners of Accounts, or of Inquiry, and amongst others, the Courts of minster Hall.

On the 2ift of February last, your Committee were re-appointed; and in the Course of their Proceeding, your Committee having required'Returns from the Offices of the several Courts of 'eft , respecting

the Total Amount of their Salaries and Emoluments, and the Increase and Diminution thereof since the Year 1782, divers Returns have been accordingly made to your Committee from the greater Part of such Offices, but the Cursitors of the Court of Chancery have infilled, for certain Reasons assigned by them under their Common Seal, that your Committee are not authorized to require such Return from them.

The Principal of the said.Curfltors being unable personally to attend your Committee, John Vernon, Esquire, one of the Two Assistant Cursitors, attended your Committee, and l'ubmitted to make such Return for himself personally as was required; but Thomas Hammond, Et'quire, the other Assistant Cursitor, and Wajldngton Cotes, Esquire, who also attended your Committee as one of the said Cursitors, have personally refused to make such Return so far as regards themselves.

Your Committee have also to state to the House, That George Woodroffe, Henry Earle, and Robert Ray, Esquires, the Three Prothonotaries of the Court of Common Pleas, have, for the Reasons by them assigned, personally and severally refused to make such Return as was required from them respectively.

Your Committee have subjo'uied to this "Report, Copies of the Orders of your Committee, and of the Answers made thereto by the several Parties above named; and also a Copy of the Minutes of their respective Examination.

And Your Committee submit the Whole of the Matters above set forth to the Considerat'on of the House, praying the Judgment and Directions of the House thereupon.

Appendix, N° 3,

In compliance with an Order of the Selcft Committee of Finance, dated the 1 cth Day of March 1798, the Corporation of Cursitors of the Court of Chancery, under their Common Seal, make the following Return:

The Office of Cursitors was incorporated, and a Seal assigned to them, by Letters Patent, in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, and confirmed by James the First, by similar Letters Patent, in the Second Year of his Reign.

The Corporation conlifts of Twenty-four Persons, appointed upon Vacancy (after having served a Clerk -ship in the Office) by the Lord Chancellor, Lord Keeper, or Lords Commissioners of the Great Seal for the Time being.

The Business of the Office consists in making ouf Writs which pass under the Great Seal,

The Receipts are uncertain (according to the Business done) like those of Counsel and Solicitor; and there are not any Salaries, Fees, or Perquisites in the Office, which attend the Receipt, Issue, or Expenditure of the Public Money.

Appendix, N° 8.

Common-Pleas Office, Temple,

5th, 1798.

Sir,

The Prothonotaries of the Court of Common Pleas most respectfully inform the Honourable the Select Committee on Finance, that their Office is Freehold, that they derive no Salary or Emolument whatever from the Public Revenue, and that their Receipts, and the Management of their Office, are not in any Way connected with the Public Expenditure.

They therefore humbly prclume the Committee will be of Opinion, that the Office of the Prothonotaries of the Court of Common Pleas is not an Object of their Inquiry: And are, with great Respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servants,

Geo.

Charles Abbot, Esqr, Hen.

Chairman of the Select Com- Rob' Ray,

mittee on Finance.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

A Petition of the Planters, Merchants, and others, interested in the British West India Islands, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the same contains Clauses which, the Petitioners apprehend, will be highly injurious to their Interests, and of others for whom they arc concerned; and that the Regulations, enacted by the Laws now in Force for carrying on the aforesaid Trade, have been found fully and effectually to answer every humane and salutary Purpose proposed thereby; and the Petitioners are not apprized that any Complaints whatever have, since the passing thereof, been made, or that any Grounds for Complaint do in any Degree exist to render an Alteration of the Law in this Respect necessary; and the Petitioners are therefore persuaded, that the additional Regulations proposed have not for their Object any requisite Accommodation to the Slaves in the Middle Past'age (which the Petitioners would gladly afient to, if the existing Provisions to that Effect were shewn to be defective) but that they tend to abolish the Trade, by rendering its Expence insupportable, and thereby to deprive the Petitioners of the Means of cultivating their Estates: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the passing of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Report be taken into further Consideration; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit. v

Ordered, That the said Report be now taken into further Consideration.

The House accordingly proceeded to take the said Report into further Consideration.

And the Counsel for the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others the Merchants of London and Liverpool, concerned in the African Slave Trade; and alto the Petition of the Merchants and others concerned in the African Slave Trade from the Port of Liverpool, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being called in;

The said Report was again read,

And the said Petitions were also read.

And the said Counsel was in Part heard.

And then he was directed to withdraw.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Petition from Council, «~if the City of Glasgozv, of the Dean of Guild, a TaxTpon' and his Council of the Merchants' House; of the Dea- Property, con. Convener, and Members, of the Trades House; and of the Chairmen and Directors of the Chamber of Commerce and Manufactures; all of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have seen, with Pleasure, the Spirit of all Ranks of People in thele Kingdoms rising in Defence of the Country against the Designs of an inveterate Enemy, who has threatened its invasion, and the Destruction of its Religion, its Liberty, and Law's; and that this Spirit, manifested by the numerous Armed Associations now forming in all Parts of the Kingdom, and by the Voluntary Contributions of Individuals in Aid to Government, while it fumifhes the surest Proof of Attachment to our happy Constitution, affords the belt grounded Hope of frustrating the boasted Threats of an insolent Foe, and of restoring to this Country the Blessings of Peace; and that, as, during the Continuation of this Contest,- a great and extraordinary Expence mu ft be incurred, to which, the Petitioners are apprehensive, neither the existing Taxes nor the Voluntary Contributions will be adequate, they are of Opinion that, in the present State of the Public Funds, it would be desirable that as great a Part of the Supplies as possible should be raised within the Year, without a Loan, and that a small Tax upon every Kind of Property or Stock would be the best Measure that could be resorted to, in order to make the Burthen fall equally upon all Descriptions of People; and that, though Inconveniences and even Difficulties to Individuals may occur . in the Execution of this Plan, yet, when the Petitioners copfider that the very Existence of the Country, and of all that is held valuable in Society, depends on the Issue of this Contest, they trust that the same Spirit, which has hitherto supported the British Name, and raised these Kingdoms so high in the Scale of the Nations of Europe, will still manifest itself in surmounting these Hardships, and will prove effectual, under the Blessing of God, for maintaining and defending them from all the Effects of the Preparations now making against them: And therefore praying, That the House would take this Matter into its Consideration, and adopt such Measures as to its Wisdom may seem most expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon thq Table, ' ,

Petition for Leave to present a Petition relative to the Town and Port of Liverpool.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses', of the Town and Port of Liverpool, in their General Corporate Capacity, and the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Common Council, of the said Town and Port, as Trustees of the Docks, and also of the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Parishioners-of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, from the critical Situation of the Nation at large, under the Apprehension of

S)anger from an inveterate Enemy, who threatens.

aily to invade our Coasts, and the particular-Mischief and Injury to which the Town and Port of „

its Docks, and Shipping, will be exposed if they should become the Objects of Attack, the Petitioners are induced to solicit the Countenance of the Legislature to authorize them to raise such a Sum of Money, by a Rate upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, as to one Moiety, and a Voluntary Contribution from the Corporate Fund, and the distinct Fund of the Trustees of the Docks, as to the other Moiety, as may be deemed sufficient to enable the Petitioners to provide suitable and adequate Floating Batteries and other Works, with Gun Boats, to be stationed at the Mouth of the Harbour, and upon the Coast, in Addition to the Military Force upon Land, under such Regulations as the House shall deem proper, in order to refill and repel any Attack that may be made upon the Town and Port of verpool;but, owing to the Time allowed for the Presentation of private Petitions having elapsed, the Petitioners are advised that they cannot, in common and regular Course, be now permitted to present the proper and necessary Petition for that Purpose: And therefore praying. Mr. cleg- Mr. Taitreported from the Committee, to whom t lon, report- e Petition of David Brewer, in Edinburgh,

«d, and refer- for himself and the other Brewers of the City of mfttee of the' Edinburgh, and its Environs, was referred; That the

House. Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, George Brown, Esquire, One of the Commissioners of Excise in Scotland, being examined, said, That the Duty of Two Pennies Scots on Ale and Beer brewed, brought into, tapped, and fold, within the said City, and Liberties thereof, has, in his Opinion, been detrimental to the Public Revenue; that the Board of Excise have repeatedly wrote to the Lords of the Treasury their hill Opinion on the Subject, in which they stated the Benefits that would be derived to the Revenue, from abolishing, or not continuing, the said Duty, in the City of Edinburgh: That it is his Opinion, that the Advantage to be derived to the Revenue by the Abolition of the Duty, would be more than sufficient to enable the Lords of the Treasury to apply an Annual Sum of Money, out of the Revenue of Excise in Scotland, for answering and defraying the Purposes for which the said Duty was originally granted and continued, and that, without any Lois or Expence to the Public Revenue.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

- Petition from A Petition of John Anderson and Alexander Anderson,

Phi/potLane, London, Merchants, Proprietors of 1(land again it Buna Island, in the River Sierra Leon, on the Westwafd'

limit ''he° Coafb of Africa, was presented to the House, and trading for read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, made in the

Slaves. Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty,

for the Application of a Sum of Money therein mentioned, granted to His Majesty for making Compenfa-

tion and Satisfaction to the Royal African Company of England, it is, amongst other Things, enacted, " that whereas it appears that a certain lfiand, situate on the River Sierra Leon, on the said Coast of Africa, called Bance Island, with a Fort and Buildings thereon, having been formerly in the Possession of the said Royal,

Company, was, in the Year 1728, deserted by the said Company 4nd their Agents, and the said Fort for some Time past has been in the Possession of Alexander.

Grant, John Sargent, and Richard of London,

Merchants, who have disbursed a considerable Sum in the Preservation and Improvement of the said Island and Fort, and for which it is just and reasonable they should have a Recompence, and that the said Alexander Grant, John Sargent, and Richard Oswald, should be at Liberty to continue in the quiet Possession of the said Island, Fort, and Buildings thereon, and that the same should from thenceforth continue and be absolutely vested in them, their Heirs, and Assigns;" and that, upon the Faith of the Right granted, and the Protection afforded them by the said Act, they established large Factories upon the said Island and in the Neighbourhood, and inverted a very great Capital therein; and that the Petitioners afterwards purchased the Right and Interest of the Persons entitled to the said Island, with the Slaves and other Property thereon and are now the foie Proprietors thereof; and that the Petitioners now have a very large Capital inverted in the Settlement and Factory, which the Petitioners have employed in the African Slave Trade, upon the Faith of the Right vested in them by the said Act, and they apprehend that, by the Bill now depending in Parliament, it is intended to prohibit the trading for Slaves on that Part of the Coast of Africa which includes the Whole of Bance Island; and that, by such Prohibition, the said Factory will become useless to the Petitioners, and the Capital employed, and now veiled therein, will be wholly loft; and that, in the Year 1794, by an Invasion of American and French fub-jedls, the Property of the Petitioners on the said Island alone, to the Amount of £.20,000 Sterling, and upwards, was destroyed, and the Petitioners have since replaced and laid out the Amount of such Property so destroyed, and have, at great Riskand Labour, and at an immense Expence, established a; great Trade at the said Island, and that they did fq upon the Assurance and Belief that by the said Act the Property of the said Island, and the Right of carrying on their Trade there, was as perfectly veiled in, and secured to them, as any other Species of, Property which the Sub-je<5ls of this Realm polfefs under the Protection and Sanction of the Law: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the fame.

Ordered, That the said Petition tie referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit the grading for Slaves on the Coast of Africa, within certain Limits, is., committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty'si Commission, for declaring His Royal Afient to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was wad, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent Vol. 53.

to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also. empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the' Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor of Great , the Lord

Chamberlain of His Majesty's Household, and the Earl Spencer, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth;

An Act for granting to His Majesty the Sum of Two Hundred Thousand Pounds, to be issued and paid to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, to be by them placed to the Account of the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt:

An Act to alter and amend so much of an Act, passed in this present Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land " Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of " the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninetyeight," as relates to the Qualification of Commissioners:

rough of A la/mejbtny, in the County of Wilts, on Behalf of them (elves and others. Capital Burgesses of the said Borough, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth. That a Select Committee of this House, appointed to tiy and determine the Merits of a certain Petition presented by Fafar,

Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough of M did, on the 10th Day of May 1797, report to the House, that, it having appeared to the said Committee that the Merits of the said Petition did wholly depend upon the Right of Election in the said Borough, the Counsel for the l'everal Parties had been required by the said Committee to deliver to the Clerk of the said Committee Statements, in Writing, of the Right of Election for which they respectively contended, and such Statements having been accordingly delivered in, as well#on the Part of the Petitioner as of the Sitting Member, the said Committee had determined, that the Right of Election, as set forth in the Statement delivered in on the Part of the Sitting Member, is' the Right of Election for the said Borough, and is as follows; that is to say, " That the Right of Election of Burgesses " to serve in Parliament for the Borough of " bury, in the County of Wis in the Alderman " and Twelve Capital Burgesses of the said Borough only and that a Petition has lately been presented to the House, by certain Persons (tiling themselves Burgesses of the said Borough of Rating,

that they had been advised, that the Right of Election, so determined by the said Committee, and reported as aforesaid on the 10th Day of 1797, is not the Right of Election for the said Borough; and praying, that they may be admitted as Parties to of-pose the Right of Election so determined and reported as aforesaid; and that the Petitioners, on the contrary, being advised that the aforesaid Right of Election, so determined and reported, is the true Right of Election for the said Borough, and that the same ought to be established, pray to be admitted by the House as Parties to defend the fame, in case it shall be deemed expedient to refer the said Petition to a Select Committee: But the Petitioners are advised further to Rate to the House, that it also appears by the Journals of the House, that, on the 7th Day of November 1796, a former Special Committee of the House, appointed to try and determine the Merits of several Petitions presented by James John Faffar, Esquire, and also by certain Persons Riling themselves the AfliRant Burgesses, Burgesses, Landholders, and other the Burgesses of the Borough of Malmesbury, in the County of complaining of an

undue Election and Return for the said Borough, reported to the House, that, it having appeared to the said Committee that the Merits of the said Petitions did in Part depend on the Right of Election, and the said Committee having thereupon required the Counsel for the several Parties to deliver to the Clerk of the said Committee Statements, in Writing, of the Right of Election for which they respectively contended, and such Statements having been delivered in accordingly, as well on the Part of the Petitioners as of the Sitting Members, the said Committee had determined that the Right, as set forth in the Statement delivered in on the Part of the Sitting Members, is the Right of Election for the said Borough of Malmesbury, and appears in the same Report to be as follows (that is to say) " that the " Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament " for the Borough of Malmesbury, in the County of " Wilts, is in the Alderman and Twelve Capital Burgesses onlyand that, from the Date of the said last mentioned Report, so made to the House on the 7th Day of November 1796, until after the Expiration of Twelve Calendar Months, no Petition appears to have been presented by any Person or Persons whatsoever to the House, praying to be admitted as Parties to oppose

the Right of Election so determined and reported as aforesaid, nor does any such Petition appear to have been hitherto presented; wherefore the Petitioners are advised that, by virtue of the Statute in that same lately made and provided, the Judgment of the said Committee, as to the Right of Election for the said Borough of Malmesbury, io reported, as aforesaid, on the 7th Day of November 1796, is now, and long before the Time of presenting the Petition above-mentioned, whereby the Petitioners pray to be admitted as Parties to oppose the Right of Election, so as aforesaid reported to the House on the 10th Day of May 1797, had become final'and conclusive to all Intents and Purposes whatsoever, and that the same cannot now, by Law, be in any Manner again called in question: And therefore praying, That the House will give such Relief in the Premises as to their Wisdom shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Monday, the 11 th Day of June next, at the same Time that the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Burgesses of the Borough of Malmesbury, in the County of Wilts, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, upon the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of the Body of Bakers resident at the Towns of Portsea, Porlfmontk, and Places adjoining, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners feel themselves much injured and oppressed by the Ma-giftates not setting the Price of Bread agreeable to the Table of the 31st Geo. II. availing themselves under the Third Clause of the said Act, and making them (the Bakers) an Allowance of Profit by much too insufficient (on an Average only Seven Shillings and Six Pence per Sack of Flour) to enable them to live by their Trade, and thereby support themselves and Families; and that thfe Petitioners have been the more sensible of such Opprefiion of late Years, incon-sequence of Servants Wages, and every Article of Life, exclusive of the late heavy additional Duty on Salt, being so much advanced: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and to afford them such Relief in the Premises as the Necessity of their same may be thought to require, by either amending or explaining the Act of the 31st Geo. II. and making the Table for the Assize of Bread therein contained the Standard for regulating the Prices, or to cause an additional Assize Table to be added, regulating the Price of Bread agreeable to the Price of Flour, in the same Manner as has lately been done for the City of London, thereby making such Allowance to the Trade of the Petitioners as may be thought just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Edward Blackjlock being examined, said. That from the critical Situation of the Nation at large, under the Apprehension of Danger from an inveterate Enemy, who threatens daily to invade our Coasts, and the particular Mischief and Injury to which the Town and Port of Liverpool, its Docks and Shipping, will be exposed, if they should become the Objects of Attack, it is necessary to rail'e such a Sum of Money, by a Rate upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, as to one Moiety, and a Voluntary Contribution from the Corporate Fund, and the distinct Fund of the Trustees of the Docks, as to the other Moiety, as may be deemed sufficient to enable them to provide suitable and adequate Floating Batteries, and other Works, with Gun Boats, to be stationed at the Mouth of the Harbour and upon, the Coast, in addition to the Military Force upon Land, under such Regulations as may be deemed proper, in order to refill and repel any Attack that may be made upon the Town and Port of Liverpool.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Craves:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to revive and continue, until the First Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-nine, an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, Chapter Forty-two, videlicet, on the Thirteenth Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-four, intituled, "An Act to prohibit the Importation of light Silver Coin of this Realm

A. 1798,

" from Foreign Countries into Great Britain or Ireland,

" and to restrain the Tender thereof beyond a certain " Sum," and to suspend the coining of Silver; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for indemnifying Governors, Lieutenant Governors, and Persons acting as such, in the India Islands, who have permitted the Importation and Exportation of Goods and Commodities ill Foreign Bottoms; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing, for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and altering the Powers, of Two several Acts, the one passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the other in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending, and keeping in Repair, the Roads leading from a Place called Friar Bacon's Study to Chilton Pond, and from the Top of Hinksey Hill to Foxcomb Hill Gate, in the Road leading to Farringdon, in the County of Berks, so far as the same relate to The Oxford District of the said Roads therein mentioned; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for more effectually repairing, widening, and improving, the Road from Tetbury, in the County of Gloucester, to and through Malmesbury, to the Churchway in Lower Stanton Field, in the County of Wilts, there to join the Turnpike Road leading from Chippenham Bridge to Lower Stanton aforesaid, and from Malmesbury to the Turnpike Road at or near Bottom,

in the said County of Gloucester, and also the Road from Farringdon to Cricklade, from thence to bury, and to the Turnpike Road at A El on and

also from Sherstone to the Turnpike Road leading from Tetbury to Bath, and for making, maintaining, widening, and improving, several other Roads communicating the rewith; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for paving the Footways, and for clean ling, lighting, and regulating, the Streets, and other public Passages and Places, within the Borough of Malmesbury, in the County of Wilts, and the Avenues leading into the lame, and for removing and preventing Nuisances, Annnoyances, and Obstructions therein; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting.inclosing, draining, and laying in Severalty, the Common and Open Fields, Common Meadows, Commonable Land, Commons, Heaths, and Waste Grounds, within the Parish of Bul-

beck, in the County of Cambridg; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for preventing the depasturing of Forests, Commons, and Open Fields, with Sheep or Lambs infefted with the Scab or Mange, in that Part of Great Britain called England; with some Amendments; to which

Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Petition from A Petition of the Freeholders, Justices of the Peace, so'/'a T«re' Commissioners of Supply, and other Proprietors of the upon Proper- County of Stirling, was presented to the House, and y- read; Setting forth, That, at a Period when our

Country is threatened with Invasion by. an inveterate Enemy, it is with peculiar Satisfaction the Petitioners have observed the many generous Efforts, in every Corner of the Kingdom, to strengthen the Hands of Government by Voluntary Contribution, but, as these must necessarily be very uncertain in their Extent, and liable to many Disadvantages from which a regular Tax imposed by the Legislature is'free, the Petitioners 4re

decidedly of Opinion, that a more efficient Measurt should be adopted at the present Juncture, in order to raise in future, as far as practicable, the necessary Supplies within the Year without any Loan — Such Exertion would convince our Enemies of the Disposition, Wealth, and Resources, of Great Britain, and how unfounded is their vain Boast of conquering her by the Increase of Public Debt; and that, owing to the Uncertainty of Income in' a Commercial and Manufacturing Country, a direct Tax upon every Kind of Property or Stock,

Real and Personal, appears to the Petitioners the only Measure which can be resorted to for accomplishing with Effect and Equality so desirable an Object-; and the Petitioners hesitate not to say, that a very small Rate thereon (which, considered merely as a Premium of Insurance for securing the Remainder, could not be deemed grievous or opprdfive) would raise the requi-. site Sum with more Ease to Individuals, Corporations, and other Societies, possessed of Property, than any other Mode which can be devised; and that the Petitioners are aware that many Objections and Difficulties may occur, and some Inconveniences be felt in carrying into Effect a Plan of this Nature; but this is no Time for such secondary Considerations to have much Weight, the Petitioners must feel such Inconveniences in common with their Fellow Subjects, and they are prepared to meet them, and even much greater, with.that Firmness and Fortitude so essential to a high spirited, a great, and a brave Nation, when its Independence, and every.

Thing valuable in Life, is at Stake: And that the Petitioners do therefore earnestly petition the House to take their Request into serious Consideration, and that a Bill may be brought into Parliament to impose a direct Tax, equal to the new Exigencies of the Country, upon Real and Personal Estates, of whatever Kind, within Great Britain, and to continue the fame-in Force, if necessary, during the Existence of the present War with France, and to come in lieu of the new Alfefled Taxes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to submit our Opinion to His Majesty,. that the.deplorable State of Ireland calls for an immediate and total Change of Counsels and Measures in that Kingdom That, if the System of Coercion, enforced in the Manner it has been, should-succeed to the full Ex-lent of the most sanguine Expectations of those who have advised it, the Conquest of a Desert is all that can be obtained by it; and that Ireland, so reduced and so desolated, can no Way be preservd but by a continued Waite of the Wealth and Strength of Great Britain, for which no other Return from that Country can be rationally expected, but implacable Hatred waiting for Revenge: — That, if these Measures fail, the Poffibi-lity of which no wife Government would leave out of its Calculation, Ireland will not merely be loft, but may become an Accession to the Power of France, and England be exposed to the I flue of a Contest, on English Ground, not for Acquisition or Dominion, but probably for Existence: — We should fail in the Duty we have undertaken, if we did not, at the same Time, express to Your Majesty our absolute Conviction, that no Change of System in Ireland would be effectual to its Purpol'c, without a Removal of those Persons, whose Counsels have produced the present Calamities, and who cannot in Reason be considered as capable of correcting their own Errors, or of attempting it with Sincerity; and whose past Conduct, both in Practice and Profession, renders it impossible for them, even were they to act on a sincere Conviction of past Error, to jaife an Expectation in Ireland of such a Government on temperate Principles as might dispose the People to submit to the regular and indispensable Restraints of Justice administered according to Law, or even to accept of Concessions without Distrust, or of Benefits with Gratitude: Nothing, in our Opinion, but a total Change of Men, as well as Measures, can prevent the otherwise certain Alienation, and, more than possible, Separation, of that Country from Great Britain;

It paired in the Negative.

MR. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That K>ng'» Melt he had a Message from His Majesty to this [ thefloffert House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the of'Militia Refame to the House; and it was read by Mr. Sjreaker S'lreJjuS (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R. '

His Majesty thinks proper to acquaint the House of Commons, that the Officers, Non-commissioned Officers, and Privates, of different Regiments of the Militia of this Kingdom, have made to His Majesty a voluntary Tender of their Services, to be employed in Aid of the Regular and Militia Forces in Ireland, for the Suppression of the Rebellion now unhappily existing in that Country. ' N

His Majesty has received with the utmost Sensibility this striking and seasonable Proof of ardent Zeal and Attachment towards His Person and Government, and of affectionate Concern for the Interests and Safety of His Majesty's faithful and loyal Subjects in; and,

conceiving that His being enabled to avail Himself of this new and distinguished Instance of Public Spirit, may eventually be of the utmost Importance for the Protection of the Lives and Properties of His Subjects, for the speedy and effectual Suppression of the Rebellion, for the Defence of Great Britain itself,. and for the general Interests and Security of the Empire, He. recommends it to His faithful Commons to ✓ consider of such Provisions as may be necessary for empowering His Majesty, for a Time and to an Extent to be limited, to accept the Services of such Parts of His Militia Forces in this Kingdom as may voluntarily offer themselves to be employed in Ireland at this important Conjuncture. G R

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

20th Day previous to the 16th Day of May 1777, from the Operation of an Act, passed in the Seventeenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for registering the Grants of Life Annuities, " and for the better Protection of Infants against such " Grants;" and Setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the Year 1776, granted an Annuity of £.400 a Year for his own Life to John Peter Blacquire, Esquire, for the Price of £. 2,400, for securing which the Petitioner executed a Bond and Warrant of Attorney for con-feffing Judgment thereon, and also demised certain his Estates to Trustees for Ninety-nine Years; and that, in the Course of the Year 1779, the Possession of all the said Estates was recovered from the Petitioner in certain Actions of Trespass and Ejectment, in Consequence of which he has been deprived of the Pofiession and Receipt of the Rents and Profits of the said Premifies ever since, during which Time the Money advanced to the Petitioner, and Interest, has been very greatly overpaid; and that the Petitioner, being advised the said Annuity was defective for Want of a due Compliance with the said Act of the Seventeenth of His present Majesty, in or about the Month of 1796, and since that Time, instituted several Proceedings at Law and in Equity , to set aside the fame, which are still depending, and in the Prosecution of which the Petitioner has incurred an Expence of near 300, but is advised, and believes, he shall ultimately succeed therein, and expected fd to have done, had not the same been delayed by the said Annuitant, but which Relief he shall be deprived of, if the said Bill pafles into a Law: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law in its present Form, and that he may be heard, by himself. Agents, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect his Interest, and may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be then heard, by himself. Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon his Petition, if he thinks' fit.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve-itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Two Months, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to prohibit the trading for Slaves on the Coast of Africa, within certain Limits.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the Merchants and Ship Owners of the Town and Port of Liver pool, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Bill is now depending in the House for raising a sufficient Sum of Money for providing suitable and adequate Floating Batteries, and other Works, with Gun Boats, for the better Defence of the Town and Port of Liverpool, by a Rate on the Parish of Liverpool, as to one Moiety, and by a Voluntary Contribution from the Corporate Fund of the said Town, and the Diffintt Fund of the Docks of the said Port, as to the other Moiety; and that the Clause in the said Bill, for raising the said Parish Rate, enadls that the , same Rate shall be made upon l'uch Inhabitants and Property as are by Law rateable for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish; and that the Petitioners, being Inhabitants of the said Parish, have always paid the Assessment laid on their Stock in Trade for the Relief of the Poor of such Parish, but of late a new and diRinift Assessment, in reipett of such Poors Rate, has been laid upon the Ships and Vessels of the Petitioners, as well as upon, and diAindlly from, their Stock in Trade; and that this Act'dfment on Ships or Vessels being of a new and extraordinary Nature, and such as never, since the first Act for Relief of the Poor passed irt the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, was heard of, or attempted, until the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty; and being also an Assessment on a Property of the most precarious and uncertain Nature which can be conceived, namely, on a Property almost perpetually floating at Sea, and liable to innumerable Losses and Accidents; and having also the Effect of laying a double Tax on the Petitioners, by taxing the Freight of such Ships, which forms Part of the aggregate Value of the Stock of the Petitioners already taxed; and that the Petitioners for these Reasons, and independently of another Question now existing between the Petitioners and the said Parish, Whether or not any Part of the said Docks (which Docks are the Place where the Petitioners Ships and Vessels are Rationed) lies within the Parish of Liverpool ? have refiRed the Payment of such Poors Rate on their Shipping, and are now legally con-teRing the Validity of the fame; and that the Petitioners are desirous to contribute, for furthering- the Purposes of the said Bill, the Sum of j£.i,obo, to be laid, assessed, and levied on them, in respect of their Ships and Vessels, by a Tonnage Duty on such Ships and Vessels respectivelyAnd therefore praying, That, as the above very important Question, Whether the Petitioners are or are not liable to be rated to the Relief of the Poor of the Parish of Liverpool, in respect of their Shipping ? is now ferioully conteRed by them in a legal Way, some Clause or Provision may be contained in the said intended Act (which is merely a temporary one) that nothing therein contained shall be conRrued to extend to charge the Petitioners with the Payment of any Rate, as a Parish Rate, in respect of their said Ships or Vessels; and they further pray, that a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, charging the Petitioners with the Sum of £.1,000 for the Purposes of the said Bill, to be laid, assessed, and levied, on them, in respect of their Ships and Vessels, by a Tonnage- Duty on such Ships and Vessels respectively.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to enable the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, in their General Corporate Capacity, and the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Common Council, of the said

Vol. 53.

Town, as TruRees of the Docks there, and the Church wardens and Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of Liverpool, to raise Money for the better and more effectual Defence and Security of the Town and Port of Liverpool again A the Invasion of the Enemy, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Inflruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

Mr. Secretary Dundas reported to the House, That their Address of Tuesday last (to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House for His most Gracious Message: To assure His Majesty, that, while we deeply regret that the Machinations of wicked Men should have induced any of His Majesty's Subjects to commit Acts of Rebellion against His Majesty's Government, we at the same Time feel the highest Satisfaction that this Occasion has afforded a fresh Proof of the Zeal and Ardour for the Service of their Country which has ever distinguished the Militia Forces of this Kingdom: That, conceiving it may be of the utmost Importance, for the Protection of His Majesty's loyal Subjects in for the speedy and effectual Suppression of the present Rebellion, and for the general Defence of the Empire, that His Majesty should avail Himself of the voluntary Offers of Service which have been made by several Regiments of Militia, we will immediately enter into the Consideration of such Provisions as may be necessary for enabling His Majesty, for a Time and to an Extent to be limited, to accept of the Services of such Militia Regiments as may wish to be employed at this important Conjuncture) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty was pleased to receive the same very eraciously.

After which. His Majesty was pleased to make a Hi most Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses Spe#c of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen.

By the Measures adopted during the present Session, you have amply fulfilled the solemn and unanimous Assurances which I received from yon at its Commencement.

The Example of your Firmnels and Constancy Inis been applauded and followed by My Subjects in every Rank and Condition of Life. A Spirit of voluntary and ardent Exertion, diffused through every Part of the Kingdom, has strengthened and confirmed Our internal Security,; the same Sentiments have continued to animate My Troops of every Description; and My Fleets have met the Menaces of Invasion, by blocking Op Our Enemies in all their principal Ports.

-'Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The extensive and equitable Scheme of Contribution, by which so large a Proportion of Our Expences will be defrayed . within the Year, has defeated the Expectations of those who had vainly hoped to exhaust Our Means, and to destroy Our Public Credit. You. have been enabled to avail yourselves of further Resources from a Commerce increased in Extent and Vigour, notwithstanding the Difficulties of War, and have had the Angular Satisfaction of deriving, at the same Moment, large additional Aid from individual Exertions of unexampled Zeal, Liberality, and Patriotism.

The Provision which has been made for the Redemption of the Land Tax has also established a System which, in its progressive Operation, may produce the happiest Consequences, by the Increase of Our Resources, the Diminution of Our Debt, and the Support of Public Credit.

My Lords, and Gentlemen;

The Designs of the Disaffected, Caitied oh in Concept with our inveterate Enemies, have been bnremittingly pursued, but have been happily and effectually counter- / acted in this Kingdom by the general Zeal and Loyalty of My Subjects.

In Ireland they have broken out into the most criminal Acts of open Rebellion. Every Effort has been employed on My Part to subdue this dangerous Spirit, which is equally hostile to the Interests and Safety of every Part of the British Empire. I cannot too strongly' commend the unlhaken Fidelity and Valour of My Regular, Fencible, and Militia Troops in Ireland, and that determined Spirit with which My Yeomanry and Volunteer Forces of that Kingdom have flood forward in Defence of the Lives and Properties of their Fellow Subjects, and in Support of the lawful Government.

The striking and honourable Proof of Alacrity and Public Spirit, which so many of My Fencible and Militia Regiments in this Kingdom have manifested on this Occasion, has already received the fullest Testimony of the Approbation of Parliament.

This Conduct, personally so honourable to the Individuals, affords the strongest Pledge both of the Military Ardor which -actuates this valuable Part of Our National Defence, and of their affectionate Concern for the Safety and Happiness of Ireland, which arc elsentially connected with the general Interests of the British Empire.

With the Advantage of this Support, and after the distinguished and important Success which has recently attended the Operations of My Arms against the principal Force of the Rebels, I trull the Time is salt approaching, when those now seduced from their Allegiance will be brought to a just Senl'e of the Guilt they have incurred, and will entitle themselves to Forgive-ness, and to that Protection which it is My conllant Wilh to afford to every Class and Condition of My

Subjects

38,39 Geo. III. ao° Junii.S0AuguJH.-'i'1709

Subje&s who manifed their Desire to pay a due Obedience, to the Laws.

This temporary Interruption of Tranquillity, and all its attendant Calamities, mud be attributed to those pernicious Principles which have been industriously propagated in that Country, and which, wherever they have prevailed, have never failed to produce the most difaflrous Effects.

With such Warnings before Us, sensible of the Danger which We are called upon to repel, and of the Blelfings We have to preserve, let Us continue firmly united in a determined Resistance to the Designs of Our Enemies, and in the Defence of that Constitution which has been found, by Experience, to enfpre to Us, in so eminent a Degree, Public Liberty, National Strength, and the Security and Comfort of all Classes of the Community.

It is' only by Perseverance in this Line of Conduct that We can hope, under the Continuance of that Divine Protection which We have so abundantly experienced, to conduct this arduous Contest to a happy Issue; and to maintain, undiminished, the Security, Honour, and lading Prosperity, of the Country.
